Start Here

CCAR-F: 60 scenario items (multiple-choice and "select N"), 120 minutes, 4 scenarios drawn from 6, pass at 720 on a 100–1,000 scale. In this reader you attempt an item first, rate your confidence, fix what you got wrong, and read only after that.

What to do, in order

The sidebar is in the same order, and so is Next at the bottom of each page.

  1. Take the Pretest in Drill before you study anything (20 min). It is the first tab. Answer all 12 official samples and rate each answer H, M or L.
  2. Read the Exam Overview, especially the out-of-scope list, because out-of-scope options are free eliminations (30 min). Then read §6 of the official PDF once, straight through.
  3. Open the 3-Day Plan and follow the day you are on. Steps 4 to 6 are what it schedules.
  4. Work through the domains from D1 to D5. For each one, run Drill → Domain focus, read the domain page or book chapter only for what you missed, then fill that domain's rows in Trap Pairs. Run Relearn that evening and again the next morning.
  5. From the evening of Day 2, run Mixed set across the domains you have covered and use the Dashboard to pick what to fix. On the last day, sit a Timed mock or two Half mocks.
  6. The evening before the exam, read the Quick Reference once and go through Exam Day. Don't start new material in the last 12–24 hours.

With only one day, follow If you only have one day instead. If you are short on time, do only the ★ blocks in the plan.

The method in five rules

# Rule Why Evidence
1 Answer before you read. Attempt every item and topic before studying it, then check the key. Retrieval beats rereading, and it transfers to application questions. Yang et al. 2021, g = 0.50, 222 studies; Pan & Rickard 2018, d = 0.40
2 Rate confidence (H/M/L) before the reveal. Your sense of knowing an answer is unreliable. Recording it lets you check it against results. Bjork et al. 2013; Butterfield & Metcalfe 2001
3 Fix confident errors first. A high-confidence miss means you hold a false belief. Those errors are quick to correct and expensive to leave. Hypercorrection effect (Butterfield & Metcalfe 2001)
4 Space and interleave. Revisit each domain about a day later. Mix domains once each is familiar. A gap of about a day beats massed study, and mixing practises telling similar questions apart. Cepeda et al. 2006/2008; Mawson & Kang 2025, d = 0.54; Brunmair & Richter 2019, g = 0.42
5 Sleep 7–8 h, every night. Lost sleep costs more than the extra study time gains. Newbury et al. 2021

The daily-user trap

Using Claude Code every day makes the material feel familiar, and familiarity makes it easy to overrate how ready you are.

  • The exam tests what sits underneath the product: the agent loop, the Batch API, structured-output validation, MCP error semantics.
  • The exam also asks for tradeoffs: it gives you several workable fixes and asks which is the best first one.
  • Pick what to study from the Dashboard priority (weight × average danger), not from how ready you feel.
  • Practice feels harder than rereading, but that doesn't mean it works worse (Deslauriers et al. 2019).
  • Walkthroughs of things you already know are wasted time (expertise reversal).

Don't bother

  • Rereading and highlighting have low utility (Dunlosky et al. 2013).
  • Learning styles have no supporting evidence.
  • Expressive writing before the exam has no effect on test anxiety (O'Meara & Lovett 2026).
  • Pomodoro as a learning technique has no controlled advantage.
  • A new Anki/FSRS deck this week is not worth it, because its benefit shows over long horizons.
  • The "AI rots your brain" EEG preprint (Kosmyna et al.) is small and not peer reviewed. The better-supported finding is narrower: unrestricted AI access harmed later unaided performance, a hint-only tutor did not (Bastani et al. 2025). Attempt first, then ask.

Drill

Answer first, then rate how sure you are, then read the rationale for every option, not only the key. Your confidence counts as much as the answer, and a confident miss gets the highest danger score. Misses come back in Relearn, and a topic only counts as secure after two confident, correct answers at least 8 hours apart. Progress is stored in this browser only; use Export JSON on the Dashboard to move it between laptop and phone.

Exam Overview — Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (CCAR-F)

This page comes from the official Exam Guide v1.0, effective July 2026 ("the exam guide" below), except logistics taken from the live Partner Academy FAQ, tagged (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21). Anything else that comes from elsewhere, or is interpretation, is marked (not in the exam guide).

Key facts
Credential Claude Certified Architect – Foundations
Exam code CCAR-F (community shorthand CCA-F; not in the exam guide)
Items 60
Item format Multiple-choice and multiple-response. Each item states how many responses to select
Structure 4 scenarios drawn from a bank of 6
Time 120 minutes of testing; ~135 minutes total seat time including check-in, instructions and survey (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)
Delivery Proctored (online proctored and/or Pearson VUE test center)
Languages English, Japanese (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)
Passing score 720 on a scaled range of 100–1,000
Fee $125 USD per attempt, up from $99 on 2026-06-30; partner-tier discounts apply at checkout (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)
Validity 12 months from award
Result reporting Pass/fail with scaled score, plus percent-correct by domain (diagnostic only; the pass decision is on total scaled score). Score shown on screen at the end (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)
Practice exam None official. The old one was retired in the move to Pearson; the only official sample questions are the 12 in the exam guide (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)

Scoring is criterion-referenced: you are measured against a fixed standard set by a formal standard-setting study, not against other candidates. 720 is a scaled score, not 72% correct, so you can't work out how many questions you can afford to miss.

Version note

v1.0 is still the current guide as of 2026-10-21. The official PDF was uploaded 2026-07-08 and there is no v1.1 or v2. Guides are subject to change, so re-check the PDF before booking.

The v0.2 draft (June 2026) and v1.0 (July 2026) have the same domains, the same 30 task statements and the same 12 sample questions. Only the surrounding material changed. The differences that affect you are:

  • v0.2 said "All questions are multiple choice… one correct response and three incorrect." v1.0 says multiple-choice and multiple-response. Expect some "select two" items, and read the instruction line on every question.
  • v1.0 adds the policy sections (retakes, ID, NDA, appeals, recertification) that v0.2 lacked. It also introduces the exam code CCAR-F and adds percent-correct by domain to the score report; v0.2 reported pass/fail only.

Blueprint

# Domain Weight ≈ items of 60
1 Agentic Architecture & Orchestration 27% ~16
2 Tool Design & MCP Integration 18% ~11
3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows 20% ~12
4 Prompt Engineering & Structured Output 20% ~12
5 Context Management & Reliability 15% ~9

Domains 1, 3 and 4 together are two-thirds of the exam.

The six scenarios (four appear on your form)

You can't choose which four you get, so study all six.

1. Customer Support Resolution Agent. A support agent built with the Claude Agent SDK handling high-ambiguity requests (returns, billing disputes, account issues) through custom MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human. Target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Primary domains: 1, 2, 5.

2. Code Generation with Claude Code. A team using Claude Code for generation, refactoring, debugging and documentation, integrating it with custom slash commands and CLAUDE.md, and deciding plan mode vs direct execution. Primary domains: 3, 5.

3. Multi-Agent Research System. A coordinator delegating to four specialized subagents (web search, document analysis, synthesis, report generation), producing comprehensive cited reports. Primary domains: 1, 2, 5.

4. Developer Productivity with Claude. An Agent SDK agent helping engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers. Primary domains: 2, 3, 1.

5. Claude Code for Continuous Integration. Claude Code in a CI/CD pipeline running automated code reviews, generating test cases and giving PR feedback, with a stated emphasis on actionable feedback and minimizing false positives. Primary domains: 3, 4.

6. Structured Data Extraction. Extracting information from unstructured documents, validating output with JSON schemas, maintaining high accuracy, handling edge cases gracefully, integrating downstream. Primary domains: 4, 5.

The scenarios are different settings for the same five domains.

Out of scope

The exam guide excludes the topics below. None of them is tested, even though Anthropic's docs and community study guides cover them:

Fine-tuning or training custom models · Claude API authentication, billing, or account management · language- and framework-specific implementation detail beyond what tool and schema configuration needs · deploying or hosting MCP servers (infrastructure, networking, containers) · Claude's internal architecture, training, or weights · Constitutional AI, RLHF, safety training · embedding models and vector database internals · computer use (browser/desktop automation) · vision and image analysis · streaming API implementation and server-sent events · rate limiting, quotas, pricing calculations · prompt caching implementation details beyond knowing it exists · token counting algorithms and tokenization · OAuth, API key rotation, authentication protocols · specific cloud provider configuration (AWS, GCP, Azure) · performance benchmarking and model comparison metrics.

Community prep material often drills prompt-cache TTLs, 429 handling, pause_turn and MCP transport specs. None of that is on this exam (inference; not in the exam guide).

In-scope topics (the exam guide's own summary)

Agentic loop implementation (control flow on stop_reason, tool result handling, termination) · multi-agent orchestration (coordinator-subagent, decomposition, parallel execution, iterative refinement) · subagent context management (explicit passing, structured state persistence, crash recovery via manifests) · tool interface design (descriptions, splitting vs consolidating, naming) · MCP tool and resource design · MCP server configuration (project vs user scope, env var expansion, multi-server access) · error handling and propagation (structured responses, transient vs business vs permission, local recovery before escalation) · escalation decision-making · CLAUDE.md configuration (hierarchy, @import, .claude/rules/ glob patterns) · custom commands and skills (scope, context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint) · plan mode vs direct execution · iterative refinement (I/O examples, test-driven iteration, interview pattern) · structured output via tool_use (schema design, tool_choice, nullable fields) · few-shot prompting · batch processing · context window optimization · human review workflows (confidence calibration, stratified sampling, accuracy segmentation) · information provenance.

Appendix: technologies named in the exam guide

The exam guide lists the specific technologies questions may refer to. Recognize each by name:

  • Claude Agent SDK: agent definitions, agentic loops, stop_reason handling, hooks (PostToolUse, tool call interception), subagent spawning via the Task tool, allowedTools configuration
  • MCP: servers, tools, resources, the isError flag, tool descriptions, tool distribution, .mcp.json, environment variable expansion
  • Claude Code: CLAUDE.md hierarchy (user/project/directory), .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter path scoping, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint), plan mode, direct execution, /memory, /compact, --resume, fork_session, the Explore subagent
  • Claude Code CLI: -p / --print, --output-format json, --json-schema
  • Claude API: tool_use with JSON schemas, tool_choice (auto, any, forced), stop_reason values (tool_use, end_turn), max_tokens, system prompts
  • Message Batches API: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour window, custom_id, polling, no multi-turn tool calling
  • JSON Schema: required vs optional, enums, nullable, "other" + detail string, strict mode
  • Pydantic: schema validation, semantic validation errors, validation-retry loops
  • Built-in tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob
  • Few-shot prompting, prompt chaining, context window management, session management, confidence scoring

Current product (not tested): this list reflects the exam guide, not the full current API and product. The domain pages mark where the product has moved on, e.g. the Task tool's current SDK name, extra stop_reason and tool_choice values, and a third MCP scope.

Intended audience

The exam guide describes the ideal candidate as a solution architect with 6+ months of hands-on experience with the Claude API, Agent SDK, Claude Code and MCP. No experience prerequisite is stated (inference), and eligibility is covered under Logistics.

Logistics and policies

Registration runs through the Anthropic Partner Academy; you then create a Pearson VUE account and schedule. The fee at checkout reflects any discount that applies to your partner tier.

Eligibility. Partner-only: you must belong to a Claude Partner Network organization, register with a company email on the partner domain (personal emails are rejected), and be 18+ with government ID. Non-partners can take Academy courses, which give a completion certificate, not the certification. (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)

Cancel or reschedule at least 48 hours before your appointment (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21). The exam guide PDF says 24 hours; the FAQ is newer, so plan on 48. Inside the window you can no longer cancel or reschedule, and the exam guide says a late change or no-show forfeits the fee.

ID. Valid, unexpired, government-issued photo ID. The name on it must match your registration exactly. Name corrections go to certifications-support@anthropic.com before scheduling.

Retakes. 14 days after a first fail, 30 days after a second, 90 days after a third. Maximum four attempts per rolling twelve months, per exam. You pay the full fee each time. (Confirmed by the Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21.)

Conduct. Stay in view of the webcam if testing online; workspace clear of notes, books, phones, secondary monitors; no communication with anyone; no capturing exam content. Prohibited: phones, smart watches, headphones, study materials, recording devices. Scratch paper only if the proctor provides it.

NDA. You accept a confidentiality agreement before the exam starts. Decline and the session ends with no refund.

Recertification. On-time renewal is a free, non-proctored assessment on the Partner Academy. Let it lapse and you retake the full exam at full price. Validity is 12 months; certifications earned before 2026-06-30 under the old 6-month rule were extended to 12. (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21)

Appeals within 14 days, via Pearson VUE support. The standard-setting outcome and individual item content are not appealable.

Accommodations must be requested and approved by Pearson VUE before you schedule, 10 or more days ahead of the exam (Partner Academy FAQ, checked 2026-10-21).

Three-Day Study Plan

Plan on 5–6 hours a day. With less, do only the ★ blocks. Modes are on the Drill page.

Standing rules:

  • Rate H/M/L before every reveal. Log every miss and every shaky answer.
  • Fixed bedtime for 7–8 h of sleep, all three nights.
  • Study a domain on its own first. Mix only after it is familiar.
  • Read a domain page or book chapter only for what Domain focus shows you missed.

Day 1: Baseline, map, Domain 1

Time Block Where Stop rule
20 min ★ Baseline. Answer all 12 official samples without studying. Drill → Pretest All 12 answered and rated. Don't peek at the explanations early.
30 min ★ Read the overview and the out-of-scope list. Out-of-scope topics are free eliminations. Exam Overview You can name the 5 domains with weights and the 6 scenarios.
30 min ★ Read §6 of the official PDF (Detailed Objectives) once, straight through. Official exam guide One pass. Don't stop to study.
2 h ★ Domain 1 (27%). Domain focus for D1, then read the page or book chapter only for the misses. Expect to be wrong on anti-patterns. Drill → Domain focus; D1 Last D1 set at 80% or more with no H-wrong answers, or the time is up.
45 min ★ Contrast drills for D1: prompt instruction vs hook, tool_choice vs gate, and the rest of the rows. Trap Pairs (D1 rows) Every D1 row filled from memory, then checked.
30 min ★ Evening: Relearn today's misses, then Recall cards for the D1 task statements (1.1–1.7). Drill → Relearn, Recall cards Every Relearn item correct once, then stop for the day.
10 min Optional: skim §8 Preparation Exercises 1 and 4 (they map to scenarios 1 and 3). Official exam guide

End of day, without looking: the five domains and weights, the six scenarios, what terminates an agent loop, why subagents start with no context, when a hook beats a prompt.

Day 2: Domains 2, 3, 4

Time Block Where Stop rule
15 min ★ First spaced pass, about a day after the first attempt: re-answer yesterday's misses and shaky items. Drill → Relearn Every item correct once.

Then run this loop for each of Domain 2, 3 and 4 (about 1.5 h each; ★):

Step Time Where Stop rule
1. Domain focus set 20 min Domain focus Set done, every answer rated.
2. Read only the weak spots 25 min Domain page or book chapter (D2, D3, D4) Only task statements you missed. Skip the rest.
3. Trap Pairs rows 20 min Trap Pairs Rows filled from memory, then checked.
4. Blank-page concept map, then explain one aloud 20 min Paper Map drawn from memory (self-generated maps: g = 0.72 vs 0.43 for studying a given map; Schroeder et al. 2018). Explain it aloud to a skeptical colleague. Stop when you find a gap, fix it, redo that branch.
5. Second Domain focus set 10 min Domain focus Ends the loop.

Domain-specific notes:

  • D2: descriptions are the primary selection mechanism and usually the correct first fix. Four error categories; only transient is retryable.
  • D3: mostly which file, which directory, which flag. Write the file map from the Quick Reference from memory.
  • D4: syntax vs semantics (a schema fixes malformed JSON, not wrong values). Batch API as one set: 50% · up to 24 h · no SLA · no multi-turn tool calling · custom_id. Batch is decided by how long the result can wait, not by cost.
Time Block Where Stop rule
40 min ★ Evening Mixed set across D1–D4 (20 items, weighted to weak spots). Drill → Mixed set All items answered, rated, explanations read.
15 min ★ Triage. Rank domains by priority = weight × average danger. Write tomorrow's repair order. Drill → Dashboard Ranked list written. Then bed on time.

Day 3: Domain 5, synthesis, then stop

Time Block Where Stop rule
30 min ★ Relearn to zero: every miss and shaky item. Drill → Relearn Each correct once, then stop.
1.5 h ★ Domain 5 (15%). Domain focus, weak spots only, Trap Pairs D5 rows. Focus: three valid escalation triggers, four-part error report, provenance checklist. Domain focus; D5 Last set at 80% or more, no H-wrong.
40 min ★ Scenario recall: free-recall each of the 6 scenarios (what it is, primary domains, three likeliest failures), self-graded. Drill → Recall cards (scenarios) All six graded. Re-read only the ones you failed.
2 h ★ Timed mock as two Half mocks (30 items / 60 min each), a few hours apart. Use the exam routine from Exam Day: instruction line, deciding phrase, rule-based elimination. Drill → Timed mock (Half mock) Hard stop at 60 min each. Log every miss and shaky item.
1.5 h ★ Weak-spot repair by Dashboard priority (weight × danger), not lowest percent. Confident-wrong items first. Dashboard, Domain focus, Trap Pairs Time boxed per domain; move on when it ends.
30 min ★ Evening: Relearn confident-wrong items only, then read the Quick Reference once. Relearn; Quick Reference No new material in the last 12–24 h. Then logistics from Exam Day and sleep.

If you have a spare 2 hours, do one full Timed mock (60 items / 120 min) before the evening instead of the two Half mocks.

If you only have one day

  1. Pretest before any study (20 min). Rate everything.
  2. Exam Overview, especially the out-of-scope list (25 min).
  3. Domain focus D1, then D3 (D1 and D3 are 47% of the blueprint), reading only the weak spots (about 2 h each with the Trap Pairs rows).
  4. Mixed set of 20 items, then Relearn to zero (1 h).
  5. Half mock (30 items / 60 min) if time allows.
  6. Quick Reference, then sleep.

Using Claude as a tutor

Attempt first, then have Claude grade you and ask you questions. Don't ask it for answers. Prompts and rules are in Study with Claude. Stop generating new items in the last 24 hours.

Domain 1 — Agentic Architecture & Orchestration (27%, ~16 items)

Most questions describe a production system that misbehaves and ask you to pick the fix. Two principles settle most of them.

  • When a mistake has real consequences (money, compliance, security), enforce the rule in code, not in the prompt. A prompt instruction is followed most of the time; code is followed every time.
  • Don't add machinery the failure doesn't need. If a small fix addresses the root cause, the bigger one is wrong.

In the book: Chapter 2 — The Agentic Loop (1.1) · Chapter 5 — Orchestration (1.2, 1.3) · Chapter 6 — Hooks & Gates (1.4, 1.5) · Chapter 1 — Agents & Workflows (1.6) · Chapter 7 — Sessions (1.7)

1.1 Design and implement agentic loops

An agentic loop is the code that sends a request to Claude, runs any tools Claude asks for, sends the results back, and repeats until Claude is done. Claude Code runs this loop every time you press enter; on the exam you are the one writing it.

The loop

1. POST /v1/messages  →  system, messages[], tools[]
2. Read response.stop_reason
3. If "tool_use":
     append the assistant message (with its tool_use blocks) to messages
     execute each requested tool
     append a USER message containing tool_result block(s)
     go to 1
4. If "end_turn": done — present the final response

The exam guide makes these points about the loop:

  • stop_reason controls the loop. "tool_use" means Claude wants a tool run, so continue. "end_turn" means Claude has finished, so stop.
  • Tool results are appended to conversation history. That history is the only place the model can see what its tools returned, so it is how the agent builds up knowledge across steps.
  • Model-driven decision-making: Claude reasons from context about which tool to call next, which is what makes the design agentic. A pre-configured decision tree or a fixed tool sequence is a different design.

The three anti-patterns

The exam guide names three wrong ways to decide the loop is finished. Expect them as distractors:

  1. Parsing natural language signals to determine loop termination: searching the response text for "done" or "I've finished."
  2. Setting arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism. A cap protects against a runaway loop. It does not tell you the task is complete.
  3. Checking for assistant text content as a completion indicator. A response with stop_reason: "tool_use" often contains text too, because Claude frequently says what it is about to do before calling a tool.

Any option that decides completion by something other than stop_reason is wrong.

Current product (not tested): the full current set is end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, tool_use, pause_turn, refusal and model_context_window_exceeded. The exam guide names only tool_use and end_turn.

1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns

Hub and spoke

In a hub-and-spoke design, one coordinator agent sits in the middle and every subagent talks only to it, so the coordinator handles all communication and routing between them.

The exam guide gives three reasons for this: observability (one place to see what happened), consistent error handling, and controlled information flow (each subagent gets exactly what the coordinator chooses to give it).

The coordinator's job:

  • break the task into pieces (decomposition)
  • hand each piece to a subagent (delegation)
  • combine the results (aggregation)
  • deciding which subagents to invoke based on query complexity, rather than running the whole pipeline every time

Subagents have isolated context. A subagent does not see the coordinator's conversation history. It knows only what the coordinator puts in its prompt. Questions in Domains 1 and 5 depend on this fact.

Failure mode: decomposition that is too narrow

The exam guide warns that a coordinator can split a broad topic too narrowly, so the subagents between them cover only part of it. Sample question 7 shows this: every subagent succeeds, yet the report on "creative industries" misses most of the topic, because the coordinator split it into three visual-arts subtasks.

When every downstream agent worked correctly but the overall coverage is wrong, the cause is the coordinator's decomposition.

Skills tested

  • The coordinator should analyze query requirements and dynamically select subagents, instead of always running the full pipeline.
  • Partition the scope so subagents don't duplicate each other, for example by giving each one distinct subtopics or distinct source types.
  • Iterative refinement loops: the coordinator reviews the synthesis for gaps, sends targeted follow-up queries to the search and analysis subagents, runs synthesis again, and repeats until coverage is sufficient.

1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning

Concept Detail
How subagents are spawned The coordinator calls the Task tool
Requirement The coordinator's allowedTools must include "Task", or it cannot spawn subagents
Context Must be explicitly provided in the prompt of the subagent. Subagents do not inherit the parent's context and do not share memory between invocations
Configuration An AgentDefinition per subagent type: its description, system prompt and allowed tools
Branching Fork-based session management lets you explore different approaches from the same starting analysis

Skills tested

  • Put the complete findings from earlier agents directly into the subagent's prompt. If the synthesis subagent needs the web search results and the document analysis, the coordinator pastes both in. A prompt that says "analyze the findings" without including them is a common wrong answer.
  • Pass context as structured data that keeps content separate from metadata (source URLs, document names, page numbers), so each claim can still be traced to its source after the handoff.
  • To run subagents in parallel, emit several Task tool calls in one coordinator response. One Task call per turn runs them one after another.
  • Give subagents goals and quality criteria, not step-by-step procedures, so they can adapt to what they find.

Quick diagnostics:

Question Answer
Why doesn't the coordinator spawn subagents? allowedTools is missing "Task"
Why is the synthesis subagent's output generic? The findings weren't in its prompt
How do I run subagents in parallel? Several Task calls in one response

Current product (not tested): the current Claude Agent SDK calls this tool Agent, and keeps Task as an alias. The exam guide says Task throughout, so answer with Task.

The SDK can also resume a specific subagent's own transcript (capture its session_id/agentId and pass resume: sessionId), instead of pasting prior findings into a fresh prompt. The exam guide's mechanism is still "provide the context explicitly in the prompt."

1.4 Multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff

Programmatic enforcement vs prompt guidance

Programmatic enforcement means a rule is checked by code; prompt guidance means the model is asked to follow it. The exam guide puts it this way: "When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate." A system prompt rule can be skipped. If skipping it costs money or breaks compliance, it needs a check in code.

A prerequisite gate is such a check. Your code refuses to execute a tool call until an earlier step has completed. The exam guide's example is to block process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID. Sample question 1 tests the same idea; its correct option gates both lookup_order and process_refund on identity verification.

Sample question 1's explanation also says why the other options fail:

  • A stronger system prompt (B) and few-shot examples (C) both "rely on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when errors have financial consequences."
  • A routing classifier (D) "addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering, which is not the actual problem."

Enforcement strength (community heuristic, not in the exam guide): tool-internal check or programmatic gate/hook > tool_choice for a single turn > prompt instruction. This applies to compliance stems (must-never rules, money, ordering guarantees); for quality or tool-routing stems the exam rewards better descriptions and prompts first (sample question 2 prefers improved tool descriptions over a routing layer).

Structured handoff to a human

When the agent escalates mid-task to a human who cannot see the conversation transcript, it should send a structured summary: customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action. A raw transcript dump makes the human redo the agent's work.

Requests with several concerns

When a customer raises several issues in one message, split them into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then combine the results into a unified resolution. Handling the first issue and asking the customer to open a second ticket is wrong.

1.5 Agent SDK hooks for interception and normalization

A hook is your code, registered with the Agent SDK, that runs automatically at a fixed point in the loop. The model cannot skip it. Claude Code's permission prompt is a similar idea: a check that runs before a tool executes, whatever the model intended.

The exam guide names two uses:

Purpose Hook Example from the exam guide
Change tool results before the model sees them PostToolUse (runs after the tool) Convert the mix of Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings and numeric status codes returned by different MCP tools into one format
Block a tool call that breaks policy Tool-call interception, implemented as PreToolUse (runs before the tool; can deny the call or rewrite its input) Block refunds over $500 and redirect to human escalation

The exam guide ties this back to 1.4: it contrasts "using hooks for deterministic guarantees versus relying on prompt instructions for probabilistic compliance." Use a hook when a business rule must always hold.

Distractors often mix up the two directions. PostToolUse sees results coming back from a tool. Interception sees calls going out. A PostToolUse hook cannot stop a refund, because by the time it runs the refund has already been processed.

The exam also tests the opposite mistake, using a hook for a soft preference such as tone.

Current product (not tested): in the SDK, a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision (allow, deny, ask or defer) inside hookSpecificOutput; matchers match tool names.

1.6 Task decomposition strategies

There are two ways to break a task into steps:

Pattern Use when Exam guide's example
Fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining): the same steps every time, each feeding the next The steps are known in advance Review each file on its own, then run a cross-file integration pass
Dynamic adaptive decomposition: the agent decides the next subtasks based on what it has found Open-ended investigation where you can't know the steps up front "Add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase"

Skills tested

  • Use prompt chaining for predictable, multi-aspect reviews. Use dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation.
  • Split a large code review into one pass per file plus a separate cross-file integration pass. The exam guide's reason is attention dilution: when one pass covers many files, the model gives each one shallower attention and can contradict itself across files. Sample question 12 (a 14-file review that comes back shallow and inconsistent) has this as its answer. Its explanation rejects two alternatives: a bigger context window "doesn't solve attention quality issues," and requiring 2 of 3 independent passes to agree "would actually suppress detection of real bugs."
  • For an open-ended task, first map the structure, then find the high-impact areas, then write a prioritized plan that changes as you discover dependencies.

1.7 Session state, resumption, and forking

Mechanism What it does When to use it
--resume <session-name> Continues a specific earlier named session, with its context The earlier context is still mostly valid
fork_session Creates an independent branch that starts from the same analysis You want to explore divergent approaches from one starting point, such as two testing strategies or two refactorings of the same codebase
Start a new session with a structured summary A fresh session seeded with the key facts The earlier tool results are stale (the files or data have changed)

The exam guide states two judgments outright:

  • "Starting a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results."
  • When you do resume after code has changed, tell the agent which files changed so it re-analyzes those, rather than re-exploring everything.

Current product (not tested): named sessions exist: claude --name/-n <name> (or /rename mid-session) names one, and claude --resume takes an ID or a name. The SDK resume option still takes a session ID. continue / continue_conversation resumes the most recent session in the working directory, with no ID. Watch for options that confuse "most recent, no ID" with "specific, by ID or name".

Domain 1 decision table

Symptom in the question Answer
Loop won't stop, or stops too early Control the loop with stop_reason
Agent skips a mandatory earlier step Prerequisite gate in code, not a prompt instruction
A policy limit is sometimes exceeded Tool-call interception hook
Tool results arrive in inconsistent formats PostToolUse normalization hook
Subagent output is generic or has no sources Put the findings and their metadata in the subagent's prompt
Coordinator can't spawn subagents Add "Task" to allowedTools
Subagents run one after another instead of in parallel Several Task calls in one coordinator response
Report misses whole subtopics, though every subagent succeeded The coordinator's decomposition is too narrow
Large multi-file review is shallow and contradicts itself One pass per file plus a separate integration pass
Need to compare two approaches from one starting analysis fork_session
Resuming after files changed Resume and say what changed; start fresh with a summary if the old results are stale
Escalating to a human who can't see the transcript Structured handoff summary

Things to remember

  • An iteration cap is a safety net, and text in a response does not mean the turn is finished.
  • Subagents inherit nothing: no conversation history, no memory between invocations.

Domain 2 — Tool Design & MCP Integration (18%, ~11 items)

The domain has five task statements. It is about how you design tool interfaces and configure MCP servers, not about the MCP protocol itself. The exam guide's out-of-scope list removes "deploying or hosting MCP servers (infrastructure, networking, container orchestration)" and "OAuth, API key rotation, or authentication protocol details", so there are no questions on transports, OAuth, protocol internals or hosting.

In the book: Chapter 3 — Designing Tools (2.1, 2.3, 2.5) · Chapter 4 — Errors & Recovery (2.2) · Chapter 8 — MCP (2.4)

2.1 Design effective tool interfaces

Descriptions drive tool selection

The model chooses which tool to call mainly by reading the tool descriptions. The exam guide says tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection, and minimal descriptions make selection between similar tools unreliable.

A good description covers:

  • what the tool does and what it returns
  • the input formats it accepts
  • example queries
  • edge cases
  • boundary explanations: when to use this tool rather than a similar one

Failure mode: misrouting

Misrouting is the model calling the wrong one of two similar tools. It happens when descriptions are vague or overlap. The exam guide's example is analyze_content and analyze_document with near-identical descriptions.

Sample question 2 has two tools, get_customer ("Retrieves customer information") and lookup_order ("Retrieves order details"). Both descriptions are minimal and both tools accept similar identifiers, so the agent confuses them. The correct answer is expand the descriptions. The explanation rejects the other options:

  • Few-shot examples "add token overhead without fixing the underlying issue."
  • A routing layer is "over-engineered and bypasses the LLM's natural language understanding."
  • Merging the two tools is "a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a first step warrants."

Keywords in the system prompt

Instructions in the system prompt that mention particular keywords can make the model associate those words with a tool, overriding good tool descriptions. If the descriptions are good and selection is still wrong, check the system prompt for such keywords.

Fixing tool selection

Fix Exam guide's example
Rename the tool and rewrite its description so it no longer overlaps with another analyze_content → extract_web_results, with a web-specific description
Split a generic tool into purpose-specific tools, each with defined inputs and outputs analyze_document → extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source
Check the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions —

Current product (not tested): tool definitions now accept "strict": true, which guarantees the tool's input matches its schema. It does not fix misrouting, because it controls whether the arguments are well-formed and has no say in which tool is chosen.> The tool search tool (tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119 / tool_search_tool_regex_20251119) keeps most tool definitions out of context and loads them when needed. It helps with very large tool sets (see 2.3), but it does not replace the exam's answer there, which is to give each agent only the tools its role needs.

2.2 Structured error responses for MCP tools

How a tool reports failure

An MCP tool reports failure by setting the isError flag on its result. The error comes back to the agent as readable content, not as an exception, so the agent can decide what to do next. Claude Code recovers from a failed Bash command the same way, because the failure output comes back as a tool result it can read.

Current product (not tested): in the Messages API, the equivalent field on a tool_result block is spelled is_error. The exam guide only uses isError.

The four error categories

Category Meaning Retry?
transient Timeouts, service unavailable Yes
validation The input was invalid No
business The request breaks a policy No
permission Access is missing or expired No

What a good error response contains

  • errorCategory: transient, validation or permission (the categories the exam guide lists in the skills bullet)
  • isRetryable: a boolean
  • a human-readable description of what went wrong
  • for a business-rule violation, retriable: false and a customer-friendly explanation, so the agent explains the policy to the customer instead of retrying

Why a generic error is wrong

A generic "Operation failed" prevents the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions. Structured error metadata prevents wasted retry attempts on errors that will never succeed.

More skills tested

  • Subagents recover locally from transient failures. They pass to the coordinator only what they cannot fix themselves, and when they do, they include partial results and what was attempted.
  • An access failure is not the same as an empty result. A timeout is a failure that needs a retry decision. A query that ran and matched nothing is a success that returned an empty set. Options that confuse the two are distractors.

2.3 Distribute tools across agents and configure tool choice

Too many tools makes selection worse

The exam guide gives a number: an agent with 18 tools instead of 4–5 picks tools less reliably, because it has more options to choose between. Agents that hold tools outside their role also tend to misuse them; the exam guide's example is a synthesis agent that starts running web searches.

The fix is scoped tool access, where each agent gets only the tools its role needs, plus limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs.

Sample question 9 is an example. The synthesis agent needs to verify facts. 85% of verifications are simple fact-checks; 15% need deeper investigation. The correct answer is a narrow verify_fact tool for the simple cases, with complex verifications still sent through the coordinator. The rejected options are giving synthesis full web search (too much access, and it mixes up the agents' responsibilities) and batching verifications (it makes synthesis wait on them).

The exam guide also names replacing a generic tool with a constrained one, for example replacing fetch_url with a load_document tool that only accepts valid document URLs.

tool_choice

tool_choice is a request parameter that controls whether and which tool the model must call.

Value Behavior Use for
"auto" The model decides, and may return text instead of calling a tool Normal open-ended agent turns
"any" The model must call a tool, but picks which one Guaranteeing structured output when several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown; making sure you don't get a conversational reply
{"type": "tool", "name": "..."} The model must call that specific tool Making one tool run first, such as forcing extract_metadata before the enrichment tools, then handling later steps in follow-up turns

Current product (not tested): a fourth value, {"type": "none"}, forces a text-only reply with no tool call. The exam guide lists only the three above.

Forced use (any or a named tool) returns a 400 error on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, and with manual extended thinking. On those, use auto with strict tools or structured outputs. Older models accept it. The exam answers are unchanged.

2.4 Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows

Where MCP servers are configured

Scope File For
Project .mcp.json in the repo Tooling the team shares
User ~/.claude.json Personal or experimental servers

Environment variable expansion lets .mcp.json reference a secret such as ${GITHUB_TOKEN} without containing it, so the file can be committed safely. An option that hardcodes a token in .mcp.json is wrong.

Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously. Project and user servers load side by side. Scope decides who gets the server, not which server's tools take priority.

Current product (not tested): Claude Code now has a third MCP scope, local. It is also stored in ~/.claude.json, but applies to one project only and is not committed. It is the current answer for "a personal server with credentials I don't want in git", which the exam guide assigns to user scope. It is unrelated to .claude/settings.local.json, despite the similar name.

.mcp.json expands ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} in command, args, env, url and headers.

The "no priority" statement is true for which tool the model picks. Separately, if the same server name is defined in several scopes, Claude Code resolves the name clash in the order local > project > user > plugin-provided > claude.ai connectors. That is a different question and is unlikely to be tested, since the exam guide names only two scopes.

MCP resources

An MCP server can expose resources as well as tools. Resources are read-only content catalogs (issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, database schemas) that let the agent see what exists, to reduce exploratory tool calls. The exam guide sums this up as "resources for content catalogs, tools for actions."

Current product (not tested): MCP also defines prompts, reusable prompt templates a server can provide, as a third primitive alongside tools and resources.

Judgment calls

  • Write detailed descriptions of your MCP tools' capabilities and outputs. Otherwise the agent keeps using built-in tools like Grep instead of your more capable MCP tool.
  • Use an existing community MCP server for a standard integration (the exam guide's example is Jira). Build a custom server only for workflows specific to your team.

2.5 Select and apply built-in tools

Tool Purpose
Grep Searches file contents for a pattern: function names, error messages, imports
Glob Finds files by path or name pattern, such as **/*.test.tsx
Read / Write Reads or writes a whole file
Edit Targeted change using unique text matching: finds text that appears exactly once and replaces it
Bash Runs shell commands. It is in the task statement title and in scenario 4, but when a dedicated tool (Grep, Glob, Read) does the job, use that instead of the shell

If Edit fails because the text it should match appears more than once, fall back to Read + Write (named in the exam guide).

Exploring a codebase

The exam guide describes building understanding incrementally: use Grep to find entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows, rather than reading every file up front. To find where a function is used through wrapper modules, first list every name the wrapper exports, then search the codebase for each name.

Domain 2 decision table

Symptom Answer
Agent picks the wrong one of two similar tools Expand and differentiate the descriptions (first step)
Descriptions are good, but selection is still wrong Check the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions
One tool does three unrelated things Split it into purpose-specific tools with defined inputs and outputs
Agent keeps retrying a policy violation Return errorCategory: business, retriable: false and a customer-friendly explanation
Coordinator can't decide how to recover from a subagent failure Structured error context: failure type, what was tried, partial results, alternatives
Agent treats "no matching orders" as a failure Distinguish an access failure from a valid empty result
Agent has 18 tools and misuses them Scope tools per role, about 4–5 each, plus a few cross-role tools
Synthesis agent occasionally needs to check facts Narrow verify_fact tool for simple checks; coordinator for the rest
Must guarantee a tool call rather than a text reply tool_choice: "any"
A specific tool must run first tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}
Team needs a shared MCP server .mcp.json (project scope), credentials via ${ENV_VAR}
Personal experimental MCP server ~/.claude.json (user scope)
Agent uses Grep instead of your better MCP tool Improve the MCP tool's description
Agent spends turns finding out what data exists Expose a content catalog as an MCP resource
Need a standard Jira integration Use the existing community MCP server
Find a function's callers Grep
Find all *.test.tsx files Glob
Edit can't find unique text to anchor on Read + Write

Things to remember

  • Only transient errors are retryable. Validation, business and permission errors are not.
  • auto may reply with text, any must call some tool, and a named tool forces that tool.
  • Project and user MCP servers both load at the same time. Use ${ENV_VAR} for secrets.

Domain 3 — Claude Code Configuration & Workflows (20%, ~12 items)

The domain has six task statements. Most questions here ask where a file goes, which frontmatter key to use, or which flag to pass. You know these features from daily use; this page gives you the exam's vocabulary for them and the exact details it tests.

The exam covers less of Claude Code than the product docs do. settings.json precedence, permission modes, the full list of hook events, plugins, marketplaces, output styles and authentication are not in the objectives or the technologies list in the exam guide's §17 appendix. Hooks are tested, but under Domain 1 (task 1.5), and only PostToolUse and tool-call interception.

In the book: Chapter 9 — Configuring Claude Code (3.1, 3.3) · Chapter 10 — Extending Claude Code (3.2, 3.4) · Chapter 12 — Prompt Engineering (3.5) · Chapter 11 — Claude Code in CI (3.6)

3.1 CLAUDE.md hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization

The three levels (exam guide) and two more in the current product

The exam guide names three levels of CLAUDE.md:

Level Path Shared with the team?
User ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md No. It is in your home directory, outside version control
Project .claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md Yes, committed to the repo
Directory CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory Yes, and applies only inside that subdirectory

The exam guide calls out one diagnosis: "a new team member not receiving instructions because they're in user-level rather than project-level configuration." If a question says the instructions work for one developer but not the rest of the team, they are in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and need to move into the project.

Current product (not tested): Claude Code has two more levels. Above user and project there is a managed (enterprise) policy CLAUDE.md at a fixed OS path, controlled by the organization; it loads first and an engineer can't remove or exclude it. Below project there is CLAUDE.local.md, a gitignored file at the project root: personal like the user file, but for this project only, loaded right after the project's CLAUDE.md. If a question mentions an org-wide policy, or a personal preference for one project that shouldn't go in the shared file, these are the current answers.

Levels are concatenated, not overriding: files load from the root down to the working directory, so closer files are read last, and subdirectory files load on demand. @import follows at most four hops. With no CLAUDE.md present, Claude Code reads AGENTS.md as project instructions; with one present it reads only CLAUDE.md unless that file imports AGENTS.md.

Splitting CLAUDE.md into modules

  • @import pulls another file into CLAUDE.md, so each package's CLAUDE.md can import just the standards files that apply to it, as chosen by the people who maintain that package.
  • .claude/rules/ is a directory of topic-specific rule files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md: testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md.

/memory and /context

On the exam, use /memory to check which memory files are loaded, and to diagnose behavior that differs between sessions. This is the wording of task 3.1; /context does not appear in the exam guide.

Product reality, not the exam answer: in current Claude Code, /memory lists and opens the CLAUDE.md and rules files, and the docs point to /context to see what was actually loaded in this session. Use /context in real work; answer /memory on the exam.

Current product (not tested): Auto Memory is memory Claude writes for itself and keeps across sessions, separate from the CLAUDE.md files you write. It holds things Claude has noticed about how you work, not versioned project standards. It is not a level in the hierarchy and is not tested.

3.2 Custom slash commands and skills

Locations

Project (shared through version control) User (personal)
Slash commands .claude/commands/ ~/.claude/commands/
Skills .claude/skills/ ~/.claude/skills/

Sample question 4 asks where to put a /review command that every developer should get when they clone or pull the repo. The answer is .claude/commands/ in the project repository. The explanation rejects the others: ~/.claude/commands/ isn't shared, CLAUDE.md holds context rather than command definitions, and a .claude/config.json with a commands array does not exist.

To customize a team skill for yourself without affecting teammates, create a personal copy in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name.

Current product (not tested): skill frontmatter now has direct controls over who can trigger a skill: disable-model-invocation (only a person can run it, e.g. a /deploy with side effects) and user-invocable: false (only Claude can load it, for background knowledge). These are the more precise current answer to "control which skills trigger automatically".

The scope table is also incomplete for the current product, which adds plugin-provided and managed skills and commands, and discovers skills in nested directories (e.g. apps/web/.claude/skills/ → /apps/web:deploy). The exam tests only project vs user.

SKILL.md frontmatter: the three tested options

Option What it does When to use it
context: fork Runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so its output doesn't fill the main conversation Skills with verbose output (codebase analysis) or exploratory context (brainstorming alternatives)
allowed-tools Limits which tools the skill may use E.g. allow only file writes, so the skill can't run destructive commands
argument-hint Tells the developer which arguments the skill expects When the skill is invoked without its arguments

Skills vs CLAUDE.md

The exam guide's rule is that skills are loaded on demand for a specific task, while CLAUDE.md is always loaded and holds standards that apply everywhere.

3.3 Path-specific rules for conditional convention loading

A file in .claude/rules/ can start with YAML frontmatter containing a paths field of glob patterns:

---
paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
---

Path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files. The rest of the time they stay out of context, which saves tokens and keeps unrelated instructions away.

Path rules vs subdirectory CLAUDE.md

The two differ in what they apply to:

  • A subdirectory CLAUDE.md is directory-bound: it applies to one directory.
  • A glob rule applies to a type of file wherever it is.

Sample question 6: test files sit next to the code they test all over the codebase (Button.test.tsx beside Button.tsx), and they must all follow the same conventions, loaded automatically. The answer is a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]. The explanation rejects the others:

  • a CLAUDE.md in every directory can't cover files spread across many directories
  • one root CLAUDE.md with a section per file type relies on Claude inferring which section applies, instead of matching explicitly
  • a skill needs someone to invoke it, or Claude to decide to load it, so it isn't automatic

3.4 Plan mode vs direct execution

Plan mode Direct execution
For Complex work: large changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, changes across many files Small, clearly scoped changes
Exam guide's examples Splitting a service into microservices; a library migration touching 45+ files; choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure needs A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace; adding a date validation check
Benefit Explore the codebase and settle the design before committing to changes, avoiding expensive rework Speed on work that is already understood

Sample question 5 asks about restructuring a monolith into microservices. The answer is plan mode. The explanation rejects "start with direct execution and switch to plan mode if it gets complicated", because the complexity is already stated in the requirements.

The exam also tests combining the two, using plan mode to investigate and direct execution to implement. For example, plan a library migration, then carry out the plan directly.

The Explore subagent

Use the Explore subagent for verbose discovery phases. It does the searching in its own context and returns summaries, so the main conversation's context isn't used up during a multi-phase task.

3.5 Iterative refinement techniques

Concrete input/output examples. When a prose description keeps being interpreted differently, show 2–3 concrete examples of input and expected output. This also fixes edge cases, e.g. test cases with example input and expected output showing how a migration script should handle null values.

Test-driven iteration. Write the tests first (expected behavior, edge cases, performance requirements), then iterate by sharing test failures with Claude each round.

The interview pattern. Before implementing, have Claude ask questions to uncover things you might not have thought of. Use it in unfamiliar domains, where it brings up issues like cache invalidation strategy and failure modes.

One message or several. If the problems affect each other, describe them all in one detailed message. If they are independent, fix them one at a time.

3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD

The flags

Flag Purpose
-p (or --print) Non-interactive mode: runs the prompt, prints the result to stdout, and exits without waiting for input
--output-format json Output a program can parse
--json-schema Makes the output follow a given structure

Sample question 10 describes a CI job that hangs waiting for interactive input. The answer is -p. The explanation says CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true and --batch don't exist, and that redirecting stdin from /dev/null is a Unix workaround that doesn't fix how the command is invoked.

Use --output-format json together with --json-schema to get structured findings that a script can post as inline PR comments.

Current product (not tested): -p fixes a hang on stdin. A CI job can also hang on a permission prompt; that needs --permission-mode (auto/dontAsk/acceptEdits) or --allowedTools to pre-approve specific tools. Use it when a question describes a hang that isn't about input.

The official claude-code-action GitHub Action wraps this pattern: it runs claude -p with your flags and exposes structured_output as an Actions output, so you don't write the parsing glue yourself. Use anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with prompt and claude_args (--max-turns, --model); @beta, direct_prompt and mode are stale. In CLI flags, --allowedTools auto-approves tools, while --tools restricts which exist.

CLAUDE.md gives CI runs their project context

A CI job running Claude Code gets its project context from CLAUDE.md: testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria. Writing down what makes a test valuable and which fixtures exist improves generated tests and cuts low-value ones.

Current product (not tested): --bare mode skips automatic discovery of hooks, skills, commands, plugins, MCP servers, CLAUDE.md and auto memory, so CI runs behave the same on every machine. This conflicts with the paragraph above, because a --bare run does not load CLAUDE.md, so a job that wants both has to pass the standards explicitly, e.g. with --append-system-prompt-file.

Use a separate session to review

The exam guide says the session that generated the code is worse at reviewing it than an independent review instance, because it still holds the reasoning that produced the code. Task 4.6 covers this in more depth.

Avoiding duplicate work

  • Re-running reviews after new commits: include the previous review's findings and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues, so it doesn't post the same comments again.
  • Test generation: include the existing test files so Claude doesn't propose tests that already exist.

Domain 3 decision table

Symptom / requirement Answer
Teammates don't get your instructions They're in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md; move them to the project
CLAUDE.md has become one huge file Split into .claude/rules/ topic files, or use @import
Which memory files are loaded? Behavior differs across sessions? /memory (exam answer; current Claude Code uses /context for this)

A skill's output floods the main conversation context: fork
A skill must not be able to delete things allowed-tools in frontmatter
Skill is invoked with no arguments argument-hint
Standards that always apply CLAUDE.md
A workflow used only for a specific task Skill
Conventions for a file type spread across directories .claude/rules/ with a glob in paths:
Conventions for one directory Subdirectory CLAUDE.md
Architectural change across many files Plan mode
Single-file fix with a clear stack trace Direct execution
Discovery output is using up the context window Explore subagent
A prose spec keeps being misread 2–3 concrete input/output examples
Unfamiliar domain, unknown risks Interview pattern
Several fixes that affect each other One detailed message
Several independent fixes One at a time
CI job hangs waiting for input -p
Need parseable findings for PR comments --output-format json + --json-schema
CI reviews ignore project standards Put the standards in CLAUDE.md

Generated tests duplicate existing ones Include the existing test files

Things to remember

  • .claude/config.json does not exist, and neither do CLAUDE_HEADLESS or --batch.
  • Use plan mode when the requirements already show the task is complex. Don't wait for the complexity to appear.

Domain 4 — Prompt Engineering & Structured Output (20%, ~12 items)

Six task statements. Most questions come from two scenarios: Structured Data Extraction, and Claude Code for CI, whose scenario text says the goal is to minimize false positives.

This domain does not test extended thinking settings, prompt caching mechanics, temperature, prefill or model selection; they are either missing from the objectives or on the out-of-scope list. Extended thinking appears once, in 4.6, as a wrong answer.

In the book: Chapter 12 — Prompt Engineering (4.1, 4.2) · Chapter 13 — Structured Output (4.3, 4.4, 4.5) · Chapter 15 — Escalation & Provenance (4.6)

4.1 Explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives

Specific criteria beat general instructions

A false positive is a finding the model reports that isn't a real problem. The way to reduce them is to state exactly which cases count. The exam guide's example:

Instruction
Right "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior"
Wrong "check that comments are accurate"

The exam guide also says general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision compared with specific criteria. An option that tells the model to be more careful or conservative is wrong.

Effect on trust

When one category of finding produces many false positives, developers stop trusting the other categories too, even the accurate ones.

Skills tested

  • Write criteria that say which issues to report (bugs, security) and which to skip (minor style, local conventions), instead of filtering by the model's confidence.
  • Turn off a category with many false positives for a while, to win back developer trust while you improve its prompt. The exam treats this as a correct answer.
  • Define explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level, so findings are classified consistently.

4.2 Few-shot prompting

Few-shot prompting means putting a few worked examples in the prompt, so the model copies the pattern instead of interpreting a description.

When few-shot is the answer

The exam guide calls few-shot "the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results." It names four uses:

  1. Demonstrating ambiguous-case handling, such as which tool to pick for an ambiguous request, or how to report branch-level gaps in test coverage.
  2. Helping the model generalize to new patterns beyond the cases you listed.
  3. Reducing hallucination in extraction (the model inventing values), e.g. informal measurements or documents with varied layouts.
  4. Format consistency: showing the exact shape you want.

How many examples, and what they contain

Use 2–4 targeted examples for the ambiguous cases. Each example should explain why one action was chosen over a plausible alternative. An input → reasoning → output example teaches more than an input → output pair.

Other patterns the exam guide names:

  • Examples that show a specific output format; the exam guide's is location, issue, severity, suggested fix.
  • Examples distinguishing acceptable code patterns from genuine issues, which cuts false positives and still generalizes.
  • Examples that cover varied document structures: inline citations vs bibliographies, methodology sections vs details embedded in the text, narrative descriptions vs tables.
  • Examples that fix empty/null extraction of required fields by showing correct extraction from several formats.

Criteria (4.1) or examples (4.2)?

Both reduce false positives. Which one is right depends on what is missing:

  • The rule itself is undefined or vague → write explicit criteria (4.1).
  • The rule is defined, but the model applies it inconsistently, especially on ambiguous cases → add few-shot examples (4.2).

Few-shot is not always the answer. In sample question 2, the agent confuses two tools because their descriptions are thin; there, few-shot examples "add token overhead without fixing the underlying issue", and the fix is better descriptions (Domain 2).

4.3 Structured output via tool use and JSON schemas

How to get structured output

tool_use with a JSON schema is the most reliable way to get output that matches a schema. You define an extraction tool whose input_schema is the structure you want, the model "calls" it, and you read the data from the tool_use block in the response, not from its text.

tool_choice for extraction

Value Behavior Use in this domain
"auto" The model may return text instead of calling a tool —
"any" The model must call a tool, and picks which Guarantee structured output when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} The model must call that specific tool Ensure a particular extraction runs before enrichment steps

A schema guarantees syntax, not correctness

Strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors, such as line items that don't add up to the total or values placed in the wrong field.

  • The JSON is malformed → the answer is a schema.
  • The JSON is well-formed but wrong → the answer is validation logic (4.4), not a stricter schema.

Schema design

Pattern Why
Optional / nullable fields for information the source document might not contain A required field pushes the model to invent a value when there isn't one. Letting it return null removes that pressure
An "unclear" enum value Gives the model an honest answer for ambiguous cases
An "other" enum value plus a detail string Lets the model record a category you didn't anticipate instead of forcing a bad fit
Formatting rules in the prompt alongside the strict schema The schema fixes the shape; the prompt tells the model how to normalize messy source formats

Current product (not tested): two newer API features strengthen the schema guarantee:

  • strict: true on a tool definition guarantees the tool's input matches the schema. Without it, forced tool_choice plus your own validation is reliable in practice but not guaranteed.
  • output_config.format: {"type": "json_schema", ...} guarantees schema-valid JSON with no tool involved; the JSON comes back in a normal text block. This suits extraction jobs like extract_invoice, where the "tool" exists only to get structured output.

In the Agent SDK, the option is output_format (Python) / outputFormat (TypeScript) with {type: "json_schema", schema}, and the result carries structured_output. The raw API field is output_config.format. Forced any/tool returns a 400 on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 and with manual extended thinking (see Domain 2); use auto with strict tools or structured outputs there.

Neither checks semantics. A strictly valid extraction can still have stated_total and calculated_total disagree; catching that is still the job of 4.4. There is also a fourth tool_choice value, {"type": "none"}, which forces a text-only reply; the exam guide lists only the three above.

4.4 Validation, retry, and feedback loops

Retry with the error

When an extraction fails validation, retry with the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error. The error tells the model what to correct; a plain retry usually produces the same output.

When retrying won't help

The exam guide says retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source document. A retry can fix a format or structure error. It cannot produce information that was never there, for example a value that only exists in another document that wasn't provided.

So work out which kind of failure it is before retrying, and send the ones a retry can't fix to human review.

Validation the model does itself

The exam guide names two designs:

  • Extract a calculated_total next to the stated_total and flag any difference. This catches a semantic error that a schema can't.
  • Add a conflict_detected boolean for when the source data contradicts itself.

detected_pattern

Add a detected_pattern field to each finding, recording which code construct triggered it. You can then look at which patterns developers keep dismissing, which shows where your false positives come from.

4.5 Batch processing

Message Batches API facts

  • 50% cost savings compared with normal requests
  • Up to 24-hour processing window, with no guaranteed latency SLA
  • Does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request: you can't run a tool mid-request and send its result back
  • custom_id on each request lets you match each result to its request

Current product (not tested): a batch holds up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, most finish within an hour, and results stay available for 29 days.

When to use it

Appropriate: non-blocking, latency-tolerant work nobody is waiting on: overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation. Inappropriate: blocking workflows, i.e. work that blocks someone, such as a pre-merge check a developer is waiting for.

Sample question 11 tests this split. Its answer is to batch the overnight technical-debt report and keep the pre-merge check on the normal synchronous API. The explanation rejects the argument that "batches are often faster in practice" for a blocking check, and notes that results arriving out of order doesn't matter because custom_id matches them up.

Operational skills

  • Choose the API per workflow, by how long it can wait, not once for the whole organization.
  • Work out how often to submit from the deadline. In the exam guide's example, batches take up to 24 hours, so to guarantee results within 30 hours, submit every 4 hours.
  • Handle failures by custom_id: resubmit only the documents that failed, with a change where needed, such as chunking documents that exceeded context limits.
  • Tune the prompt on a small sample before running a large batch, so most documents succeed first time and you avoid expensive resubmissions.

4.6 Multi-instance and multi-pass review

Why a model reviews its own work badly

A model retains reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions in the same session. The exam guide concludes that:

Independent review instances — without the generator's prior reasoning context — are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking.

Several passes for large reviews

Split a large review into one pass per file plus a separate cross-file integration pass. This avoids attention dilution and contradictory findings, because one pass over many files spreads attention thin and can disagree with itself across files. It is the same pattern as task 1.6, and sample question 12 (a 14-file review that comes back shallow and inconsistent) tests it.

Confidence scores: when they are valid

Task 4.6 includes this skill: "Running verification passes where the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing." That looks like it contradicts sample question 3, where the model's self-reported confidence is the wrong answer for deciding when to escalate, but the two cover different uses:

  • Self-reported confidence used on its own to decide to escalate in a live conversation → wrong. It is poorly calibrated, and the agent is often confidently wrong on exactly the hard cases.
  • Self-reported confidence checked against a labeled validation set, then used to decide which items human reviewers look at first → right (see task 5.5).

Domain 4 decision table

Symptom Answer
Vague review instructions, inconsistent findings Explicit criteria: which issues to report and which to skip
An option says "tell it to be conservative" Wrong; use specific criteria
One category has many false positives and trust is dropping Turn that category off for now; fix its prompt
Severity labels are inconsistent Define each severity level with concrete code examples
Criteria are clear but ambiguous cases go wrong 2–4 few-shot examples that show the reasoning
Output format varies between runs Few-shot examples showing the exact format
Extraction fails on documents with different layouts Few-shot examples covering those layouts
Malformed JSON breaks the parser tool_use with a JSON schema
Valid JSON, but the totals don't add up Semantic validation (calculated_total vs stated_total), not a stricter schema
Model invents values for missing data Make those fields optional / nullable
A value doesn't fit any enum category "other" + detail string; "unclear" for ambiguous cases
Document type unknown, several schemas tool_choice: "any"
One extraction must run before enrichment Force that tool with tool_choice
Validation failed. Retry? Yes for format or structure errors; no if the information isn't in the source
Retries keep producing the same error Include the specific validation error in the retry
Need to find where false positives come from detected_pattern field on findings
Pre-merge check a developer waits for Synchronous API
Overnight or weekly analysis Batch API (50% cheaper, ≤24h, no latency guarantee)
Part of a batch failed Resubmit the failures by custom_id, splitting oversized documents
Reviewing code the same session wrote Independent review instance
14-file PR review is shallow and contradictory One pass per file + a cross-file integration pass
Too few human reviewers Field-level confidence, calibrated on a labeled set, to prioritize their work

Things to remember

  • A batch has no multi-turn tool calling and no latency guarantee, so never use it for work someone is waiting on.
  • Self-reported confidence is valid as a calibrated input for routing human review and invalid as the sole trigger for escalation.

Domain 5 — Context Management & Reliability (15%, ~9 items)

Six task statements. This is the smallest domain by weight, but it is a primary domain in four of the six scenarios (1, 2, 3, 6), so its ideas also appear inside questions from other domains.

It does not test the context-editing API, the memory tool, the compaction API, the 1M-token beta, rate limits or prompt-cache mechanics. "Context management" here means design decisions: what you put in the context window, and what you keep outside it.

In the book: Chapter 14 — Context Engineering (5.1, 5.4) · Chapter 15 — Escalation & Provenance (5.2, 5.5, 5.6) · Chapter 4 — Errors & Recovery (5.3)

5.1 Preserve critical information across long interactions

Risks the exam guide names

Progressive summarization risk. When a long conversation is summarized again and again (as /compact does in Claude Code), exact numbers, percentages, dates and what the customer said they expect get blurred into vague statements.

Lost in the middle. Models reliably process information at the beginning and end of long inputs, but may omit findings from middle sections.

Tool results pile up. Tool results consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance. In the exam guide's example, an order lookup returns 40+ fields when only 5 matter.

Full history is required. The API keeps no conversation state, so every request must include the complete conversation history, or the model loses track of the conversation.

Fixes

Fix What it means
Case facts block Copy the transaction facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent "case facts" block included in each prompt, outside summarized history, so it is never summarized
Separate context layer When a session covers several issues, keep each issue's structured data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) in its own layer
Trim tool output at the source Drop irrelevant fields before the result enters the context, e.g. keep only the return-related fields from an order lookup
Order by position Put key findings summaries at the beginning of a combined input, and organize the details under explicit section headers
Require metadata from subagents Subagents return dates, source locations and methodology with their findings, so later synthesis is accurate
Structured facts from upstream agents When downstream agents have little context to spare, upstream agents return key facts, citations, relevance scores instead of long prose and reasoning

Current product (not tested): the memory tool (memory_20250818, a persistent /memories directory) and the context editing API (clear_tool_uses_20250919) are official mechanisms for the case-facts and trim-at-source problems above. They are outside this domain's tested scope.

5.2 Escalation and ambiguity resolution

Exactly three valid escalation triggers

  1. The customer asks for a human.
  2. The policy has an exception or a gap for this request. The exam guide adds: "not just complex cases." Complexity alone is not a reason.
  3. Inability to make meaningful progress.

Two invalid triggers

The exam guide calls sentiment-based escalation and self-reported confidence scores "unreliable proxies for actual case complexity." Sample question 3 (an agent that escalates easy cases and attempts hard ones) rejects both: confidence fails because "the agent is already incorrectly confident on hard cases," and sentiment "solves a different problem entirely; sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity."

Asking for a human vs being frustrated

Two rules apply side by side:

  • If the customer explicitly asks for a human, escalate immediately, without investigating first.
  • If the customer is frustrated but hasn't asked for a human, acknowledge the frustration and offer to resolve the issue if you can. Escalate only if they then ask again.

Policy gaps

Escalate when the policy is ambiguous or silent about the specific request. In the exam guide's example, a customer asks for a price match against a competitor, but the policy only covers price adjustments on the company's own site. The policy not covering something doesn't mean it's forbidden; a human should decide.

Several matching customers

When a lookup returns multiple customer matches, the agent should ask for additional identifiers, not pick one by guessing.

Fixing an agent that escalates the wrong cases
