Sample question 3's answer is to write explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt, with few-shot examples of when to escalate and when to resolve. It is the proportionate first fix. A trained classifier, sentiment analysis and confidence thresholds are all wrong.

5.3 Error propagation across multi-agent systems

What a subagent's error report should contain

A subagent's report should give the type of failure, what was attempted, any partial results and possible alternative approaches. With these four, the coordinator can choose a recovery: retry with a changed query, try another approach, or carry on with the partial results.

Two anti-patterns the exam guide names

  • Silently suppressing errors: returning an empty result as if it were a success. Nothing can recover from it, and the final output may be incomplete without anyone knowing.
  • Stopping the whole workflow because one step failed.

A milder third anti-pattern is returning generic error statuses such as "search unavailable", which hide what the coordinator needs to know. Sample question 8 (a search subagent timing out) rejects an option that retries with backoff and then returns a generic status on this basis, even though the retry part is fine.

Recover locally first

Subagents implement local recovery for transient failures, and pass up only what they can't resolve, including what was attempted and partial results.

Access failure vs valid empty result

This is the same distinction as in task 2.2, applied to multi-agent systems. A timeout needs a retry decision. A query that succeeded but matched nothing does not.

Coverage annotations

Mark in the synthesis output which findings are well supported and which topics have gaps because a source was unavailable. Partial results are acceptable; partial results presented as complete are not.

5.4 Context in large codebase exploration

Context degradation

The exam guide describes the symptom. In long sessions, the model starts giving inconsistent answers and refers to "typical patterns" instead of the specific classes it found earlier. If a question describes an agent that has drifted into generic advice about a codebase it explored an hour ago, this is the diagnosis.

Exploration techniques

Technique What it means
Scratchpad files Write key findings to a file, and refer back to it for later questions, so they survive when the context fills up or is compacted
Subagent delegation Give specific questions ("find all test files", "trace refund flow dependencies") to subagents. Their long exploration output stays in their context, and the main agent keeps the overall picture
Phase summaries At the end of one exploration phase, summarize the key findings before starting the next, and put that summary in the next phase's subagent prompts
Saved state and a manifest Each agent saves its state to a known location. After a crash, the coordinator loads a manifest on resume listing that state and puts it into the agents' prompts. This is the exam guide's crash-recovery design
/compact Shrink the context during a long exploration once it fills with discovery output

Current product (not tested): the memory tool closely matches the scratchpad and manifest patterns: a persistent /memories directory Claude reads and writes across sessions. Server-side compaction (compact_20260112) accepts an instructions field, so you can tell it to keep dollar amounts and dates verbatim instead of relying only on a case-facts block.

5.5 Human review workflows and confidence calibration

The main risk

An overall accuracy figure can hide poor accuracy on particular document types or fields. 97% overall can include 60% on one class of document. Check accuracy per document type and per field before letting high-confidence extractions skip human review.

Review techniques

  • Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions: keep reviewing a random sample from each segment of the extractions the model is sure about, to measure the ongoing error rate and detect novel error patterns. You sample the ones you believe are correct because that is where unnoticed errors collect.
  • Accuracy broken down by document type and field, to confirm performance holds in every segment before cutting human review.
  • Field-level confidence scores, calibrated against a labeled validation set, to decide where reviewers look. Calibrated means you have checked that, say, 90% confidence really is right about 90% of the time.
  • Send to human review any extraction with low confidence, or whose source document is ambiguous or contradictory, so limited reviewer time goes where it's needed.

Confidence is legitimate here because it is per field, calibrated against labeled data, and used to prioritize review (compare 5.2 and 4.6).

5.6 Provenance and uncertainty in multi-source synthesis

Provenance means being able to trace each claim in the output back to its source.

How it gets lost

Source attribution is lost during summarization steps when findings are compressed without preserving claim-source mappings. The structural fix is to require structured claim-source mappings (source URL, document name, relevant excerpt) that every later agent must preserve and merge through synthesis.

Sources that disagree

Report both values with their sources instead of picking one. If two credible sources give different figures, show both, attributed. More fully, finish the document analysis with the conflicting values included and marked as conflicting, and let the coordinator decide how to reconcile them before synthesis.

Dates

Require publication or data collection dates in structured outputs, to prevent temporal differences from being misinterpreted as contradictions. Two "conflicting" figures may just be from different years.

Current product (not tested): the citations API (citations: {"enabled": true} on a document content block) does claim-to-source mapping automatically when Claude reads a document directly, returning the cited text and its location. You still need your own mapping for handoffs between subagents, where there is no document block, only the previous subagent's findings.

Report structure

  • Separate sections distinguishing well-established findings from contested ones, keeping each source's own wording and methodological context.
  • Present each kind of content in a suitable form: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists, rather than one uniform format.

Domain 5 decision table

Symptom Answer
Amounts, dates and order numbers become vague in a long chat Persistent "case facts" block, outside the summarized history
Findings from the middle of a long input get dropped Key findings summary at the top; clear section headers
Order lookups return 40+ fields and 5 are relevant Trim tool output before it enters the context
Downstream agent has little context to spare Upstream agents return structured facts and citations, not prose
Customer says "get me a human" Escalate immediately, without investigating first
Customer is angry but the issue is simple Acknowledge it, offer to resolve; escalate if they ask again
Policy says nothing about the request Escalate: policy gap
get_customer returns three matches Ask for another identifier
Someone proposes escalating on sentiment or confidence Wrong; use explicit criteria + few-shot examples
Subagent times out Structured error context: type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives
Subagent returns empty results as a success Anti-pattern: silently suppressing the error
One subagent fails and the whole workflow stops Anti-pattern: carry on with partial results
Report is based on partial coverage Coverage annotations separating supported findings from gaps
Agent starts citing "typical patterns" late in a session Context degradation → scratchpad files
Exploration output is filling the context window Delegate to subagents; /compact
Long exploration needs crash recovery Saved agent state + a manifest the coordinator loads on resume
97% accuracy, want to reduce human review Check accuracy per document type and field first
Need to keep catching errors in the "safe" high-confidence bucket Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions
Not enough human reviewers Route by calibrated field-level confidence
Citations disappear after synthesis Claim-to-source mappings kept through every step
Two credible sources disagree Report both with sources; don't pick one
Figures look contradictory Require publication or collection dates

Things to remember

  • There are three valid escalation triggers: the customer asks, the policy has a gap, or the agent cannot make progress. Sentiment and self-reported confidence are not triggers.

Trap Pairs

Cover the answer. For each pair, write both conditions on paper or say them aloud, and name the deciding phrase. Then open Check. A pair is done when you can fill it from memory twice, on different days. Then run a Drill set: Drill → Domain focus, on the task number in the Drill: line. The drill engine filters by domain and task statement only, so there is no per-pair filter. Use the Check only to compare your own answer with the key.

Domain 1: Agentic Architecture and Orchestration

stop_reason vs text content

Which signal ends the loop: stop_reason or text content? Why does the other fail?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • stop_reason is "tool_use": run the tools, append results, call again.
  • Never for loop control. Only "end_turn" ends the loop; an iteration cap is a safety net.
  • Deciding phrase: e.g. "how should the loop decide it is finished"; "the model returned text".
  • Distractor: Parsing the text for "I'm done" phrases, or checking whether any text block exists. Text can accompany a tool_use turn.
  • Drill: 1.1

Prerequisite gate vs prompt rule

Use Prerequisite gate when ___. Use prompt rule when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Gate (code): the step order or check is critical business logic (verify identity before refund) and a skipped step has financial or compliance cost.
  • Prompt rule / few-shot: the failure is soft, such as tone, phrasing or ambiguous judgment, and an occasional miss is acceptable. Money, identity, compliance and ordering get code (gate, hook, schema, validation).
  • Deciding phrase: "in 12% of cases ... skips get_customer entirely"; "financial consequences"; "specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic".
  • Distractor: Stronger system-prompt wording and few-shot examples ("probabilistic LLM compliance"); a routing classifier ("addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering").
  • Drill: 1.4, 1.5, 4.3

PostToolUse vs tool-call interception

Use PostToolUse when ___. Use tool-call interception when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • PostToolUse: a result has come back and must be changed before the model sees it (timestamps, status codes, heterogeneous formats).
  • Interception (pre-call): an outgoing call must be blocked or redirected before it executes (refund over $500 to escalation).
  • Deciding phrase: "normalize" or "heterogeneous formats" points to PostToolUse; "block", "exceeding $500", "before it executes" points to interception.
  • Distractor: PostToolUse to stop a refund: it fires after execution, so the money has already moved.
  • Drill: 1.5

Prompt chaining vs dynamic decomposition

Use Prompt chaining when ___. Use dynamic decomposition when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Prompt chaining: the steps are known in advance and fixed (per-file pass, then integration pass).
  • Dynamic adaptive decomposition: the subtasks depend on what each step finds (open-ended investigation of a legacy codebase).
  • Deciding phrase: "predictable multi-aspect review" versus "open-ended", "unknown structure".
  • Distractor: One single pass over 14 files ("inconsistent depth"), or an adaptive plan for a task whose steps are already known.
  • Drill: 1.6

Coordinator-routed vs direct subagent communication

Who carries information between subagents: the coordinator or the subagents directly? Why does the other fail?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Coordinator-routed (hub-and-spoke): always. The coordinator owns observability, consistent error handling and controlled information flow.
  • Direct subagent-to-subagent: not an exam answer. Subagents have isolated context and inherit nothing.
  • Deciding phrase: "observability", "consistent error handling", "controlled information flow".
  • Distractor: Letting subagents share context or call each other; a shared global memory that subagents read implicitly.
  • Drill: 1.2, 1.3

Fix the coordinator's decomposition vs fix downstream agents

Use Fix the coordinator's decomposition when ___. Use fix downstream agents when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Decomposition: every subagent ran correctly but the final coverage has gaps (only visual arts of "creative industries").
  • Downstream agent: a subagent's own output is wrong for the task it was given.
  • Deciding phrase: "each subagent completes successfully"; "it decomposed the topic into three subtasks" (logs show the narrow subtasks).
  • Distractor: Blaming the search agent, the synthesis agent or the document analysis agent; widening their prompts.
  • Drill: 1.2 · sample Q7

Resume vs fork_session vs fresh session with summary

Use --resume when ___. Use fork_session when ___. Use a fresh session with a structured summary when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • --resume <session-name>: prior context is still valid and you continue the same line of work (tell it which files changed). fork_session: you want two divergent approaches from one shared baseline. Fresh session + structured summary: earlier tool results are stale.
  • Deciding phrase: "files changed since", "stale tool results", "compare two approaches from the same analysis".
  • Distractor: Resuming with stale tool results as if still true; forking when there is no divergence to compare.
  • Drill: 1.7

Domain 2: Tool Design and MCP Integration

Tool description fix vs routing layer or consolidation

Two similar tools get confused and their descriptions are minimal. What is the first step, and why do a routing layer and consolidation fail as a first step?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Rewrite descriptions: two tools get confused and descriptions are minimal. Include input formats, example queries, edge cases, when to use this one instead of the neighbour.
  • Routing layer: "over-engineered", bypasses the model's language understanding. Consolidation: valid but more effort than a first step warrants. If the tools do overlap, the exam guide's fix is to rename or split them into purpose-specific tools with clear contracts, not to merge them.
  • Deciding phrase: e.g. "most effective first step" (Q2 stem); "minimal descriptions".
  • Distractor: A routing classifier ("over-engineered"), few-shot examples ("token overhead without fixing the underlying issue"), consolidating tools ("more effort than a first step warrants").
  • Drill: 2.1

tool_choice any/forced vs better descriptions or a gate

Use tool_choice any/forced when ___. Use better descriptions or a gate when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • tool_choice: "any" when the model must return a tool call (structured output) and not text; a named tool when a specific extraction must run first.
  • Descriptions or a gate: selection between similar tools (descriptions) or a required order across several calls (gate). tool_choice forces one turn only.
  • Deciding phrase: e.g. "must return structured output" versus "keeps picking the wrong tool" or a required order on every request.
  • Distractor (inference): Forcing a tool to fix ordering that must hold on every request. Forcing get_customer once does not verify identity on later process_refund calls (sample Q1 needs a programmatic prerequisite). auto may reply with text.
  • Drill: 2.3

Retryable transient vs business, validation or permission error

Use Retryable transient when ___. Use business, validation or permission error when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Retry: the error is transient (timeout, service unavailable) and isRetryable is true. The subagent retries locally.
  • Do not retry: validation (fix the input), business (policy rule: retriable: false, customer-friendly explanation), permission (needs different access).
  • Deciding phrase: "timed out" versus "exceeds policy limit" or "not authorized".
  • Distractor: Retrying a business-rule violation; returning one generic "operation failed" status that hides the category.
  • Drill: 2.2

Empty result vs access failure

Use Empty result when ___. Use access failure when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Empty result: the query ran and found zero matches. It is a success; report "no matches".
  • Access failure: timeout or unreachable source. It is an error with a category, and the coverage gap must be reported.
  • Deciding phrase: "returned no results" versus "timed out" or "unavailable".
  • Distractor: Treating a timeout as an empty success ("suppresses the error"), or retrying a legitimate zero-match.
  • Drill: 2.2, 5.3

MCP resource vs tool

Use MCP resource when ___. Use tool when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Resource: read-only content catalog the agent should browse without exploratory calls (issue summaries, schemas, doc hierarchy).
  • Tool: an action, or a query with parameters that does work.
  • Deciding phrase: "catalog", "visibility into what is available", "reduce exploratory tool calls".
  • Distractor: Wrapping a static catalog as a tool, forcing the agent to call it blind to discover contents.
  • Drill: 2.4

Project .mcp.json vs user ~/.claude.json

Use Project .mcp.json when ___. Use user ~/.claude.json when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • .mcp.json: the server is shared with the team through version control. Use ${GITHUB_TOKEN} expansion so secrets are not committed.
  • ~/.claude.json: personal or experimental servers only you need.
  • Deciding phrase: "every developer on clone" versus "experimental", "only me".
  • Distractor: Putting a team server in user scope (not shared); hard-coding the token in .mcp.json; assuming one scope has priority (both load together).
  • Drill: 2.4

Grep vs Glob

Use Grep when ___. Use Glob when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Grep: you search file contents (function names, error strings, callers).
  • Glob: you match file paths or names (**/*.test.tsx).
  • Deciding phrase: "files that contain" versus "files named" or "with extension".
  • Distractor: Glob to find callers; Grep to list files by extension; reading every file up front.
  • Drill: 2.5

Edit vs Read + Write

Use Edit when ___. Use Read + Write when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Edit: a targeted change where the anchor text appears exactly once.
  • Read + Write: the anchor is not unique and Edit fails, or the whole file changes.
  • Deciding phrase: "Edit fails", "non-unique match".
  • Distractor: Retrying Edit with the same anchor; falling back to Bash sed (a common wrong answer, not exam-sourced; the exam fallback is Read + Write).
  • Drill: 2.5

Domain 3: Claude Code Configuration and Workflows

Directory CLAUDE.md vs .claude/rules with paths glob

Use Directory CLAUDE.md when ___. Use .claude/rules with paths glob when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Directory CLAUDE.md: the convention belongs to one directory tree.
  • .claude/rules/*.md with paths: glob: the convention follows a file type spread across directories (tests next to code).
  • Deciding phrase: "spread throughout the codebase", "regardless of directory", "automatically".
  • Distractor: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files (directory-bound); a skill (needs manual invocation); inference from one big CLAUDE.md (unreliable).
  • Drill: 3.3

User vs project CLAUDE.md

Use User when ___. Use project CLAUDE.md when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md): personal preferences that travel with you across projects. Not shared.
  • Project (CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md): team standards, committed. Fixes "works for me, not for teammates".
  • Deciding phrase: "new teammate doesn't get the instructions"; "shared via version control".
  • Distractor: Putting the team rule in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (not shared via version control). Also: verify what loaded with /memory.
  • Drill: 3.1

Skill vs CLAUDE.md

Use Skill when ___. Use CLAUDE.md when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Skill: a task-specific workflow loaded on demand.
  • CLAUDE.md: universal standards that must always be loaded.
  • Deciding phrase: "on demand", "occasional task" versus "every session", "always apply".
  • Distractor: Putting a rare multi-step procedure in CLAUDE.md (bloats every session); putting always-on standards in a skill (may not load).
  • Drill: 3.2

context: fork vs allowed-tools

Use context: fork when ___. Use allowed-tools when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • context: fork: the skill produces verbose output or exploration that should not pollute the main conversation.
  • allowed-tools: restrict which tools the skill may use. argument-hint prompts for the parameter.
  • Deciding phrase: "output pollutes the conversation" versus "limit what the skill can do".
  • Distractor: Using allowed-tools to reduce verbosity; using context: fork as a permission control.
  • Drill: 3.2

Plan mode vs direct execution

Use Plan mode when ___. Use direct execution when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Plan mode: large-scale change, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, complexity already stated in the requirements.
  • Direct execution: single-file fix, clear stack trace, well-understood change. Combine: plan to investigate, direct to implement.
  • Deciding phrase: "dozens of files", "decisions about boundaries" versus "single-file", "clear stack trace".
  • Distractor: Starting direct and switching "if it gets complex" (the complexity is already known); deciding the structure before exploring.
  • Drill: 3.4

Explore subagent vs main context

Use Explore subagent when ___. Use main context when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Explore subagent: discovery that generates verbose output; only the summary returns.
  • Main context: a short, targeted lookup whose result you need in the conversation.
  • Deciding phrase: "verbose", "fills the context", "multi-phase task".
  • Distractor: Reading dozens of files into the main session; keeping on exploring in the same long session.
  • Drill: 3.4, 5.4

Domain 4: Prompt Engineering and Structured Output

Explicit criteria vs few-shot examples

Use Explicit criteria when ___. Use few-shot examples when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Explicit criteria: the rule is missing or vague ("be conservative"). State what to report and what to skip, with severity definitions.
  • Few-shot (2-4, with reasoning): the rule exists but ambiguous cases are handled inconsistently.
  • Deciding phrase: "be conservative" / "only report high-confidence" with no categories defined points to explicit criteria; "detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results" or "ambiguous cases" points to few-shot. The two can be combined, as sample Q3 answer A does.
  • Distractor: "Only report high-confidence findings", or a confidence threshold. Neither defines the category.
  • Drill: 4.1, 4.2

Schema (syntax) vs validation logic (semantics)

Output is valid JSON but line items do not sum to the stated total. Which mechanism catches it: schema or validation logic? Which errors does each one prevent?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Schema via tool_use (strict): eliminates JSON syntax errors.
  • Validation logic: catches values that parse but are wrong (line items that do not sum, wrong field). Add calculated_total next to stated_total.
  • Deciding phrase: "values don't sum", "valid JSON but wrong".
  • Distractor: A stricter schema or more required fields to fix a wrong value; a longer prompt.
  • Drill: 4.3, 4.4

Nullable field vs required field

Use Nullable field when ___. Use required field when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Nullable / optional: the source may not contain the value. The model returns null instead of inventing one.
  • Required: the value is always present in every source document.
  • Deciding phrase: "fabricated", "invented a value", "not in every document".
  • Distractor: A "never guess" prompt line alone; making the field required to "force completeness".
  • Drill: 4.3

Retry with error feedback vs futile retry

Which failures can a retry fix, and which can it never fix? Retry with error feedback vs stop retrying.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Retry with feedback: the failure is format or structure. Send the original document, the failed extraction and the specific error.
  • Do not retry: the information is absent from the source. Route to human review or mark unclear.
  • Deciding phrase: "information is in a document that wasn't provided" versus "misplaced field".
  • Distractor: Retrying with the same prompt and no error; retrying to "find" data that does not exist.
  • Drill: 4.4

Sync API vs Batch API

Use Sync API when ___. Use Batch API when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Synchronous: someone waits (pre-merge check, interactive).
  • Batch: latency-tolerant (overnight, weekly). 50% cheaper, up to 24 h, no SLA, no multi-turn tool calling; custom_id matches results and drives resubmission of failures.
  • Deciding phrase: "blocking", "developers wait" versus "overnight", "next morning".
  • Distractor: Batching both workflows because "often faster"; a timeout fallback; claiming results cannot be correlated (custom_id does it).
  • Drill: 4.5

Same-session self-review vs independent instance

Who should review generated code: the same session or an independent instance? Why does the other fail?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Self-review (same session): retains the generator's reasoning, so it is biased toward its own output.
  • Independent instance: fresh context reviews the work; beats self-review and extended thinking. Use per-file passes plus an integration pass for large PRs.
  • Deciding phrase: "the same session that generated it", "missed its own bug".
  • Distractor: A "review your work" instruction; extended thinking; a bigger context window.
  • Drill: 4.6, 3.6

Domain 5: Context Management and Reliability

Summarized history vs persistent case-facts block

Use Summarized history when ___. Use persistent case-facts block when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Case-facts block: numbers, dates, IDs and stated expectations that must survive; keep outside the summarized history and include in every prompt.
  • Summarized history: the conversational narrative, which can be compressed.
  • Deciding phrase: "customer's refund amount drifted", "details lost after summarization".
  • Distractor: A larger context window; summarizing more often.
  • Drill: 5.1

The three valid escalation triggers vs sentiment or confidence

Escalate on the three valid triggers or on sentiment / self-reported confidence? Name the triggers and why the other fails.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Valid: customer asks for a human (escalate immediately), policy gap or exception, no meaningful progress.
  • Invalid: sentiment analysis, self-reported confidence, apparent complexity.
  • Not an escalation: several matches means ask for another identifier, do not guess. Frustration with a simple issue means acknowledge and offer resolution; escalate only if the customer reiterates.
  • Deciding phrase: e.g. "frustrated", "agent is 40% confident" (illustrations) versus "asks for a human", "policy is silent".
  • Distractor: A sentiment classifier or a confidence threshold ("poorly calibrated", "solves a different problem"). Explicit criteria plus few-shot is the fix.
  • Drill: 5.2

Self-reported confidence for escalation vs calibrated confidence for review routing

Use Self-reported confidence for escalation when ___. Use calibrated confidence for review routing when ___.

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Invalid: the agent grades itself and escalates automatically below a threshold.
  • Valid: field-level confidence, calibrated on a labeled validation set, prioritizing limited human reviewers.
  • Deciding phrase: "calibrated against labeled data", "prioritize human review" (4.6: the model self-reports confidence per finding to enable calibrated review routing).
  • Distractor: Rejecting every confidence score, or accepting an uncalibrated one for autonomous escalation.
  • Drill: 5.2, 5.5, 4.6

Aggregate vs segmented accuracy

Before reducing human review, which accuracy view do you trust: aggregate or segmented? What does the other hide?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Aggregate: hides segment failures (97% overall, poor on one document type).
  • Segmented / stratified sampling: measure by document type and field, sample high-confidence extractions too, before reducing human review.
  • Deciding phrase: "97% overall", "before automating", "reduce review".
  • Distractor: Cutting review because overall accuracy is high; sampling only low-confidence items.
  • Drill: 5.5

Annotate conflict vs resolve it

Two credible sources report different figures. Annotate both or pick one? Who decides how to reconcile?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Annotate: two credible sources disagree. Report both with attribution and dates, in separate sections for established and contested findings.
  • Pick one arbitrarily: wrong. If reconciliation is needed, the coordinator decides it after the subagent returns both values annotated, before synthesis.
  • Deciding phrase: "sources report different figures"; different publication dates (not a real conflict).
  • Distractor: Silently choosing the more recent or more authoritative one; dropping claim-source mappings during synthesis.
  • Drill: 5.6

Structured error report vs generic status or swallowed failure

A subagent times out. What should reach the coordinator: a structured error report, a generic status, an empty success, or an abort? Why do the other three fail?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Structured report: failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives. The coordinator then decides.
  • Generic status / empty success / terminate all: hides the cause, suppresses recovery, or abandons good partial work.
  • Deciding phrase: "enables intelligent recovery".
  • Distractor: "Search unavailable" alone, returning empty as success, or ending the entire workflow.
  • Drill: 5.3, 2.2 · sample Q8

Across domains

Proportionate first fix vs added infrastructure

A stem asks for the "most effective first step". When is the cheap fix right, and when is the heavier fix (a gate) right? What makes a classifier, trained model or bigger context window over-engineered?

Deciding phrase in the stem: ___

Check
  • Cheap fix: rewrite the description, add explicit criteria, split the pass, add the nullable field.
  • Added infrastructure: only when the cheap fix has been tried and the failure is a real guarantee gap.
  • Exception: when the stem requires a guarantee (Q1: financial consequences), the heavier programmatic fix is correct.
  • Deciding phrase: e.g. "most effective first step" (Q2 stem), "proportionate first response".
  • Distractor: Routing classifier, trained model, labeled data pipeline, bigger model, bigger context window.
  • Drill: any task; Q1-Q3 sample questions

How the exam words its verdicts

Phrases from the official sample questions and explanations (guide §9). For each, write what it signals about the option, then open Check.

  • "probabilistic LLM compliance": ___
  • "addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering": ___
  • "over-engineered": ___
  • "most effective first step": ___
  • "is a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a first step warrants": ___
  • "poorly calibrated": ___
  • "solves a different problem entirely": ___
  • "proportionate first response": ___
  • "relies on inference rather than explicit matching": ___
  • "directory-bound": ___
  • "doesn't exist" / "non-existent features": ___
  • "incorrectly blame downstream agents that are working correctly": ___
  • "hides valuable context" / "suppresses the error" / "terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily": ___
  • "least privilege" / "over-provisions" / "separation of concerns": ___
  • "attention dilution": ___
  • "shifts burden to developers without improving the system": ___
  • "adds unnecessary complexity": ___
  • "complexity is already stated in the requirements": ___
  • "misconception": ___
Check
  • "probabilistic LLM compliance": A prompt or few-shot fix offered where a guarantee is needed. Wrong when the cost is financial or compliance.
  • "addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering": The option fixes a different problem than the one stated. Wrong. Check which failure the stem describes.
  • "over-engineered": Classifier, trained model or labeled-data pipeline before the cheap fix was tried. Wrong.
  • "most effective first step" (Q2 stem): Pick the lowest-effort fix at the root cause (descriptions, criteria), not the larger valid design.
  • "is a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a first step warrants": A valid design, but not the answer to a "first step" question.
  • "poorly calibrated": Self-reported confidence as an autonomous trigger. Wrong.
  • "solves a different problem entirely": Sentiment (or similar) does not track the underlying issue. Wrong.
  • "proportionate first response": Prompt-level fix before infrastructure. Right.
  • "relies on inference rather than explicit matching": Unreliable. Deterministic path-glob matching is the answer where files match by type.
  • "directory-bound": Subdirectory CLAUDE.md cannot cover files spread across directories.
  • "doesn't exist" / "non-existent features": Fictional flag or file (CLAUDE_HEADLESS, --batch, .claude/config.json). Wrong.
  • "incorrectly blame downstream agents that are working correctly": The fault is the coordinator's decomposition.
  • "hides valuable context" / "suppresses the error" / "terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily": Generic status, empty success, abort-all. Wrong; structured error context is right.
  • "least privilege" / "over-provisions" / "separation of concerns": Give an agent only the tools its role needs, not all tools.
  • "attention dilution": Split into per-file passes plus an integration pass; a bigger window does not fix it.
  • "shifts burden to developers without improving the system": Pushing the work onto humans is wrong.
  • "adds unnecessary complexity": Match each workload to its API instead of building a hybrid.
  • "complexity is already stated in the requirements": Plan mode now, not later.
  • "misconception": The option states something false (batch results cannot be correlated: custom_id does it).

Quick Reference — final-hour review

One page to read on the morning of the exam.

Exam mechanics

60 items · 120 min (2 min/item) · 4 of 6 scenarios · pass 720/1000 scaled · multiple-choice and multiple-response. Read how many to select.

D1 27% · D2 18% · D3 20% · D4 20% · D5 15%.

Five rules that answer most questions

  1. When a mistake has real consequences, enforce the rule in code. Money, compliance, security, identity checks, required order of steps → prerequisite gate or hook. Not a system prompt instruction, not few-shot examples.
  2. Otherwise, pick the smallest fix that addresses the root cause. The exam guide's answers reject "over-engineered" options (routing classifiers, trained models, extra infrastructure) when rewriting a description or writing explicit criteria would work.
  3. Fix the root cause, not the symptom. If every downstream component works, the problem is upstream. If tool descriptions are thin, fix the descriptions rather than adding examples.
  4. Anything that must survive a handoff goes in structured fields. Sources, error details, case facts and escalation summaries should be fields, not prose the next step has to interpret.
  5. A bigger model or a bigger context window is almost never the answer.

Phrases in the question that decide the answer

Phrase Points to
"must never", "always before", "guaranteed" Programmatic enforcement (gate / hook)
"most effective first step" Lowest-effort root-cause fix
"developers wait for the result", "blocking", "pre-merge" Synchronous API, not batch
"overnight", "weekly", "nightly" Batch API
"spread throughout the codebase", "regardless of location" .claude/rules/ glob
"available to every developer on clone" .claude/commands/ (project)
"multiple valid approaches", "architectural" Plan mode
"single-file", "clear stack trace" Direct execution
"the same session that generated it" Independent review instance
"inconsistent depth", "contradictory across files" Per-file passes + integration pass
"customer asks for a human" Escalate immediately
"policy is silent on" Escalate: policy gap
"multiple matches returned" Ask for another identifier
"values don't sum", "wrong field" Semantic validation, not a stricter schema
"model fabricated a value" Make the field nullable/optional
"information isn't in the document" Retry won't help; send to human review
"job hangs waiting for input" -p
"verbose output pollutes the conversation" context: fork / Explore subagent

Fixed facts

stop_reason: "tool_use" → continue the loop · "end_turn" → stop. On the exam, nothing else ends a loop. (Current API also has max_tokens, stop_sequence, pause_turn, refusal and model_context_window_exceeded; not tested.)

Spawning subagents: the Task tool; allowedTools must include "Task"; parallel = multiple Task calls in one response; subagents inherit nothing. (The current SDK calls it the Agent tool, with Task kept as an alias; the exam says Task.)

tool_choice: "auto" may return text · "any" must call some tool · {"type":"tool","name":"x"} forces one. (Current API also has {"type":"none"}, forcing a text-only reply; not tested. Forced any/tool returns 400 on the newest models and with manual extended thinking.)

Error categories: transient · validation · business · permission. Transient is the retryable one; business violations carry retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation. Payload: errorCategory, isRetryable, human-readable description. MCP flag is isError.

Empty result ≠ error. Timeout = error. Zero matches = success.

Tool count: ~4–5 per agent; 18 degrades selection.

Batch API: 50% off · ≤24h · no SLA · no multi-turn tool calling · custom_id correlates and drives selective resubmission.

CI flags: -p / --print · --output-format json · --json-schema. (CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch don't exist.)

File and directory map

~/.claude/CLAUDE.md          user-level, NOT shared
~/.claude/commands/          personal slash commands
~/.claude/skills/            personal skills (rename to avoid clashing)
~/.claude.json               user-scope MCP servers (personal/experimental)

CLAUDE.md  or  .claude/CLAUDE.md    project-level, committed
<subdir>/CLAUDE.md                  directory-scoped conventions
.claude/rules/*.md                  topic files; YAML `paths:` globs for conditional loading
.claude/commands/*.md               team slash commands, version-controlled
.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md      team skills
.mcp.json                           project-scope MCP servers, ${ENV_VAR} for secrets

SKILL.md frontmatter tested: context: fork · allowed-tools · argument-hint. Commands used: /memory (check which memory files are loaded; exam answer. Current product uses /context for this) · /compact · --resume <session-name> (named sessions exist now via --name/-n or /rename; SDK resume takes an ID) · fork_session.

Current product (not tested): there is also a managed (enterprise) policy CLAUDE.md, a gitignored project-root CLAUDE.local.md (personal, one project only), and a third MCP scope, local (one project, private, not in git).

Built-in tools

Read · Write · Edit · Bash · Grep · Glob. Task 2.5 names all six.

Grep = search file contents. Glob = match file paths/names. Read/Write = whole file. Edit = targeted, needs unique anchor text → on failure fall back to Read + Write. Bash exists, but don't shell out where a dedicated tool does the job. Exploration order: Grep for entry points → Read to follow imports. Don't read everything up front.

Confidence scores: when they are valid

Use Verdict
Agent reports its own confidence and escalates automatically below a threshold Wrong (5.2): poorly calibrated, often confidently wrong on hard cases
Field-level confidence, calibrated against a labeled validation set, used to prioritize limited human reviewers Right (5.5, 4.6)

Few-shot vs explicit criteria vs enforcement

The problem is… The fix is…
The rule doesn't exist or is vague Explicit criteria
The rule exists but ambiguous cases go wrong 2–4 few-shot examples with reasoning
The rule exists, is clear, and must never be violated Programmatic gate or hook

Escalation triggers

Valid: customer asks for a human (escalate immediately, no investigation first) · policy exception or gap · no meaningful progress

Invalid: sentiment analysis · self-reported confidence · "the case seems complex" · turn count

Provenance checklist for multi-source synthesis

Structured claim-to-source mappings (URL, document name, excerpt) kept at every step · publication or collection dates required · conflicts reported with both sources, never silently resolved · separate report sections for well-established and contested findings · coverage annotations for gaps · each content type in a suitable form (tables for financial data, prose for news, lists for technical findings).

Answer-selection procedure (community-derived heuristic)

  1. Find the qualifier in the stem (first, most, must never, least effort).
  2. Label the failure mode (ambiguity, missing rule, ordering, stale context, silent failure).
  3. Fix the earliest controllable layer: description, example, schema, validation, context, boundary.
  4. Compliance, money or ordering: a deterministic gate beats a prompt.
  5. Prefer the option that preserves information and removes the least context.
  6. Eliminate options that rely on the Off the table list below or on fabricated flags and features.

Off the table

Fine-tuning and training custom models · Claude API auth, billing, account management · language- and framework-specific implementation detail · deploying or hosting MCP servers (infrastructure, networking, containers) · Claude's internal architecture and weights · Constitutional AI / RLHF · embedding models and vector DBs · computer use · vision · streaming / SSE · rate limits, quotas, pricing calculations · OAuth and key rotation · cloud provider config · performance benchmarking · prompt caching beyond knowing it exists · tokenization.

An option that depends on one of these is very likely a distractor.

Exam Day

Night before

  • No new material. Skim your error log, the confident-wrong list and the Quick Reference, then stop by early evening.
  • Eat a normal dinner, skip alcohol and keep your caffeine routine unchanged.
  • Bed on time for 7–8 h of sleep. If you can't sleep, rest anyway: one short night hurts less than a night of worry about it (Newbury et al. 2021).
  • Set out ID, water, and (online) clear the room.

Morning

  • Usual breakfast and usual caffeine only. Light movement.
  • 2 minutes of slow breathing before you start.
  • Arrive or log in early (30 min of buffer).

Logistics checklist:

  • [ ] ID name matches your registration exactly.
  • [ ] Pearson VUE system test done (online delivery).
  • [ ] Room and desk clear; route or login planned.
  • [ ] Cancel or reschedule needs 48 h notice (the PDF says 24 h; the live FAQ says 48 h).
  • [ ] Plan for ~135 min in the chair: 120 testing plus check-in, instructions and survey. The score shows on screen at the end.

Pacing

Measure Target
Per item ~2 min
Per 15-item scenario block ~23 min (about 2 min reading the scenario, then ~1.4 min per item)
Soft cap per item 2.5 min, then pick your best answer and move on
Review ~20 min at the end, if navigation allows

Neither exam guide says whether you can go back to earlier items or flag them. Read the tutorial's navigation instructions before item 1.

  • Can go back: four blocks of ~23 min, then ~20 min review (flagged items first, then select-N items), then confirm every item has an answer.
  • Can't go back: fold the review time into each block. Spend it on the close calls as you go.

The platform requiring an answer before moving on (a v0.2 draft note, see the exam overview) only rules out blank answers; it says nothing about going back.

Reading routine

For every item:

  1. Read the instruction line: how many to select.
  2. Read the stem and find the deciding phrase before looking at the options.
  3. Predict the answer, then match it to an option.

Deciding phrases: must never · before any · every time · available to every developer · developers wait for · regardless of directory · the same session · first step · most effective.

Elimination rules

Eliminate by rule, not by how plausible an option sounds.

  • Remove any option that meets a must always requirement with a prompt instruction.
  • Remove any option that adds infrastructure (classifier, trained model, routing layer, bigger model, bigger context window) when a description, criterion or schema field would do.
  • Remove any option that pushes work onto a human or the customer when the system should handle it.

When two options both look right, pick the one that fixes the root cause described in the question. The exam guide's explanations often reject fixes that help but address a different problem.

Select-N items

  • No research exists on strategy for these. Treat each as all-or-nothing.
  • Pick exactly N. Fewer or more loses the item.
  • Judge each option on its own against the stem. Don't pick by pairing.

Changing answers

  • Change an answer only for a reason you can state (a missed phrase, a recalled fact).
  • Don't change on unease alone. Changes are more often wrong-to-right than the reverse (Kruger et al. 2005; USMLE Step 2 CK, N = 27,830).
  • Answer every item. There is no stated penalty for guessing.

Nerves

  • Reappraise arousal as readiness. Tell yourself that a racing heart means your body is preparing.
  • 30–60 s of slow breathing (about 5–6 breaths per minute) if panic hits.
  • The effects are small, but both cost nothing.
  • The scale is criterion-referenced, so a hard item tells you nothing about your score and you can't count misses.

From candidate reports

Community reports, not official.

  • Stems are dense, with a key qualifier buried inside. One word often decides the answer.
  • Pacing is tight at ~2 min per item. A first pass at ~90 seconds, flag and return, works if navigation allows.
  • CI/git with Claude Code (3.6) was heavier than many expected.
  • High practice scores did not guarantee a pass.

Preface — from using Claude Code to building with Claude

You already use Claude Code daily: CLAUDE.md, plan mode, slash commands, MCP servers. Many of the exam's judgement questions can be answered from that experience.

What you haven't done is build the thing. You haven't sent a Messages API request, written the while loop that turns a stateless call into an agent, authored an MCP server, or designed a schema that stops a model fabricating values. The exam assumes that work and asks about stop_reason, tool_result, AgentDefinition, and tool_choice, the machinery the product hides from you.

You have already operated most of the architectures the exam tests, from the outside, so the work is attaching each exam term to behaviour you have seen.

What you already know, and what it is called here

What you do in Claude Code What the exam calls it Chapter
Press enter, watch it grep, read, edit, run tests The agentic loop, driven by stop_reason 2
The tool output indented in your transcript tool_result blocks in a user message 2
A Bash command fails and Claude adapts is_error: true on a tool result (the failure comes back as readable content, not an exception) 4
Your CLAUDE.md The system parameter, and a three-level configuration hierarchy 2, 9
Approving or denying a permission prompt A human-in-the-loop gate between the model asking and your code executing; PreToolUse interception 2, 6
Installing an MCP server from a config file Tool definitions crossing the API boundary; .mcp.json project scope vs ~/.claude.json user scope 3, 8
Claude reaching for the wrong one of two similar tools Tool descriptions as the primary selection mechanism 3
Claude spawning subagents on its own Orchestrator-workers; the Task tool and AgentDefinition; isolated subagent context 1, 5
A subagent that cannot see your main conversation Subagents inherit nothing not written into their prompt 5, 14
Running /compact and watching context shrink The messages array being rewritten; what survives summarization 2, 14
Plan mode A programmatic gate between steps of a chain 1, 10
.claude/commands/ and .claude/skills/ Project vs user scope; SKILL.md frontmatter 10
--resume on yesterday's session Session state, and tool results that were true when fetched 7
The Explore subagent Context isolation for verbose discovery 10, 14
claude -p in a shell script Headless invocation for CI 11

The four things you have never done

  1. Written the loop. Start with Chapter 2, and do its exercises as well as reading it. Writing the loop yourself, about forty lines, turns half of Domain 1 from reasoning into recognition.
  2. Authored a tool. A tool description is a prompt competing for the model's attention, not documentation (Chapter 3). In Chapter 8 you write an MCP server as well as use one.
  3. Designed for structured output. tool_use with a JSON schema eliminates malformed JSON and does nothing about line items that don't sum (Chapter 13).
  4. Made behaviour reliable at volume. Chapter 12 covers explicit categorical criteria, few-shot examples that show reasoning, and why "be more conservative" never fixes precision.

How the book is arranged

The book has fifteen chapters, and each of the 30 task statements has exactly one home chapter.

  • 1–8 build the agent: patterns, loop, tools, errors, orchestration, hooks, sessions, MCP.
  • 9–11 cover Claude Code configuration. You'll move fastest here, because you already have the concepts and only need the vocabulary and exact paths.
  • 12–15 cover prompting, structured output, context, and Domain 5's reliability judgements.

If you are short on time, read Chapter 2 in full, read Chapter 6 for the rule behind tasks 1.4 and 1.5, and skim Chapters 9–11 for the configuration details.

Each chapter ends with What the exam tests (task statements and judgement calls) and Exercises.

Where the exam guide and the product disagree

The guide dates from July 2026, and Claude Code has moved since. Seven points no longer match current docs:

  • Wrong semantics (3): allowedTools gating subagent delegation; allowed-tools restricting a skill's tools; Read + Write as the fallback when Edit hits a non-unique match.
  • Overtaken (3): Task renamed to Agent; /memory reporting what's loaded; MCP having two scopes rather than three.
  • Cosmetic (1).

On these points your instincts will be right about the product and wrong for the exam, so answer the guide's version. Chapters keep the guide's answer in the main text and add a marked note on current reality. The full list with sources is in REVIEW-FINDINGS.md at the repo root. Read it once before the exam.

Six of the seven concern Claude Code and Agent SDK configuration, and Domains 4 and 5 are almost unaffected.

A note on the code

Substantive examples come in Python then TypeScript, using the exam scenarios' tool names (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human, extract_invoice). Four of the six scenarios appear on your form, and the same mechanism recurs across them in different settings. A deterministic gate on a refund is the same idea as a gate in a CI pipeline, and the exam can test it in whichever setting you know less well.

Examples use claude-sonnet-5, a still-available model that accepts forced tool_choice. The newest models (Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1) reject forced tool_choice with a 400, which the exam does not test.

Chapter 1 — Agents, workflows, and knowing which one you need

A support agent refunds the wrong account because identity verification was requested in a prompt rather than enforced in code. A 14-file review contradicts itself because one call was asked to do 14 jobs. The central question is how much of the control flow belongs in your code and how much is left to the model's judgement. Too little structure gives you non-determinism where you needed guarantees. Too much gives you a brittle, expensive state machine.

Claude Code is itself an agent built from the primitives this chapter covers: a loop, tools, a system prompt, and gates. The vocabulary comes from Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (workflow vs agent, the pattern catalogue) and the Agent SDK work (the loop).

The augmented LLM

The building block is the augmented LLM: a model plus tools, retrieval, and memory.

Underneath it is the Messages API, a single stateless call. It takes a system prompt, alternating user and assistant messages, and optional tool definitions, and returns one assistant message. It has no memory, cannot run anything, and cannot read files. Everything Claude Code does beyond that (reading the repo, editing, running tests, remembering earlier steps) is scaffolding built around this call.

Each augmentation is a design decision:

  • Tools set what the model can do, and their descriptions steer what it will do. A description is a prompt (Chapter 3). When Claude Code picks the wrong MCP tool, the description is at fault.
  • Retrieval sets what the model knows when it acts: pre-fetched (CLAUDE.md, injected up front) or fetched on demand (the file Claude opens on turn six).
  • Memory sets what survives between turns and sessions. Subagents inherit nothing except their prompt, which is why a Claude Code subagent can't see your main thread.

For each exam scenario, ask which augmentation matters most. The support agent's refund depends on memory of a verified customer ID. The research system's hard problem is what the coordinator carries between subagents. Extraction barely needs tools, and its success depends on schema design.

Workflows and agents

Exam options are written against Anthropic's exact definitions:

  • Workflow: LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths. You write the sequence, and the model fills in the steps.
  • Agent: the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool usage. You give it a goal and tools, and it decides each next step from what it just learned.
  • Agentic systems: the umbrella term for both. It does not imply autonomy.

In Claude Code, a bare request is an agent, since nobody told it to grep, read three files, edit, then test. A slash command whose body lists the steps in order is a workflow. The model and tools are the same in both, and only the location of the control flow differs.

The distinction is architectural. Task statement 1.1 tests it as model-driven decision-making versus pre-configured decision trees or fixed tool sequences. Neither is the default answer.

The agentic loop

Anthropic describes the loop as gather context → take action → verify work → repeat.

  • Gather: fetch what's needed rather than being handed everything, e.g. grep/tail on a log instead of reading all of it.
  • Act: call a tool that changes something.
  • Verify: check the result against the goal.

Verification is skipped because in most domains it is expensive or impossible to automate. Nothing cheaply tells you whether a summary is good or a report has gaps. The loop decays into gather-act-gather-act, and errors compound unnoticed.

Coding became the first strong agent domain because it has free, fast, deterministic verifiers: compiler, type checker, tests. Outside coding, ask what is my test suite? It might be a JSON Schema validator (Chapter 13), or a second model call with a rubric (evaluator-optimizer, below). If no verifier exists, keep the design a workflow with human review rather than an autonomous agent.

Mechanically, the loop is a while you write. The API is stateless, so you own the message list, resending it every iteration. Each response's stop_reason says whether Claude is done or wants a tool run. Termination is a protocol signal, not a judgement call. Chapter 2 builds the loop.

The five workflow patterns

Pattern Shape Choose it when
Prompt chaining Fixed sequence of calls with programmatic gates between steps Subtasks are fixed and known in advance; you trade latency for per-step accuracy
Routing Classify input, send to a specialised prompt/model/toolset Inputs fall into distinct categories and misrouting is rare and recoverable
Parallelization Concurrent calls, aggregated Subtasks are independent (sectioning), or you want confidence from repeats (voting)
Orchestrator-workers A central model decomposes at runtime, delegates, synthesises Subtasks depend on what the input contains
Evaluator-optimizer Generator + critic in a loop until a bar is met Clear evaluation criteria exist and iteration measurably improves output
Autonomous agent Goal + tools + loop Step count is unpredictable, the flow can't be drawn in advance, and the environment gives actionable feedback

Details by pattern:

  • Chaining: the gates matter most. Without them you have a long prompt split across calls, and with them a malformed extraction is caught at step 2 instead of step 5. Plan mode is a gate, because nothing executes until the plan clears a check. The blueprint's example is per-file review passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass.
  • Parallelization has two forms. Sectioning runs independent subtasks at once, e.g. one instance answers while another screens for policy violations. Voting runs the same task several times to raise recall. A common mistake is requiring 2-of-3 agreement, which suppresses real findings rather than filtering false ones.
  • Parallelization vs orchestrator-workers: ask whether you can write the subtask list before seeing the input. If you can, it's parallelization and the split belongs in code. If you can't, it's orchestrator-workers and a model must decompose. When Claude Code decides for itself to spawn subagents, that is orchestrator-workers.
  • Orchestrator-workers fail at the decomposition step, not in the workers. Chapter 5 covers it.
  • Evaluator-optimizer loops uselessly when no reliable criterion exists, because the critic can't tell good from bad.
  • Autonomous agents trade cost and latency for adaptability, so they need guardrails: sandboxing, checkpoints, human review at consequential boundaries.

Choosing

Ask in order:

  1. Can you draw the decision tree? If it's finite on a whiteboard, build the workflow. Readable code is cheaper to debug than a reasoning trace and doesn't vary between runs.
  2. Are the subtasks predictable? That is, can you enumerate them before seeing the input? This settles parallelization vs orchestrator-workers, and fixed pipeline vs dynamic decomposition.
  3. Is the task worth the tokens? An agent resends its growing history every iteration, so cost grows super-linearly with steps, and subagents multiply it. The exam tests no exact multiplier, only that more steps and more agents cost more.
  4. What does an error cost, and would you notice? Cost and discoverability are separate axes. A wrong refund is expensive and visible, while a silent coverage gap is cheap per incident and invisible. Low discoverability argues for structure and explicit verification even when errors look cheap.

The overriding rule is to pick the simplest solution that works and add complexity only when it demonstrably helps. Often a single well-specified call with good examples beats any agentic design.

Task statement 1.6

Task 1.6 (design task decomposition strategies) comes down to one choice, between a fixed sequential pipeline (prompt chaining) and dynamic adaptive decomposition based on intermediate findings.

Prompt chaining Dynamic decomposition
Subtasks known before you start Yes No
Who decomposes Your code The model, at runtime
Blueprint's example Per-file review passes plus a cross-file integration pass "Add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase"
Cost of getting it wrong Rigid: unanticipated input falls through Coverage gaps from a narrow initial split
Failure to look for Missing gates between steps Orchestrator's decomposition, not the workers

The legacy-tests example shows what "adaptive" means. You map the structure, identify high-impact areas from that map, then build a prioritised plan that keeps adapting as dependencies come to light. The plan can't be written up front because it depends on the codebase.

The same task, two ways

The example task is triaging a support ticket. The workflow fixes the path: classify, fetch the records the class implies, draft. Each helper is one Messages API call, and the control flow between them is your code.

Python

async def triage_workflow(ticket: str) -> Resolution:
    # Step 1 — classify. Forced tool call guarantees structured output.
    category = await classify_ticket(ticket)  # "billing" | "shipping" | "account"

    # Programmatic gate: unroutable tickets never reach the drafting step.
    if category.confidence < 0.7:
        return escalate_to_human(ticket, reason="low_confidence_classification")

    # Step 2 — predetermined context fetch per category.
    if category.name == "billing":
        context = await get_customer(category.customer_id)
    elif category.name == "shipping":
        context = await lookup_order(category.order_id)
    else:
        context = await get_customer(category.customer_id)

    # Step 3 — draft against fetched context only.
    return await draft_resolution(ticket, context)

TypeScript

async function triageWorkflow(ticket: string): Promise<Resolution> {
  const category = await classifyTicket(ticket);

  if (category.confidence < 0.7) {
    return escalateToHuman(ticket, "low_confidence_classification");
  }

  const context =
    category.name === "shipping"
      ? await lookupOrder(category.orderId)
      : await getCustomer(category.customerId);

  return draftResolution(ticket, context);
}

The agent version gives a goal and constraints, then loops on stop_reason. The message list is the conversation, SYSTEM is the system prompt, and TRIAGE_TOOLS stands for tool definitions (name, description, input_schema), which is what a .mcp.json entry becomes at the API boundary. Chapter 2 shows their real shape.

Python

TRIAGE_TOOLS = [get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human]

SYSTEM = """Resolve the customer's ticket. Verify the customer's identity with
get_customer before any financial operation. Escalate when the request falls
outside documented policy or the customer asks for a human."""

async def triage_agent(ticket: str) -> Resolution:
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": ticket}]

    while True:
        response = await client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-5",
            system=SYSTEM,
            tools=TRIAGE_TOOLS,
            messages=messages,
            max_tokens=2048,
        )
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        if response.stop_reason == "end_turn":
            return Resolution.from_content(response.content)

        results = [await execute_tool(block) for block in response.content
                   if block.type == "tool_use"]
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

TypeScript

async function triageAgent(ticket: string): Promise<Resolution> {
  const messages: MessageParam[] = [{ role: "user", content: ticket }];

  for (;;) {
    const response = await client.messages.create({
      model: "claude-sonnet-5",
      system: SYSTEM,
      tools: TRIAGE_TOOLS,
      messages,
      max_tokens: 2048,
    });
    messages.push({ role: "assistant", content: response.content });

    if (response.stop_reason === "end_turn") {
      return resolutionFrom(response.content);
    }

    const toolResults = await Promise.all(
      response.content
        .filter((b): b is ToolUseBlock => b.type === "tool_use")
        .map(executeTool),
    );
    messages.push({ role: "user", content: toolResults });
  }
}

The tools and model are unchanged, and only the decomposition has moved from if statements into the model. This version handles a ticket that is both a billing dispute and a shipping complaint, which the workflow can't express without a new branch. The cost is non-deterministic ordering, so the identity-verification rule in the prompt is not sufficient. Prompts have a non-zero failure rate, just as CLAUDE.md instructions are usually but not always followed. A rule with financial consequences needs a programmatic prerequisite gate or an interception hook (Chapter 6).

In production the answer is usually a composite: an agent loop for the investigative middle, with hard gates around operations that must not go wrong. Patterns compose (routing feeds a chain; an orchestrator wraps evaluator-optimizer workers).

What the exam tests

  • Task 1.6: choose fixed pipeline or dynamic decomposition and justify it from the scenario's predictability. The two blueprint cases are per-file plus cross-file passes for a large PR (the stated cause is attention dilution), and map-then-prioritise for legacy-code tests (the plan can't exist until the structure is known).
  • Task 1.1: model-driven decisions versus pre-configured tool sequences.
  • Task 1.2: a coverage gap with healthy subagents is fixed in the decomposition (Chapter 5).
  • Distractors are competent engineering at the wrong layer: a bigger context window for an attention problem, a consensus rule that suppresses real findings, an extra agent where a gate would do.
  • Scoring rule: proportionality. Name the described failure and pick the least complex fix. When two options both work, the simpler one is correct.

Exercises

  1. Build both triage versions against four mock MCP tools. Run 20 tickets (10 single-concern, 10 with two concerns), logging tokens and tool calls per ticket, and find the ticket the workflow mishandles. Do this one first, because writing 40 lines of tool-use loop by hand teaches more than reading.
  2. For the 14-file review, implement one call over all files, then per-file passes plus an integration pass. Feed both a PR with one planted cross-file bug and three single-file bugs, and record what each catches.
  3. Write an orchestrator's decomposition step for "research the impact of AI on creative industries" and inspect the subtasks before any worker runs. If they're all visual arts, rewrite the coordinator prompt to specify coverage criteria rather than procedure. Claude Code hides this step from you.
  4. For one exam scenario, write its verifier in one sentence. If you can't, write what would have to be true for one to exist, and decide whether it should be an agent at all.

Chapter 2 — The agentic loop in code

The loop that drives an agent like Claude Code fits in about forty lines. The backtracking and recovery you see in Claude Code come from Claude deciding each next step by reasoning over the conversation history. The loop only ferries messages and checks one field. This chapter builds that loop by hand (task statement 1.1) against the customer-support scenario: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human.

The Messages API, from zero

One endpoint, POST /v1/messages. The request fields that matter:

Field What it is
model Model identifier.
max_tokens Ceiling on reply length.
system Persistent instructions (role, policy, tone). Separate from messages because it is not part of the conversation.
messages The conversation, oldest first. Each entry has role ("user" / "assistant") and content.
tools Tool definitions: name, natural-language description, input_schema (JSON Schema).

content can be a plain string, but its real form is a list of typed blocks:

  • text: prose.
  • image: an image.
  • tool_use (assistant messages only): Claude asking you to run something.
  • tool_result (user messages only): you handing back what happened.

One message can mix several block types, so a loop has to handle them all.

The response is an assistant message: role: "assistant", a content list of blocks, and a stop_reason saying why generation ended. Because it is already shaped like a message, you append it straight onto messages.

tools declares tools without installing anything. Nothing runs on Anthropic's side: Claude emits a tool_use block and stops, you run the function, and you send the result back. Execution is local, so your code decides whether a tool runs at all.

The API is stateless. There is no session and no server-side memory. Every request re-sends the whole messages array, and the model knows only what is in it. /compact rewrites that array.

One turn of the cycle

  1. Send system, the full messages array, and tools.
  2. Claude replies with an assistant message: text blocks, possibly tool_use blocks, and a stop_reason. The stop_reason, not the content, decides what happens next.
  3. If stop_reason == "tool_use", append the assistant message in full, run every requested tool, append one user message holding all the tool_result blocks, and loop.
  4. If stop_reason == "end_turn", stop. The text blocks are the answer.

The tool output you see indented in a Claude Code transcript is how it renders tool_result blocks. Memorise both shapes:

Field tool_use (assistant) tool_result (user)
type "tool_use" "tool_result"
identifier id, server-generated, e.g. toolu_01A… tool_use_id, which must match the id character for character
payload name (tool name) and input (object matching the schema) content, either a string or a list of text/image blocks
failure signal — is_error: true, optional; the message goes in content

The API enforces three pairing rules and rejects any violation with a 400:

  • Every tool_use must be answered by a tool_result in the immediately following message. Return two results for three calls and the request is rejected.
  • Every tool_result needs a preceding tool_use with that id. This is what breaks when you truncate history to save context and the conversation ends up opening on a tool_result.
  • All results go in one user message, and the tool_result blocks must come first in its content. Any extra text goes after them.

Human-in-the-loop review sits between tool_use and execution, when Claude has asked but nothing has run yet. Approving runs the tool, and denying sends back a tool_result saying so.

The loop, written out

Python

import json
import time
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "get_customer",
        "description": (
            "Retrieve a customer record by email or account ID. Returns the "
            "verified customer_id, tier, and account status. Call this before "
            "any order lookup or refund."
        ),
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"identifier": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["identifier"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "lookup_order",
        "description": "Fetch an order by order_id, including line items, "
                       "ship date, and current refund eligibility.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["order_id"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "process_refund",
        "description": "Issue a refund against a verified customer and order. "
                       "Amount is in USD cents.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "customer_id": {"type": "string"},
                "order_id": {"type": "string"},
                "amount_cents": {"type": "integer"},
                "reason": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["customer_id", "order_id", "amount_cents", "reason"],
        },
    },
    {
        "name": "escalate_to_human",
        "description": "Hand the case to a human agent with a structured "
                       "summary. Use when policy blocks resolution or the "
                       "customer asks for a person.",
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "customer_id": {"type": "string"},
                "root_cause": {"type": "string"},
                "recommended_action": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["customer_id", "root_cause", "recommended_action"],
        },
    },
]

TOOL_IMPLS = {
    "get_customer": get_customer,
    "lookup_order": lookup_order,
    "process_refund": process_refund,
    "escalate_to_human": escalate_to_human,
}


def execute_tool(block):
    """Return a tool_result block for one tool_use block."""
    try:
        result = TOOL_IMPLS[block.name](**block.input)
        return {
            "type": "tool_result",
            "tool_use_id": block.id,
            "content": json.dumps(result),
        }
    except Exception as exc:
        return {
            "type": "tool_result",
            "tool_use_id": block.id,
            "content": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
            "is_error": True,
        }


def run_agent(user_message, max_iterations=25, budget_seconds=120):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]
    deadline = time.monotonic() + budget_seconds

    for iteration in range(max_iterations):
        if time.monotonic() > deadline:
            raise TimeoutError("wall-clock budget exhausted")

        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-5",
            max_tokens=2048,
            system=SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            tools=TOOLS,
            messages=messages,
        )
        log.info("iteration=%d stop_reason=%s", iteration, response.stop_reason)

        # The assistant message goes back verbatim, text blocks and all.
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        if response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
            tool_uses = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
            results = [execute_tool(b) for b in tool_uses]
            messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
            continue

        if response.stop_reason == "end_turn":
            return response

        if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
            raise RuntimeError("response truncated; raise max_tokens")

        raise RuntimeError(f"unhandled stop_reason: {response.stop_reason}")

    raise RuntimeError("iteration cap hit — investigate, do not just raise it")

TypeScript

import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

const client = new Anthropic();

type Impl = (input: any) => Promise<unknown>;
const toolImpls: Record<string, Impl> = {
  get_customer: getCustomer,
  lookup_order: lookupOrder,
  process_refund: processRefund,
  escalate_to_human: escalateToHuman,
};

async function executeTool(
  block: Anthropic.ToolUseBlock,
): Promise<Anthropic.ToolResultBlockParam> {
  try {
    const result = await toolImpls[block.name](block.input);
    return {
      type: "tool_result",
      tool_use_id: block.id,
      content: JSON.stringify(result),
    };
  } catch (err) {
    return {
      type: "tool_result",
      tool_use_id: block.id,
      content: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err),
      is_error: true,
    };
  }
}

export async function runAgent(
  userMessage: string,
  { maxIterations = 25, budgetMs = 120_000 } = {},
): Promise<Anthropic.Message> {
  const messages: Anthropic.MessageParam[] = [
    { role: "user", content: userMessage },
  ];
  const deadline = Date.now() + budgetMs;

  for (let iteration = 0; iteration < maxIterations; iteration++) {
    if (Date.now() > deadline) throw new Error("wall-clock budget exhausted");

    const response = await client.messages.create({
      model: "claude-sonnet-5",
      max_tokens: 2048,
      system: SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
      tools: TOOLS,
      messages,
    });
    log.info({ iteration, stop_reason: response.stop_reason });

    messages.push({ role: "assistant", content: response.content });

    if (response.stop_reason === "tool_use") {
      const toolUses = response.content.filter(
        (b): b is Anthropic.ToolUseBlock => b.type === "tool_use",
      );
      const results = await Promise.all(toolUses.map(executeTool));
      messages.push({ role: "user", content: results });
      continue;
    }

    if (response.stop_reason === "end_turn") return response;
    if (response.stop_reason === "max_tokens") {
      throw new Error("response truncated; raise max_tokens");
    }
    throw new Error(`unhandled stop_reason: ${response.stop_reason}`);
  }

  throw new Error("iteration cap hit — investigate, do not just raise it");
}

The only branch is on stop_reason. The loop never inspects Claude's text, keeps no whitelist of which tool may follow which, and has no workflow state machine. Swap in Read/Bash/Edit/Grep, put a permission gate before execute_tool, and you have the skeleton of Claude Code's loop.

stop_reason is the control signal

Value Meaning What the loop does
"tool_use" The turn ended because Claude wants tools run. At least one tool_use block is present. Execute all of them, append results, iterate.
"end_turn" Claude finished naturally. No tools pending. Terminate; the text blocks are the answer.
"max_tokens" The response hit the max_tokens ceiling mid-generation and was truncated. Treat as an error condition. Any partial tool_use block is unusable, so do not execute it.
"stop_sequence" Hit one of your stop_sequences. A requested stop. Treat like "end_turn".
"model_context_window_exceeded" Claude 4.5+: the context window filled mid-generation. Older models return a validation error instead. The conversation is too big. Trim or compact history; raising max_tokens won't help.

Continue on "tool_use", terminate on "end_turn", and handle unknown values in an explicit else that raises. A loop that falls through treats a new stop reason as completion.

Strict tool use and thinking blocks

  • "strict": true next to a tool's input_schema makes schema-valid arguments guaranteed rather than merely very likely. The only cost is that one field. Chapter 3 covers the JSON Schema subset it supports.
  • Extended thinking: when a tool_use block sits alongside thinking or redacted_thinking blocks, send those thinking blocks back unmodified and in the same position on the next turn. Editing, reordering, or dropping one breaks its signature, and the request fails.

Why history is the agent's memory

Tool results are appended to history so the model can reason about the next action, and this is how the agent accumulates knowledge. In the support case:

  1. get_customer("dana@example.com") → history now holds customer_id: "cus_8812", tier: "enterprise".
