  2. Claude reads that and calls lookup_order → shipped 19 days ago, inside a 30-day window.
  3. Claude calls process_refund with arguments it derived from history. You did not route them.

Ways to break it:

  • Drop the assistant message, keep the results. 400: a tool_result with no tool_use.
  • Keep the assistant message, drop the results. 400. If it somehow got through, Claude would re-request the same tool forever.
  • Summarise the result into your own prose. You have become the decision-maker without meaning to, filtering what the model can reason over.

All three treat history as a log when it is state. The same applies to /compact: whatever it drops, the agent no longer knows. That is why a long session "forgets" a decision from an hour ago.

Model-driven decisions versus decision trees

The exam contrasts Claude choosing the next tool from context with a pre-configured decision tree or fixed sequence. A fixed sequence (always get_customer → lookup_order → branch on amount) assumes every case has the same shape. Real cases don't:

  • Customer gives an order number → no email lookup needed.
  • Three disputed charges → three order lookups.
  • "Just let me talk to someone" → escalate_to_human, nothing else.

The loop above handles all of these with no routing code. You control the envelope: which tools exist, what their schemas allow, and which calls a hook may block (Chapter 6). Claude chooses within it. Plan mode is an example, since it narrows the envelope to read-only tools and Claude still decides everything inside it.

When ordering must be guaranteed, use a programmatic prerequisite gate (task 1.4, e.g. block process_refund until get_customer returns a verified id). Don't hard-code the call order in the loop.

Three anti-patterns the guide names

These three come from task 1.1's skills list.

Parsing natural language for termination

Python

# WRONG
text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
if "let me know if" in text.lower() or "anything else" in text.lower():
    return response

TypeScript

// WRONG
const text = response.content
  .filter((b) => b.type === "text")
  .map((b) => (b as Anthropic.TextBlock).text)
  .join("");
if (/let me know if|anything else/i.test(text)) return response;

This fails both ways. "Let me know if you need anything else" can arrive alongside a pending tool_use, so the loop exits early and the refund never happens. "Your refund of $84.99 has been submitted." matches no phrase, so a finished conversation keeps looping.

An iteration cap as the stopping mechanism

Python

# WRONG
for _ in range(5):
    response = client.messages.create(...)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    tool_uses = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    if not tool_uses:
        break
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [execute_tool(b) for b in tool_uses]})
return response   # after 5 turns, whatever we have

TypeScript

// WRONG
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  response = await client.messages.create({ /* ... */ });
  messages.push({ role: "assistant", content: response.content });
  const toolUses = response.content.filter((b) => b.type === "tool_use");
  if (toolUses.length === 0) break;
  messages.push({
    role: "user",
    content: await Promise.all(toolUses.map(executeTool)),
  });
}
return response; // after 5 turns, whatever we have

A 5-turn finish and a runaway both leave through the same return, and nothing tells them apart. A three-issue billing dispute that needs 8–9 turns is silently cut off. Keep a cap, but exceeding it must raise an error, not return.

Assistant text as a completion indicator

Python

# WRONG
if any(b.type == "text" for b in response.content):
    return response

TypeScript

// WRONG
if (response.content.some((b) => b.type === "text")) return response;

This sounds structural, but a tool_use response often carries text too. It is the sentence of narration you see above every tool call in Claude Code:

{
  "stop_reason": "tool_use",
  "content": [
    { "type": "text",
      "text": "I've confirmed Dana's account. Let me pull up order SO-44120." },
    { "type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01Xy…", "name": "lookup_order",
      "input": { "order_id": "SO-44120" } }
  ]
}

tool_choice and the loop

Value Behaviour Loop impact
{"type": "auto"} (default) Claude decides whether to call a tool. Either stop reason is possible. This is the agentic setting.
{"type": "any"} Claude must call some tool, its choice which. Guarantees "tool_use", so the loop cannot terminate on this turn. Use it to stop the model answering conversationally when an action is required.
{"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"} Claude must call that named tool. Also guarantees "tool_use", with the tool fixed.
{"type": "none"} Claude must not call a tool. Forces a text-only "end_turn".

Forcing applies per turn, not to the whole loop. Force get_customer on iteration one, then go back to auto. If you leave it forced, the loop can never reach "end_turn".

Current product (not tested): on the newest models (Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1), any and tool return a 400; only auto and none work. Use auto plus strict: true tool use, or output_config.format. Manual extended thinking also rejects any/tool, and a forced call skips thinking. Older models (e.g. Sonnet 5, used in these examples) accept forced use.

Parallel tool calls

One assistant turn can hold several tool_use blocks, for example two lookup_order calls for two disputed orders. It is the same as Claude Code firing three Reads at once. Run them concurrently (Promise.all, or asyncio.gather for slow I/O; the Python listing runs them sequentially for clarity) and return every result in one user message.

Claude parallelises only calls it believes are independent, and it can be wrong when one call's input should come from another's output. Safeguards:

  • State prerequisites in descriptions, e.g. "process_refund needs a verified customer_id from get_customer". This nudges the model to sequence the calls itself.
  • Gate the dependent tool programmatically when correctness can't rely on the model. A premature call then gets a structured error it can recover from.
  • disable_parallel_tool_use alongside tool_choice caps a response at one tool call. The cost is latency.

tool_use_id binds each result to its call. Keeping results in order is good hygiene but not required for validity.

Guardrails that are not termination logic

Only stop_reason decides that the task is complete. Separate operational guardrails decide that the loop is no longer allowed to run:

  • Max iterations bounds cost and catches cycles, such as retrying a tool that fails the same way every time. Exceeding it should raise, alert, and keep the transcript. Never return a partial answer as final.
  • Wall-clock budget covers what an iteration count can't. One slow MCP call can take 90 s inside a single iteration.
  • Structured logs record iteration, stop_reason, tool names, and durations, so an incident has a trace to read. Chapter 5 makes the same observability argument for routing subagent traffic through a coordinator.

The same loop, at a higher level

The Claude Agent SDK's query() runs this loop for you and yields typed messages. It is the engine Claude Code runs on.

MCP tool names are namespaced mcp__<server>__<tool>. <server> is the key in your config, not the server's internal name. Server key support plus tool get_customer gives mcp__support__get_customer. The namespacing exists because two servers can both expose search. Rename the config key and every allowlist entry for it breaks, which is the usual cause of a tool that "exists but Claude never calls".

Python

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt=SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    mcp_servers={"support": {"command": "node", "args": ["./support-mcp.js"]}},
    allowed_tools=[
        "mcp__support__get_customer",
        "mcp__support__lookup_order",
        "mcp__support__process_refund",
        "mcp__support__escalate_to_human",
    ],
)

async for message in query(
    prompt="Dana (dana@example.com) says order SO-44120 arrived damaged.",
    options=options,
):
    log.info("%s", message)

TypeScript

import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Dana (dana@example.com) says order SO-44120 arrived damaged.",
  options: {
    systemPrompt: SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    mcpServers: {
      support: { command: "node", args: ["./support-mcp.js"] },
    },
    allowedTools: [
      "mcp__support__get_customer",
      "mcp__support__lookup_order",
      "mcp__support__process_refund",
      "mcp__support__escalate_to_human",
    ],
  },
})) {
  log.info(message);
}

The SDK builds tools from the MCP servers, branches on stop_reason, dispatches each tool_use, and batches the results, all as you did by hand. It also adds permission modes, hooks, and subagents. For your own code:

  • A custom handler that throws kills the loop, and Claude never sees the error. Returning an error result (isError) puts the failure into history, where the agent can react. It is is_error one level up.
  • maxTurns/max_turns defaults to unlimited, so the iteration cap and wall-clock budget are still your job. Retrying failed HTTP requests belongs to the client, not the loop.

What the exam tests

  • Task 1.1, mostly diagnostic: "this loop misbehaves; why?" It has three knowledge bullets: the stop_reason lifecycle, results appended to history, and model-driven decisions versus decision trees.
  • Completion determined by scanning text, hitting an iteration cap, or the presence of prose is wrong. Continue on "tool_use", terminate on "end_turn".
  • Expect an item that turns on a tool_use response that also contains narration text.
  • Task 2.3 tool_choice: "any" guarantees an action instead of chat. A forced named tool pins the first step, then you return to auto.
  • Task 1.4: enforcing order with a gate is a different design from hard-coding the call order in the loop.
  • Streaming, token counting, and rate limits are out of scope.

Exercises

  1. Send one request with no tools and print the raw response: find role, content, the block types, and stop_reason. Add one tool and a prompt that needs it, then diff the two responses.
  2. Implement run_agent from scratch, in your less-used language, against stub tools. Don't look at the listing until it runs, then diff and account for every difference.
  3. Break it four ways and record what happens: omit the assistant message; return one result for two tool_use blocks; change one character of a tool_use_id; set max_tokens to 64. Which give a 400, which give a silent behaviour change, which loop forever?
  4. Add a stdin approval prompt before process_refund. On refusal, return a tool_result saying a human denied it, and watch what Claude does. That is the same mechanism as Claude Code's permission prompt.
  5. Send a message disputing three orders, and log the tool_use blocks per turn. Then set disable_parallel_tool_use and compare iterations and wall-clock time.
  6. Write the smallest conversation that makes the iteration-cap anti-pattern silently return an incomplete resolution. Keep the transcript.

Chapter 3 — Designing tools Claude can choose between

Claude Code's built-in tools are described in detail, which is probably a large part of why it picks between Grep, Glob, and Edit reliably. Write two tools you think are obviously distinct and you may see coin-flip selection between them. The exam's position is that tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection, and minimal descriptions produce unreliable selection among similar tools.

What a tool definition is

A tool definition has three fields: name, description, input_schema (a JSON Schema object). The model sees nothing else. Anything you know about the tool (which database it hits, what ID it needs, overlapping fields) is invisible unless it's in the description.

The description is prompt text. It is injected into context at selection time and read like any other instruction, by a reader who can't see the source. If you treat it as an API contract, you'll write two lines where you needed twenty.

Python

extract_data_points = {
    "name": "extract_data_points",
    "description": (
        "Extract structured numeric and categorical data points from a research "
        "document that has already been loaded. Returns a list of records, each with "
        "a field name, a value, a unit where applicable, and the page and paragraph "
        "the value was read from.\n\n"
        "Input: document_id from load_document, plus the field names to extract.\n"
        "Use this when you need specific values out of a document — revenue figures, "
        "sample sizes, publication dates, dosage tables.\n"
        "Do NOT use this to understand what a document argues; use summarize_content. "
        "Do NOT use this to check whether an external claim is supported; use "
        "verify_claim_against_source.\n"
        "Edge case: if a requested field is absent, the record is returned with a null "
        "value and a reason, rather than being omitted."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "document_id": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Identifier returned by load_document.",
            },
            "field_names": {
                "type": "array",
                "items": {"type": "string"},
                "description": "Field labels to extract, e.g. ['sample_size', 'p_value'].",
            },
        },
        "required": ["document_id", "field_names"],
    },
}

TypeScript

const extractDataPoints: Anthropic.Tool = {
  name: "extract_data_points",
  description: [
    "Extract structured numeric and categorical data points from a research document",
    "that has already been loaded. Returns a list of records, each with a field name, a",
    "value, a unit where applicable, and the page and paragraph the value was read from.",
    "",
    "Input: document_id from load_document, plus the field names to extract.",
    "Use this when you need specific values out of a document — revenue figures, sample",
    "sizes, publication dates, dosage tables.",
    "Do NOT use this to understand what a document argues; use summarize_content.",
    "Do NOT use this to check whether an external claim is supported; use",
    "verify_claim_against_source.",
    "Edge case: if a requested field is absent, the record is returned with a null value",
    "and a reason, rather than being omitted.",
  ].join("\n"),
  input_schema: {
    type: "object",
    properties: {
      document_id: { type: "string", description: "Identifier returned by load_document." },
      field_names: {
        type: "array",
        items: { type: "string" },
        description: "Field labels to extract, e.g. ['sample_size', 'p_value'].",
      },
    },
    required: ["document_id", "field_names"],
  },
};
  • The field is input_schema, and tools are a flat list. OpenAI's shape (type: "function" wrapper, nested function.parameters) is not accepted, and parameters appears in distractors.
  • Per-property description strings are prompt text too. Put format constraints there that the schema can't express, e.g. "#-prefixed, eight digits" or "must point at a document, not an arbitrary page".

What a good description contains

Audit any description against five elements:

  1. What it does and returns: what fields come back, not how the tool is implemented.
  2. Accepted input formats, including ones that look valid but aren't.
  3. Example queries in the user's language.
  4. Edge cases, especially "failed" versus "succeeded and found nothing".
  5. Boundaries against sibling tools, by name.

With near-neighbour tools, #5 outweighs the other four, because it's the only information the model can't infer from the tool in isolation.

Bad:

name: lookup_order
description: Retrieves order details.

Good:

name: lookup_order
description: >
  Look up a single order by its order number and return status, line items,
  fulfilment and delivery dates, carrier tracking, and the refund state of each
  line. Accepts an order number with or without the leading '#' (e.g. "#48812",
  "48812"). Does NOT accept email addresses, names, or account IDs.

  Use for queries like "where is my order 48812", "was #48812 delivered",
  "which items shipped in my last order".

  Use get_customer instead when the request identifies a person rather than an
  order ("look up my account", "what's on file for jane@example.com") or when
  you need the customer's order history rather than one order.

  If the order number is well-formed but not found, returns an empty result with
  found: false — this is a successful call, not an error, and usually means a
  typo or an order belonging to a different account.

What each part of the good version prevents:

  • Return description: the model no longer calls get_customer just to find out whether tracking data exists.
  • "Does NOT accept" clause: no email passed in, no turn burned on a validation error.
  • Example queries: they do the job of system-prompt few-shot examples, for fewer tokens, and they're maintained with the tool.
  • Boundary sentence naming get_customer: draws the line between the two tools.
  • Empty-result note: stops the agent treating "not found" as a failure and retrying or escalating, when it should ask the customer to re-check the number.

A description of 150 to 250 tokens costs less than a misrouted call plus the recovery turn.

strict: true and input schemas

Descriptions fix which tool is called. A perfect description still leaves a separate failure, the right tool called with a malformed argument, such as a string for a number or a missing required field. "strict": true beside input_schema constrains generation so the input matches the schema exactly, much as strict JSON output does in Chapter 13. Add it wherever a malformed input is costly (e.g. process_refund.amount_cents). It doesn't help selection, so a strict tool still needs a good description.

input_examples lets you attach example input objects as structured data. It is an alternative to writing example queries in prose, but prose still carries when to use the tool, which bare inputs don't.

Diagnosing misrouting

Misrouting shows up as consistently picking the wrong member of a specific pair on a consistent class of query. For example, get_customer gets called on order queries, or analyze_content and analyze_document (near-identical descriptions) are picked interchangeably regardless of input type.

Diagnose in order of cost:

  1. Compare the two descriptions. Could a new engineer, given only those strings, pick correctly for every failing query? If not, the descriptions are the cause.
  2. Check the schemas. If both take a bare string query, the schema offers no signal either.
  3. Only if the descriptions already discriminate, read the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions. "Always begin by understanding the customer" pulls calls toward get_customer whatever its description says. It overrides good descriptions and is invisible unless you look.

These don't fix it:

  • A deterministic routing layer that pre-selects tools from the input. It discards the model's language understanding and fails on every phrasing you didn't anticipate.
  • 5–8 few-shot examples in the system prompt. They add tokens to every request and leave the cause untouched. The model memorises surface patterns but still can't tell the tools apart.

Fixing misrouting

  1. Rename and rewrite to remove overlap. analyze_content becomes extract_web_results: it takes search snippets and URLs, returns passages with source attribution, and explicitly routes loaded documents to the document tools. The rename matters as much as the rewrite, because the name is what the model sees first.
  2. Split a generic tool into purpose-specific tools. If one tool does unrelated jobs, no description can fix it, because the ambiguity is in the tool. An analyze_document that summarises, extracts, or fact-checks depending on phrasing becomes extract_data_points, summarize_content, and verify_claim_against_source, each with defined I/O contracts and each naming the other two in its boundaries.
  3. Review the system prompt. It's the cheapest fix. Remove keywords that collide with tool names, and move real sequencing out of prose and into tool_choice or a programmatic prerequisite.

Use one naming convention across the inventory, snake_case verb plus resource, namespaced by service when there are several backends. billing_get_invoice and fulfilment_get_shipment are easy to tell apart; two get_records are not.

Distributing tools across agents

Selection reliability is a property of the tool set, not the individual tool. In the exam's numbers, an agent with 18 tools selects less reliably than one with 4–5.

Agents also misuse tools outside their specialisation. Give a synthesis agent web search and it will search, because the tool is there and a gap seems to fit it. You get mediocre research instead of good synthesis, and blurred responsibility.

The default is scoped tool access, where each agent holds only what its role needs. In the research system:

  • Search agent: search and fetch tools.
  • Document agent: load_document plus the three extraction tools.
  • Synthesis agent: none of those.
  • Report agent: formatting and citation tools.
  • Coordinator: delegation tools only.

The verify_fact case. Strict scoping means synthesis must go through the coordinator to reach search, which adds 2–3 round trips and about 40% latency. Measurement shows 85% of verifications are simple (dates, names, statistics) and 15% need real investigation. The fix is to give synthesis a limited, scoped verify_fact tool for the 85% and keep routing the 15% through the coordinator. The wrong answers are:

  • The full search toolkit for synthesis: over-provisioned, and it dissolves the separation of concerns.
  • Batching verifications to the end: later steps depend on earlier facts, so it creates blocking dependencies.

Apply the same instinct to individual tools by replacing generic ones with constrained ones. fetch_url (fetches anything) becomes load_document (validates that the URL is a document and rejects the rest).

The tool search tool, as an alternative to manual scoping

For an agent that legitimately needs many tools of one kind, the tool search tool (tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119 for keyword search, tool_search_tool_regex_20251119 for patterns) defers most definitions and lets Claude search for the relevant one on demand. It solves the context and selection-load problem, but not separation of concerns: a synthesis agent that shouldn't research still shouldn't have search. Scoping answers "who should be able to do this". Tool search answers "how do I keep a large legitimate inventory usable".

tool_choice as a sequencing instrument

Setting Behaviour Use when
"auto" The model decides whether to call a tool at all and which one. May return conversational text. Ordinary agent turns where a text answer is a valid outcome.
"any" The model must call some tool, but chooses which. You need structured output and a prose reply would be a failure.
{"type": "tool", "name": "..."} A specific named tool is called. A particular tool must run first, before the model has discretion.
{"type": "none"} No tool may be called. You want plain text and must rule out a premature call.

When enrichment depends on extract_metadata's output, don't write "always call extract_metadata first" in the prompt. Force it on turn one, then return to "auto".

Python

first = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[extract_metadata, enrich_company, enrich_filing],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Process the Q3 filing at doc_8814."}],
)
# ... append the tool_use block and its tool_result, then continue:
followup = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[extract_metadata, enrich_company, enrich_filing],
    tool_choice={"type": "auto"},
    messages=conversation,
)

TypeScript

const first = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-sonnet-5",
  max_tokens: 2048,
  tools: [extractMetadata, enrichCompany, enrichFiling],
  tool_choice: { type: "tool", name: "extract_metadata" },
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Process the Q3 filing at doc_8814." }],
});

const followup = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-sonnet-5",
  max_tokens: 2048,
  tools: [extractMetadata, enrichCompany, enrichFiling],
  tool_choice: { type: "auto" },
  messages: conversation,
});

tool_choice applies to one request. It can't enforce a prerequisite across an open-ended multi-turn loop. For business-critical sequencing (verify the customer before refunding), block the call in your own code. In order of strength: prompt < tool_choice < programmatic gate. Sample question 1 turns on this. Chapter 6 covers gates.

Current product (not tested): forced tool_choice (any/tool) returns a 400 on Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1; see Chapter 2. The examples use claude-sonnet-5, which accepts it.

The built-in Claude Code tools

You know these tools already. The table lists the distinctions the exam draws.

Tool Use for
Grep File contents: callers of reconcileInvoice, error strings, imports
Glob File paths/names: **/*.test.tsx, src/**/handler.py
Read / Write Whole files
Edit Surgical change at a unique anchor string; fails if the anchor repeats
Bash Builds and tests. Not for grep/cat where a dedicated tool exists, because you lose structured results, the permission model, and guardrails
  • Edit fallback (the guide's answer): when Edit can't find unique text, use Read to load the whole file, then Write to save the reconstructed version. It's slower and costs more tokens, but it's deterministic, and it is the exam's answer. Current Claude Code documents a different first move: widen old_string with context, or set replace_all: true.
  • Incremental exploration: Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports. Don't read everything up front. Forty files for one code path wastes context and pushes the relevant part into the weak-attention middle.
  • Tracing through wrapper modules: re-exports rename things, so one Grep for the original name misses callers. First identify the exported names (Grep the barrel file or export statements), then search for each.

What the exam tests

  • Task 2.1: descriptions are the primary selection mechanism. Given a misrouting symptom (get_customer/lookup_order, analyze_content/analyze_document), the best first step is expanding the descriptions: formats, examples, edge cases, sibling boundaries. Few-shot examples, a routing layer, and consolidating tools are the wrong first steps.
  • Match each repair to its example: rename + rewrite for overlap; split with defined I/O contracts for a generic tool; system prompt review when good descriptions are overridden by keywords.
  • Task 2.3: 18 tools vs 4–5; out-of-specialisation misuse; scoped access by default; a limited verify_fact when a measured majority of cases are simple, with the rest via the coordinator; fetch_url → load_document. tool_choice: forced to run extract_metadata first, "any" to guarantee a call rather than text.
  • Task 2.5: Grep = contents, Glob = paths, Read/Write = whole files, Edit = unique anchor with Read + Write fallback, Bash only when no dedicated tool exists. Two strategies: incremental exploration from Grep, and exported-names-first tracing through wrappers.
  • MCP deployment, auth, and transports are out of scope.

Exercises

  1. Give get_customer and lookup_order one-line descriptions. Run 20 queries (10 each) with tool_choice: "auto" and record accuracy. Rewrite both with all five elements and re-run. For queries still failing, decide whether the description or the schema is at fault.
  2. Write a generic analyze_document with a mode parameter, then split it into extract_data_points, summarize_content, and verify_claim_against_source with distinct schemas, in Python and TypeScript. Check that each description names the other two.
  3. Build a two-turn harness: force extract_metadata, append the tool_use/tool_result, then follow up with "auto". Change the follow-up to "any" and see what happens when nothing useful is left to call. That shows where "any" is a trap.
  4. Audit a Claude Code built-in tool's description against the five elements, then write one of your own to that standard.

Chapter 4 — Errors, recovery, and telling the agent the truth

When a Bash command fails in Claude Code, Claude reads stderr, adjusts, and tries something else. No handler knows what command not found: uv means. Recovery works because the failure arrives as content the model can read, not as an exception that ends the turn.

In an agentic system, an error is a message to the model, and the model is its primary consumer. The operator and the log come second. If you raise an exception out of the loop, you remove the one participant that could narrow the query, try another source or carry on with what it has. Given "the pricing service did not respond within 30 seconds; this is usually transient", the model can plan recovery from the task as a whole, which hand-written branches cannot see. Backend reflexes like "fail fast" and "let it crash" are right for failures people read. Here they do harm, because failing fast kills the reasoning that might have solved the problem.

Two task statements share this material:

  • 2.2: structured error responses from MCP tools. The recipient is the calling agent.
  • 5.3: error propagation in multi-agent systems. The recipient is a coordinator handling a subagent that couldn't finish.

Both use the same taxonomy, the same access-failure versus empty-result distinction, and the same rule that partial results travel with the error.

Scope. Rate limits, quotas, and pricing are out of scope. Retry strategy is in scope as design judgement (attempt budgets, idempotency).

Don't conflate these layers:

  • isError/is_error and the categories below cover your tool failing while the API is healthy.
  • overloaded_error (HTTP 529) and rate_limit_error (HTTP 429) mean the API call itself failed. They never reach the model as a tool_result. The SDK retries them beneath your loop with a small default budget, exponential backoff, and retry-after. Don't build a competing retry policy for this layer.
  • stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded" (Claude 4.5+) means the conversation ran out of room. Fix it by trimming or compacting history, not by retrying.

The two spellings of the same flag

A tool result is content plus one boolean saying "this is a failure":

  • MCP: isError on the tool result.
  • Messages API: is_error on a tool_result block.

isError is not a thrown exception. The tool returns normally with the flag set and a description. The model reads it as the outcome of its call, and the turn continues.

Protocol error Tool error
What broke The MCP server itself (malformed request, transport failure) The operation. The server worked fine.
Model sees it? Generally no Yes, via isError
Examples — Upstream payment failure, missing document, customer ID fails validation

Four categories, one retryable

Category Typical cause Retryable What the agent should do
transient Upstream timeout, service unavailable, connection reset Yes Retry within a bounded budget, ideally inside the subagent; escalate only if the budget is exhausted
validation Malformed or out-of-range input, missing required field No Correct the arguments from the error description and call again with a materially different input
business Policy violation (refund window elapsed, item non-returnable) No Stop, and explain the policy to the user in the customer-friendly terms the error supplies
permission Missing scope, expired credential, record outside the caller's tenant No Stop and escalate to a human or to a differently-scoped path; never loop

Only transient errors are retryable. Retrying the others fails the same way and wastes tokens and latency. "Not retryable" doesn't mean hopeless. After a validation error the agent should call again with corrected input, which is a different act from retrying.

The guide is inconsistent here. The knowledge statements name four categories, but task 2.2's skills bullet lists errorCategory as only transient/validation/permission. Business-rule violations are instead described as the case needing retriable: false plus a customer-friendly message. Default to four categories, recognise the three-value list, and remember that retriable: false is attached to business violations by name.

Generic error text

Generic, uniform error text is a named anti-pattern. If every failure reads Operation failed, the model can't tell a network blip from a policy refusal. Its only strategy is to retry, so it retries a refund that is out of policy on attempt one and still out of policy on attempt four. Structured metadata prevents those wasted retries. The payload carries:

  • errorCategory
  • isRetryable boolean
  • A description written for a reader who must decide what to do next
  • For business violations: retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation the agent can relay

Python

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict

@dataclass
class ToolFailure:
    errorCategory: str          # transient | validation | business | permission
    isRetryable: bool
    description: str            # for the model: what happened, what to try
    customerMessage: str | None = None   # for business errors: safe to relay verbatim

def process_refund(order_id: str, amount_cents: int) -> dict:
    order = orders.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        return error_result(ToolFailure(
            errorCategory="validation",
            isRetryable=False,
            description=(
                f"No order matches id '{order_id}'. Order ids look like 'ORD-8842911'. "
                "Confirm the id with the customer before calling again."
            ),
        ))
    if order.days_since_delivery > 30:
        return error_result(ToolFailure(
            errorCategory="business",
            isRetryable=False,
            description="Refund window closed; policy REFUND-30D. Do not retry.",
            customerMessage=(
                "This order was delivered 47 days ago and our refund window is 30 days, "
                "so I can't process a refund automatically — but I can raise it with a specialist."
            ),
        ))
    ...

def error_result(failure: ToolFailure) -> dict:
    return {
        "isError": True,
        "content": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(asdict(failure))}],
    }

TypeScript

type ErrorCategory = "transient" | "validation" | "business" | "permission";

interface ToolFailure {
  errorCategory: ErrorCategory;
  isRetryable: boolean;
  description: string;
  customerMessage?: string;
}

const errorResult = (failure: ToolFailure) => ({
  isError: true,
  content: [{ type: "text" as const, text: JSON.stringify(failure) }],
});

export async function processRefund(orderId: string, amountCents: number) {
  const order = await orders.get(orderId);
  if (!order) {
    return errorResult({
      errorCategory: "validation",
      isRetryable: false,
      description:
        `No order matches id '${orderId}'. Order ids look like 'ORD-8842911'. ` +
        "Confirm the id with the customer before calling again.",
    });
  }
  if (order.daysSinceDelivery > 30) {
    return errorResult({
      errorCategory: "business",
      isRetryable: false,
      description: "Refund window closed; policy REFUND-30D. Do not retry.",
      customerMessage:
        "This order was delivered 47 days ago and our refund window is 30 days, so I can't " +
        "process a refund automatically — but I can raise it with a specialist.",
    });
  }
  // ...
}

The description is a prompt fragment, not a log line. The model weighs it like CLAUDE.md text, so write it as an instruction.

Access failure is not an empty result

This appears in both Domain 2 and Domain 5.

  • Access failure: couldn't reach the data. It failed and needs a retry decision.
  • Valid empty result: the query reached the data and nothing matched. That is a success, and the answer is "none".

Collapse them and you lose information both ways. A timeout marked as an empty success produces a confident "no records" with no basis. An empty match marked as an error burns the retry budget re-asking an answered question. Make them differ in structure as well as wording.

Python

def search_incident_reports(query: str, since: str) -> dict:
    try:
        rows = incident_index.search(query, since=since, timeout=20)
    except SearchTimeout:
        return error_result(ToolFailure(
            errorCategory="transient",
            isRetryable=True,
            description=f"Incident index timed out after 20s for query {query!r}.",
        ))
    payload = {
        "isError": False,          # explicit, not the absence of the field
        "resultCount": len(rows),  # 0 is a real, trustworthy answer
        "results": rows,
        "queryExecuted": query,
    }
    return {"isError": False, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(payload)}]}

TypeScript

export async function searchIncidentReports(query: string, since: string) {
  try {
    const rows = await incidentIndex.search(query, { since, timeoutMs: 20_000 });
    const payload = { isError: false, resultCount: rows.length, results: rows, queryExecuted: query };
    return { isError: false, content: [{ type: "text" as const, text: JSON.stringify(payload) }] };
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof SearchTimeout) {
      return errorResult({
        errorCategory: "transient",
        isRetryable: true,
        description: `Incident index timed out after 20s for query "${query}".`,
      });
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

resultCount: 0 with no error flag tells the model the search ran and found nothing.

Local recovery, then escalation

The subagent is the right place to absorb transient failure. It is closest to the tool, knows expected latency, and retrying there costs the coordinator nothing. Handle transients locally and propagate only what you couldn't resolve, always with partial results and what was attempted.

Task 5.3's structured error context has four parts, each of which feeds a coordinator decision:

Part Lets the coordinator…
Failure type decide whether retrying is coherent
What was attempted avoid reissuing the identical query
Partial results decide whether it already has enough
Alternative approaches go somewhere other than "give up"

Python

async def market_research_subagent(topic: str) -> dict:
    attempts, partial = [], []
    for query in expand_topic(topic):           # e.g. three narrower sub-queries
        attempts.append(query)
        try:
            partial.extend(await web_search(query, timeout=25, retries=2))
        except SearchTimeout:
            continue                             # local recovery: keep going
    if not partial:
        return {
            "status": "failed",
            "failureType": "transient",          # timeout, not "no such topic"
            "attempted": attempts,
            "partialResults": [],
            "alternatives": [
                "Retry with a single narrowed query such as 'EU battery recycling mandates 2026'",
                "Route to the internal-archive subagent, which has cached analyst notes",
            ],
        }
    if len(partial) < expected_minimum(topic):
        return {
            "status": "partial",
            "failureType": "transient",
            "attempted": attempts,
            "partialResults": partial,
            "coverageGaps": ["regulatory outlook — all three source queries timed out"],
            "alternatives": ["Re-run only the regulatory sub-query"],
        }
    return {"status": "complete", "results": partial}

TypeScript

export async function marketResearchSubagent(topic: string) {
  const attempted: string[] = [];
  const partial: Finding[] = [];

  for (const query of expandTopic(topic)) {
    attempted.push(query);
    try {
      partial.push(...(await webSearch(query, { timeoutMs: 25_000, retries: 2 })));
    } catch (err) {
      if (!(err instanceof SearchTimeout)) throw err;   // local recovery only for transient
    }
  }

  if (partial.length === 0) {
    return {
      status: "failed",
      failureType: "transient",
      attempted,
      partialResults: [],
      alternatives: [
        "Retry with a single narrowed query such as 'EU battery recycling mandates 2026'",
        "Route to the internal-archive subagent, which has cached analyst notes",
      ],
    };
  }
  if (partial.length < expectedMinimum(topic)) {
    return {
      status: "partial",
      failureType: "transient",
      attempted,
      partialResults: partial,
      coverageGaps: ["regulatory outlook — all three source queries timed out"],
      alternatives: ["Re-run only the regulatory sub-query"],
    };
  }
  return { status: "complete", results: partial };
}

Walking sample question 8

A web-search subagent times out mid-research. The correct answer is the four-part structured payload above. The distractors are:

  • Retry with backoff, then return generic "search unavailable". The retry is fine and belongs there. The defect is the generic status, which throws away the queries tried and the data collected.
  • Catch the timeout, return an empty result marked successful. This suppresses the error, so no recovery is possible, and synthesis treats absence of findings as evidence of absence.
  • Terminate the workflow from a top-level handler. This reports the failure but is out of proportion, because it kills the whole run when a narrowed retry or another source would likely have worked.

The last two are task 5.3's named anti-patterns: suppressing errors as empty success, and terminating an entire workflow on one subtask failure.

Coverage annotations

Synthesis output must mark which findings are well supported and which topic areas have gaps because sources were unavailable. "Competitor pricing: three independent sources; regulatory outlook: no sources retrieved, all queries timed out" is useful. If the same report silently drops the regulatory section, the reader can't tell "investigated, found nothing" from "never reached". Partial results are acceptable as long as they are disclosed.

Idempotency

process_refund posts the refund, then the response times out. The tool correctly reports a retryable transient error, the agent retries, and the customer is refunded twice. The category was right, but the operation wasn't safe to retry.

Retryability is a property of the operation as well as the error. Make mutating tools idempotent: the client supplies a key derived from the request's intent, not the attempt, and the server returns the original outcome for a repeated key.

Python

def refund_result(refund_id: str, replayed: bool) -> dict:
    payload = {"isError": False, "refundId": refund_id, "replayed": replayed}
    return {"isError": False, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": json.dumps(payload)}]}

def process_refund(order_id: str, amount_cents: int, idempotency_key: str) -> dict:
    prior = refund_ledger.get(idempotency_key)
    if prior is not None:
        return refund_result(prior.id, replayed=True)
    receipt = payments.refund(order_id, amount_cents, key=idempotency_key)
    refund_ledger.put(idempotency_key, receipt)
    return refund_result(receipt.id, replayed=False)

TypeScript

const refundResult = (refundId: string, replayed: boolean) => {
  const payload = { isError: false, refundId, replayed };
  return { isError: false, content: [{ type: "text" as const, text: JSON.stringify(payload) }] };
};

export async function processRefund(
  orderId: string, amountCents: number, idempotencyKey: string,
) {
  const prior = await refundLedger.get(idempotencyKey);
  if (prior) return refundResult(prior.id, true);

  const receipt = await payments.refund(orderId, amountCents, { key: idempotencyKey });
  await refundLedger.put(idempotencyKey, receipt);
  return refundResult(receipt.id, false);
}

Make the key a required schema parameter and describe it as identifying the refund attempt, so the model reuses it on retry. The caller is a model choosing arguments from prose, so the description is the only thing that prevents a duplicate payment. If the model generates a new key on each call, the key protects nothing.

Retry strategy as a design decision

  • Exponential backoff with jitter for transients. Backoff gives the dependency room to recover. Jitter stops parallel subagents retrying in lockstep (thundering herd).
  • Bound attempts: 2–3 when a human is waiting, more for batch.
  • Retries the model sees cost tokens. Each failed attempt stays in context for the rest of the session, crowding out useful material. Absorb retries inside the subagent and report one summarised outcome.
  • Set a per-turn budget alongside the per-call one. When it's exhausted, escalate with the four-part payload.

What the exam tests

  • The four categories, and that only transient is retryable.
  • isError (MCP) and is_error (Messages API) by name. Their purpose is to make failure visible to the model.
  • Access failure versus valid empty result (Domains 2 and 5). A timeout reported as empty success, or an empty match reported as an error, is wrong on sight.
  • The four-part payload for multi-agent failures. A generic "search unavailable" is always the trap, even with sound retry logic around it.
  • The two named anti-patterns: suppressing as empty success, and terminating the whole workflow on one failure.
  • Local recovery first. Escalation carries partial results rather than replacing them.
  • Coverage annotations (task 5.3): partial is fine, undisclosed is not.

Exercises

  1. Write an MCP tool wrapping a service you have credentials for. Give every exit path an errorCategory, an isRetryable, and a model-oriented description. In Claude Code, trigger each failure: it should retry the timeout and stop on the policy refusal. Then change every description to Operation failed and compare.
  2. Build a search tool with structurally distinct empty and timeout results. With the source unreachable, confirm the agent retries. With the source reachable and the query unmatchable, confirm it reports "no matches" with zero retries.
  3. Implement the market-research subagent and force one sub-query to time out permanently. Check that the coordinator gets partial results plus coverageGaps, and that the synthesis names the gap. Then make the subagent return {"status": "complete", "results": []} and record what the synthesis claims.
  4. Add a required idempotency key to a mutating tool and simulate a timeout after commit. Confirm the retry replays the receipt. Then reword the key's description to sound per-call and watch the model mint a fresh one.

Chapter 5 — Orchestration

When Claude Code fans a broad request out to subagents, it is running a small distributed system. A coordinator decides to delegate, isolated workers each see only what they are told, and a synthesis step reconciles results that never talked to each other. This chapter covers building that system yourself with the Agent SDK (task statements 1.2 and 1.3), so you can diagnose it and use it outside Claude Code.

The running example is the exam's Multi-Agent Research System. A coordinator delegates to search and document-analysis subagents, and a synthesis subagent writes the report. Customer support is the secondary example.

Why orchestration is a separate problem from the loop

Chapter 2's loop is one agent with one growing messages array. Orchestration applies when one context can't hold the whole problem well:

  • Tool load: 18 tools select worse than 4–5, and out-of-specialisation tools get misused (Chapter 3).
  • Context load: a single conversation accumulates every document, result, and draft, so by synthesis time the signal is buried. Separate bounded contexts are a context-management technique as well as a division of labour (Chapter 14).

Hub-and-spoke

The default architecture puts one coordinator at the centre. Subagents talk only to the coordinator, never to each other. The coordinator decomposes the task, delegates the parts and aggregates the results. A finished search subagent returns to the coordinator, which decides what synthesis sees.

The exam names three benefits of giving up direct subagent-to-subagent communication:

  1. Observability: everything passes through one place, so one log tells the whole story.
  2. Consistent error handling: one place decides whether to retry, substitute, or pass on partial results.
  3. Controlled information flow: the coordinator can filter, summarise, or redact before passing data on, e.g. keep sensitive document content away from the report agent.

In support, a case that needs order history and a fraud check before process_refund routes both through a coordinator, not a fraud agent reading the order agent's output directly. The coordinator sees the whole case and decides what an inconclusive fraud check means.

Subagent context isolation

A subagent's context is isolated. It does not inherit the coordinator's history, and separate invocations of "the same" subagent share nothing. The Task tool starts a subagent with only the prompt you write. Anything the coordinator or an earlier subagent learned exists for it only if it is in that prompt.

In the exam's example, a synthesis subagent is prompted with just "Synthesize the research findings into a report." The findings are in the coordinator's history, so the subagent has none, and its output is generic and uncited. The fix is to put the findings in the prompt, not to use a bigger model or give synthesis a WebSearch tool. A search tool would move research into the wrong agent and break separation of concerns.

Python

# WRONG — the coordinator assumes shared memory that doesn't exist
synthesis_prompt = "Synthesize the research findings into a report."

# RIGHT — the coordinator passes what it actually collected
synthesis_prompt = f"""
Write a research report answering: {research_question}

You have no access to the search or document tools. Work only from the
findings below. Cite every claim using the bracketed source ids.

## Web search findings
{format_search_findings(search_results)}

## Document analysis findings
{format_document_findings(document_results)}

Quality criteria: every factual claim must carry a citation id. Flag any
subtopic in the original question that the findings below do not cover.
"""

TypeScript

// WRONG — the coordinator assumes shared memory that doesn't exist
const synthesisPrompt = "Synthesize the research findings into a report.";

// RIGHT — the coordinator passes what it actually collected
const synthesisPrompt = `
Write a research report answering: ${researchQuestion}

You have no access to the search or document tools. Work only from the
findings below. Cite every claim using the bracketed source ids.

## Web search findings
${formatSearchFindings(searchResults)}

## Document analysis findings
${formatDocumentFindings(documentResults)}

Quality criteria: every factual claim must carry a citation id. Flag any
subtopic in the original question that the findings below do not cover.
`;

The corrected prompt ends with a goal and quality bar (cite every claim, flag coverage gaps) and leaves the subagent free to structure the report to fit the material. It does not give a numbered procedure.

Structured findings and attribution

If a subagent returns prose that mixes claims with URLs, synthesis has to re-parse attribution from running text. Sometimes it drops or garbles the sources, and the report makes confident claims nobody can trace. Separate content from metadata at return time: every finding carries its source URL, or document name and page, as a field alongside the content.

Python

search_findings = [
    {
        "claim": "The library dropped support for callback-style APIs in v5.",
        "source_url": "https://example.com/library/changelog/v5",
        "retrieved_at": "2026-08-30",
    },
    {
        "claim": "Migration guides recommend the async adapter for v4 codebases.",
        "source_url": "https://example.com/library/migration-guide",
        "retrieved_at": "2026-08-30",
    },
]

document_findings = [
    {
        "claim": "Internal usage of the callback API appears in 14 call sites.",
        "document_name": "internal-audit-q3.pdf",
        "page": 6,
    },
]

TypeScript

const searchFindings = [
  {
    claim: "The library dropped support for callback-style APIs in v5.",
    sourceUrl: "https://example.com/library/changelog/v5",
    retrievedAt: "2026-08-30",
  },
  {
    claim: "Migration guides recommend the async adapter for v4 codebases.",
    sourceUrl: "https://example.com/library/migration-guide",
    retrievedAt: "2026-08-30",
  },
];

const documentFindings = [
  {
    claim: "Internal usage of the callback API appears in 14 call sites.",
    documentName: "internal-audit-q3.pdf",
    page: 6,
  },
];

format_search_findings / format_document_findings render these with metadata still attached to each claim.

The Task tool and the AgentDefinition

The Task tool looks like any tool (name, description, schema), but calling it starts a new agentic loop with its own messages array and returns that loop's final result as the tool result. Claude Code spawns its subagents this way.

Two configuration facts matter here:

  1. allowedTools must include "Task" for the coordinator to delegate. When a coordinator never spawns subagents despite its prompt, the cause is structural rather than a reasoning failure, so check this first. (Claude Code renamed Task to Agent in v2.1.63 and keeps Task as an alias: tool_use blocks name the tool "Agent", while system:init still lists "Task", so match both in code. The guide and exam say Task, so answer Task.)
  2. Each spawnable role is an AgentDefinition: name, description (when the coordinator should use it), prompt (scopes behaviour), and tools (restriction). It is the SDK equivalent of a Claude Code subagent definition.

Python

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt=COORDINATOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
    allowed_tools=["Task"],
    agents={
        "search_agent": AgentDefinition(
            description="Runs web searches for a specific subtopic and "
                        "returns findings with source URLs attached.",
            prompt=SEARCH_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            tools=["WebSearch", "WebFetch"],
        ),
        "document_agent": AgentDefinition(
            description="Loads and extracts claims from a specific set of "
                        "documents, returning findings with document name "
                        "and page number attached.",
            prompt=DOCUMENT_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            tools=["load_document", "extract_data_points"],
        ),
        "synthesis_agent": AgentDefinition(
            description="Writes a cited research report from findings "
                        "supplied in its prompt. Has no research tools.",
            prompt=SYNTHESIS_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            tools=[],
        ),
    },
)

TypeScript

import { AgentDefinition } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

const options = {
  systemPrompt: COORDINATOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
  allowedTools: ["Task"],
  agents: {
    search_agent: {
      description: "Runs web searches for a specific subtopic and returns " +
        "findings with source URLs attached.",
      prompt: SEARCH_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
      tools: ["WebSearch", "WebFetch"],
    } satisfies AgentDefinition,
    document_agent: {
      description: "Loads and extracts claims from a specific set of " +
        "documents, returning findings with document name and page " +
        "number attached.",
      prompt: DOCUMENT_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
      tools: ["load_document", "extract_data_points"],
    } satisfies AgentDefinition,
    synthesis_agent: {
      description: "Writes a cited research report from findings supplied " +
        "in its prompt. Has no research tools.",
      prompt: SYNTHESIS_AGENT_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
      tools: [],
    } satisfies AgentDefinition,
  },
};
  • Caveat on allowedTools: the SDK documents it as an auto-approve list that "does not restrict Claude to only these tools". Omitting "Task" won't reliably block delegation in real code, but it is still the exam's answer to "why won't my coordinator spawn subagents?". AgentDefinition.tools does restrict the subagent, since an omitted tool "isn't in the subagent's session at all."
  • description is what the coordinator routes on. A vague one misroutes between subagent types, just as a vague tool description does between tools.
  • synthesis_agent has no tools by design, which enforces the Chapter 3 scoping argument in configuration.

Other AgentDefinition fields (not tested field by field):

Field Purpose
disallowedTools Remove specific tools (incl. mcp__server, mcp__*) from an otherwise permissive role
model Full ID, alias, or 'inherit': cheaper model for search, stronger for synthesis
skills, memory ('user'/'project'/'local'), mcpServers, initialPrompt Subagent's own skills, memory scope, MCP connections, seed message
maxTurns Caps the subagent's loop. At the cap it returns a resumable partial result rather than failing
background Run without blocking the coordinator's turn
effort How much the subagent reasons
permissionMode Subagent's own permission mode

Resuming a subagent

A Task/Agent result carries a session_id (shown as agentId in current tooling) for that subagent's transcript. Pass it back as resume: sessionId on a later Task call to continue that subagent's history instead of starting from nothing. This is useful when a document subagent has built up expensive context on a document set. Resume when the prior context is still valid and worth its cost; otherwise spawn fresh (the same judgement as Chapter 7).

Spawning in parallel

Parallel delegation = multiple Task calls in a single coordinator response. Four Task calls in one turn run four subagents side by side. One call per turn over four turns runs them in sequence, which takes far longer because each is its own multi-step loop.

There is no parallelism flag. Distractors offer real parameters that govern something else, such as disable_parallel_tool_use, which controls batching of ordinary tool calls in a turn.

With query(), the SDK harness sees the four tool_use blocks and runs the four loops concurrently, while your code supplies options and reads typed messages.

Python

from claude_agent_sdk import query

async for message in query(
    prompt="Research the market impact of generative AI on creative "
           "industries: visual arts, music, writing, and film/video, "
           "each as a distinct workstream.",
    options=options,  # the ClaudeAgentOptions defined above
):
    log.info("%s", message)
# Internally, the coordinator's turn carries four Task tool_use blocks
# naming "search_agent", each with a distinct, non-overlapping subtopic
# in its input — the SDK runs the four resulting subagent loops concurrently.

TypeScript

import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

for await (const message of query({
  prompt: "Research the market impact of generative AI on creative " +
    "industries: visual arts, music, writing, and film/video, each as " +
    "a distinct workstream.",
  options, // the ClaudeAgentOptions defined above
})) {
  log.info(message);
}
// Internally, the coordinator's turn carries four Task tool_use blocks
// naming "search_agent", each with a distinct, non-overlapping subtopic
// in its input — the SDK runs the four resulting subagent loops concurrently.

Fan-out ceilings exist because anything that can spawn more of itself needs a hard cap:

  • CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH: nesting depth (default 3).
  • CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS: concurrent loops (default 20).
  • maxBudgetUsd / max_budget_usd: total spend across the delegation tree. Exceeding it stops with result subtype error_max_budget_usd.

Partitioning scope without narrowing the topic

Splitting "creative industries" into visual arts, music, writing, and film/video partitions scope correctly, with full coverage and no duplication. The exam calls this partitioning research scope to minimise duplication: assign each subagent distinct subtopics or source types (e.g. one agent on regulatory filings, one on news, one on vendor pages).

Now split it into gallery representation, digital art marketplaces, and museum curation, which are all visual arts. Every subagent succeeds with well-cited findings, and synthesis produces a confident report covering about a quarter of the topic.

When every subagent succeeds and aggregate coverage is still wrong, the defect is in the coordinator's decomposition. Error handling can't catch it, so you have to compare the decomposition against the original question's breadth, before delegating and again after synthesis.

Iterative refinement

A one-pass pipeline (decompose → delegate → synthesise) can't catch narrow decomposition after the fact. Make it a loop: evaluate synthesis for gaps against the original question, re-delegate targeted queries for the gaps, re-synthesise, and repeat until coverage is sufficient.

Python

def run_research_coordinator(question, max_refinement_rounds=3):
    findings = delegate_initial_research(question)   # parallel Task calls
    report = invoke_synthesis(question, findings)

    for round_num in range(max_refinement_rounds):
        gaps = evaluate_coverage(question, report)    # coordinator's own check
        if not gaps:
            return report
        log.info("refinement round=%d gaps=%s", round_num, gaps)
        targeted_findings = delegate_targeted_research(gaps)  # more Task calls
        findings = findings + targeted_findings
        report = invoke_synthesis(question, findings)

    report["coverage_warning"] = (
        "Refinement rounds exhausted; known gaps may remain unresolved."
    )
    return report

TypeScript

async function runResearchCoordinator(
  question: string,
  maxRefinementRounds = 3,
) {
  let findings = await delegateInitialResearch(question); // parallel Task calls
  let report = await invokeSynthesis(question, findings);

  for (let round = 0; round < maxRefinementRounds; round++) {
    const gaps = await evaluateCoverage(question, report); // coordinator's own check
    if (gaps.length === 0) return report;
    log.info({ round, gaps });
    const targetedFindings = await delegateTargetedResearch(gaps); // more Task calls
    findings = [...findings, ...targetedFindings];
    report = await invokeSynthesis(question, findings);
  }

  report.coverageWarning =
    "Refinement rounds exhausted; known gaps may remain unresolved.";
  return report;
}

evaluate_coverage must look for named subtopics that never got a subagent, not just check for non-empty output. The three visual-arts subagents all returned good, non-empty results. The loop is bounded, and when it runs out of rounds it attaches a warning instead of returning incomplete work as complete.

Query complexity

The opposite failure is over-processing. "What year was [a well-known data regulation] enacted?" doesn't need search, then document analysis, then synthesis. The coordinator's prompt should have it assess complexity first (simple lookup, comparison, or open investigation) and invoke only the subagents needed. A coordinator told to always run the full team spends four invocations on a one-agent question. In support, a plain order-status request doesn't need a fraud check.

Fork-based sessions, briefly

Forking branches a session into independent copies from a shared baseline, so you can explore two divergent approaches (e.g. two report framings) without re-deriving the shared analysis. It is a session mechanism, covered in Chapter 7.

Scaling past hub-and-spoke, and the default subagent

  • Workflow tool (separate from Task/Agent) orchestrates dozens to hundreds of agents outside the coordinator's conversation. Hub-and-spoke keeps everything in the coordinator's context, which is what buys observability and controlled flow, and that context would overflow at large scale. The two suit different problem sizes, and hub-and-spoke still applies at small to moderate scale.
  • general-purpose is a built-in subagent always available even with no agents defined, unless disabled with CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_DISABLE_BUILTIN_AGENTS=1. A coordinator with an empty agents map can still delegate.

What the exam tests

Tasks 1.2 and 1.3 are diagnostic: name the cause of a symptom.

  • Coordinator never spawns subagents: check allowedTools for "Task".
  • Generic or uncited subagent output: put the findings in its prompt. Don't add tools or restructure turns.
  • Parallel delegation: multiple Task calls in one coordinator response. Distractors are real parameters that govern adjacent things.
  • Narrow decomposition: clean logs, wrong coverage. The defect is upstream in decomposition, found by comparing the question's breadth with what was delegated.
  • Complexity assessment versus routing everything through the full pipeline.
  • Hub-and-spoke benefits (observability, consistent error handling, controlled information flow) versus direct subagent communication.
  • Structured findings with separated content and metadata; coordinator prompts stating goals and quality criteria, not procedure.

Exercises

  1. Build the research coordinator with search_agent, document_agent, and synthesis_agent (tools scoped per Chapter 3), with the synthesis prompt as just "Synthesize the research findings into a report." Observe the generic output, then pass structured, attributed findings and compare.
  2. Have a coordinator decompose "the effects of remote work on urban commercial real estate" twice: once narrowly (three subtopics, same angle) and once broadly. Compare reports and write one sentence on what a reader of the narrow one would wrongly believe is covered.
  3. Add the refinement loop to exercise 2's narrow decomposition. Confirm it finds the gap, re-delegates, and closes it. Then remove the cap and make evaluate_coverage impossible to satisfy.
  4. Have the coordinator assess complexity first. Run a single-fact lookup, a two-way comparison, and an open investigation, and log which subagents run for each.

Chapter 6 — Hooks and gates

Claude Code's permission prompt is one instance of a general pattern. The model emits a tool_use block, and code outside the model inspects the call before it runs and can refuse it. When the prompt stops an rm -rf, the model's instructions play no part in that, because the check runs outside the model.

The rule behind tasks 1.4 and 1.5 is that prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate. However carefully you write "always verify the customer before refunding", some runs will refund anyway once there are enough conversations, long contexts and adversarial customers. The model weighs an instruction against everything else in its context. A gate is code that runs on every call and gives the same answer each time.

In the support scenario the model can make most decisions itself, such as which order, which policy and what to say. Two conditions have to hold on every run:

  1. A refund is never issued against an unverified identity.
  2. A refund never exceeds the policy threshold without a human.

Claude Code's hook system gives you two places to run code: PreToolUse (before a call executes) and PostToolUse (after a result returns). The permission prompt is a PreToolUse hook with a UI. The sections below implement both in code. Chapters 9–10 cover the configuration files.

The enforcement ladder

Mechanism What it constrains Scope Guarantee
System prompt instruction What the model is told to prefer Every turn, informally None. The model can be wrong or overridden by competing context
tool_choice forcing Which tool the next response must call One request Strong, but only for a single turn
Programmatic gate or hook Whether a call is allowed to execute, or what a result looks like once it returns The whole session, or however long your code holds the state Absolute. The check runs in your code, outside the model

A common wrong answer forces get_customer with tool_choice. That guarantees only that the next response calls it. Three turns later tool_choice is back on "auto" and nothing stops an unverified process_refund. A prerequisite that has to hold for a whole conversation needs code that keeps state and checks every call, which is what a gate is.

Use deterministic enforcement when a miss would have financial, compliance or security consequences, or when a step must never be skipped, such as verifying identity before payment. For anything less serious a good prompt is enough, and a hook is the wrong tool (see "When a prompt is enough" below).

Prerequisite gates

A prerequisite gate sits between the model's request and execution and refuses the call until an earlier condition holds. The exam's example: block process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID. The code is only a dict lookup and an if, but three details are easy to get wrong:

  1. Keep the state per conversation. With one process-wide boolean, session B can refund on session A's verification. Nothing reports an error, so the bug looks like a working gate, which is worse than having no gate. Key the state by conversation ID.
  2. Return the block as a result instead of raising. An exception kills the loop like any uncaught exception (Chapter 4). Return a normal tool_result with is_error and a description of what's missing, and the model recovers: it calls get_customer, then retries.
  3. Gate every call that can act on the wrong account. In sample question 1 the agent sometimes skips get_customer and calls lookup_order with only the customer's stated name, which leads to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. The correct option blocks both lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID. The code below shows the process_refund half; lookup_order gets the same check.

Python

verified_customers: dict[str, str] = {}  # conversation_id -> customer_id

def gated_process_refund(conversation_id: str, order_id: str,
                          amount_cents: int, reason: str) -> dict:
    customer_id = verified_customers.get(conversation_id)
    if customer_id is None:
        return {
            "is_error": True,
            "content": (
                "process_refund blocked: no verified customer on this "
                "conversation. Call get_customer first, then retry with "
                "the returned customer_id."
            ),
        }
    return process_refund(customer_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason)

def gated_get_customer(conversation_id: str, identifier: str) -> dict:
    result = get_customer(identifier)
    if result.get("verified"):
        verified_customers[conversation_id] = result["customer_id"]
    return result

TypeScript

const verifiedCustomers = new Map<string, string>(); // conversationId -> customerId

async function gatedProcessRefund(
  conversationId: string, orderId: string, amountCents: number, reason: string,
) {
  const customerId = verifiedCustomers.get(conversationId);
  if (!customerId) {
    return {
      is_error: true,
      content:
        "process_refund blocked: no verified customer on this conversation. " +
        "Call get_customer first, then retry with the returned customer_id.",
    };
  }
  return processRefund(customerId, orderId, amountCents, reason);
}

async function gatedGetCustomer(conversationId: string, identifier: string) {
  const result = await getCustomer(identifier);
  if (result.verified) verifiedCustomers.set(conversationId, result.customerId);
  return result;
}

Interception versus PostToolUse

Both hooks sit in the loop, but they differ in timing:

  • Interception (PreToolUse, pre-call) inspects a call before dispatch and can block it.
  • PostToolUse inspects a result after it returns. The action has already happened.

Once process_refund returns, the money has moved. A PostToolUse hook can log the refund, flag it or page someone, but it can't reverse it. A rule like "refunds over $500 never go out without a human" has to be enforced before the call, by interception.

Python

REFUND_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 50_000

def intercept_process_refund(conversation_id: str, order_id: str,
                              amount_cents: int, reason: str) -> dict | None:
    """Return a blocking result if the call must not proceed, else None."""
    if amount_cents > REFUND_THRESHOLD_CENTS:
        return {
            "is_error": True,
            "content": (
                f"process_refund blocked: ${amount_cents/100:.2f} exceeds the "
                "$500 auto-approval threshold. Call escalate_to_human with a "
                "root cause and recommended action instead."
            ),
        }
    return None

def dispatch_process_refund(conversation_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason):
    blocked = intercept_process_refund(conversation_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason)
    if blocked is not None:
        return blocked
    return gated_process_refund(conversation_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason)

TypeScript

const REFUND_THRESHOLD_CENTS = 50_000;

function interceptProcessRefund(
  conversationId: string, orderId: string, amountCents: number, reason: string,
) {
  if (amountCents > REFUND_THRESHOLD_CENTS) {
    return {
      is_error: true,
      content:
        `process_refund blocked: $${(amountCents / 100).toFixed(2)} exceeds the ` +
        "$500 auto-approval threshold. Call escalate_to_human with a root cause " +
        "and recommended action instead.",
    };
  }
  return null;
}

async function dispatchProcessRefund(
  conversationId: string, orderId: string, amountCents: number, reason: string,
) {
  const blocked = interceptProcessRefund(conversationId, orderId, amountCents, reason);
  if (blocked) return blocked;
  return gatedProcessRefund(conversationId, orderId, amountCents, reason);
}

The blocking result redirects the agent by naming escalate_to_human, so it has a next step and doesn't retry or give up.

How the options in a typical refund-threshold question score:

Option Verdict
System prompt: escalate refunds over $500 Probabilistic. Insufficient for money
Few-shot example escalating a $600 refund Probabilistic
Interception blocking > $500, redirecting to escalation Correct
PostToolUse flagging > $500 for audit Right family, wrong direction. Every refund still goes out

PostToolUse: normalizing what comes back

PostToolUse solves data quality, not compliance. Real support tooling spans systems: lookup_order returns Unix epoch timestamps, get_customer returns ISO 8601, a third returns status codes 0/1/2 with the meaning in an unattached lookup table. If the model has to translate between formats on top of its real work, it will misread one now and then.

A PostToolUse hook rewrites every result into one shape (field names, date format, status vocabulary) before the model sees it.

Python

from datetime import datetime, timezone

STATUS_CODES = {0: "active", 1: "suspended", 2: "closed"}

def normalize_tool_result(tool_name: str, raw: dict) -> dict:
    result = dict(raw)
    if tool_name == "lookup_order" and isinstance(result.get("ship_date"), int):
        result["ship_date"] = datetime.fromtimestamp(
            result["ship_date"], tz=timezone.utc
        ).date().isoformat()
    if tool_name == "get_customer" and isinstance(result.get("status"), int):
        result["status"] = STATUS_CODES.get(result["status"], "unknown")
    return result

TypeScript

const STATUS_CODES: Record<number, string> = { 0: "active", 1: "suspended", 2: "closed" };

function normalizeToolResult(toolName: string, raw: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const result = { ...raw };
  if (toolName === "lookup_order" && typeof result.ship_date === "number") {
    result.ship_date = new Date(result.ship_date * 1000).toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  }
  if (toolName === "get_customer" && typeof result.status === "number") {
    result.status = STATUS_CODES[result.status as number] ?? "unknown";
  }
  return result;
}

Wire it into execute_tool from Chapter 2: call the tool, normalise, then serialise into content.

Agent SDK names (task 1.5 is phrased in SDK terms):

  • PreToolUse callback returns hookSpecificOutput with permissionDecision ("allow", "deny", "ask", "defer") and permissionDecisionReason. It can rewrite arguments via updatedInput instead of blocking.
  • PostToolUse callback returns additionalContext to append, or updatedToolOutput to replace the output before Claude sees it. This is how you normalise results in the SDK.

A prompt line such as "dates may be Unix or ISO; interpret carefully" usually works, but it costs tokens on every turn and the model still has to apply it correctly each time. If lookup_order is a third-party MCP server, you can't change what it returns, only what the model sees. A hook converts each result once, so every turn gets clean data.

When a prompt is enough

Hooks are code, so they can have bugs and need maintenance. For soft preferences, such as polite phrasing, offering store credit first or mentioning the loyalty programme, a prompt is enough because a miss costs little.

Ask whether an occasional miss would justify code that can never be skipped. For money, identity checks and compliance it would. For tone, phrasing or a choice between two acceptable orderings it wouldn't. Over-gating brings back the rigidity of the decision trees criticised in Chapter 2.

Multi-concern decomposition

"SO-44120 arrived damaged, and I was also charged twice for last month's subscription" is two concerns in one message. Two ways to handle it badly:

  • Resolving one and telling the customer to open a second ticket.
  • Handling independent concerns serially.

Both hurt first-contact resolution, the scenario's headline metric.

The correct pattern is to decompose the message into distinct items, investigate in parallel on shared context, and synthesise one unified resolution. Shared context means fetching the customer once and passing the same verified customer_id to both branches. If each branch calls get_customer itself, each one re-verifies through the gate. The two lookups are independent once the customer is known, so they can be parallel tool_use blocks.

Python

async def resolve_multi_concern(conversation_id: str, customer_identifier: str,
                                 concerns: list[dict]) -> dict:
    customer = gated_get_customer(conversation_id, customer_identifier)
    findings = await asyncio.gather(*(
        investigate(concern, customer_id=customer["customer_id"])
        for concern in concerns
    ))
    return synthesize_resolution(customer, concerns, findings)

TypeScript

async function resolveMultiConcern(
  conversationId: string, customerIdentifier: string, concerns: Concern[],
) {
  const customer = await gatedGetCustomer(conversationId, customerIdentifier);
  const findings = await Promise.all(
    concerns.map((concern) => investigate(concern, customer.customerId)),
  );
