  return synthesizeResolution(customer, concerns, findings);
}

Synthesis produces one reply that resolves both concerns.

Structured handoff

escalate_to_human fires when interception blocks a refund, policy is silent, or the customer asks for a person. The person who receives it has no access to the transcript and starts with nothing. Sending them the raw transcript leaves them to research the case under time pressure.

A structured handoff carries four fields:

Field Answers
Customer ID Who is this?
Root cause What happened?
Refund amount How much money is at stake?
Recommended action What should happen next?

Python

def escalate_to_human(customer_id: str, root_cause: str, amount_cents: int,
                       recommended_action: str) -> dict:
    return {
        "is_error": False,
        "content": json.dumps({
            "customer_id": customer_id,
            "root_cause": root_cause,
            "refund_amount_cents": amount_cents,
            "recommended_action": recommended_action,
        }),
    }

TypeScript

function escalateToHuman(
  customerId: string, rootCause: string, amountCents: number, recommendedAction: string,
) {
  return {
    is_error: false,
    content: JSON.stringify({
      customerId,
      rootCause,
      refundAmountCents: amountCents,
      recommendedAction,
    }),
  };
}

Wrong answers in the select-two version:

  • Raw transcript: what the structured handoff replaces.
  • Agent's self-reported confidence: the same unreliable signal rejected for autonomous escalation (Chapter 15), and just as unreliable here.
  • Tool calls with timings: debugging telemetry the human can't act on.

What the exam tests

  • Tasks 1.4 and 1.5: prompts have a non-zero failure rate, so enforcement for financial, compliance, or security misses belongs in code. The usual example is identity verification before a refund.
  • Agent occasionally skips a mandatory step: add a programmatic prerequisite gate. Not a stronger instruction, more few-shot examples, or an iteration-cap workaround.
  • Direction (a common 1.5 distractor): PostToolUse can't stop what already happened. Interception blocks before dispatch. PostToolUse for a refund threshold is the right family, wrong direction.
  • Interception redirects to escalate_to_human rather than issuing a bare denial.
  • Heterogeneous formats (Unix, ISO 8601, numeric codes): PostToolUse normalisation, not "interpret carefully".
  • Multi-concern: decompose, parallel on shared context, one resolution. Not serial, not escalated for being compound.
  • Handoff fields: customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action. Reject transcript, confidence score, and telemetry.
  • When not to hook: hooks are for guarantees, not preferences such as tone or phrasing.

Exercises

  1. Add verified_customers to Chapter 2's run_agent, wire in gated_get_customer/gated_process_refund, and push the model to refund before verifying. Confirm the block arrives as a normal tool_result and the model recovers.
  2. Put the $500 interception in front of gated_process_refund. Run a $200 and a $650 request, and confirm only the second is blocked and redirected to escalate_to_human.
  3. Build two lookup_order stubs (Unix and ISO ship_date) and make normalize_tool_result produce identical output. Then replace it with "interpret dates carefully" in the prompt, run 20 conversations, and compare delivery-window reasoning accuracy.
  4. Write resolve_multi_concern with two stub investigations sharing one customer fetch. Then make each call get_customer itself and observe the extra round trip the gate forces.

Chapter 7 — Sessions

You resume a two-day-old Claude Code session and Claude confidently describes a file you rewrote yesterday. Claude is reading its history correctly, but the history predates your change. Task statement 1.7 covers when to resume, when to fork, and when resuming is worse than starting over.

What a session is

A session is the running list of blocks: user turns, the model's text and tool calls, and the tool_result blocks that came back. It is replayed to the model every turn. Resuming reloads that list without revalidating any of it. Every tool result in it is treated as still describing the world.

That is why a resumed refactor remembers the plan and naming decisions. The list is also a cache, and it is correct only while the world still matches what it recorded.

Resuming a named session

The tested skill is using --resume <session-name> to continue a specific investigation, not just the latest one, because you usually have several lines of work going. Name a session at launch with claude -n <name> (or /rename mid-session), then resume it with claude --resume <name>. The SDK's resume option takes a session ID instead.

Say that on Monday Claude explored a legacy billing module, designed a split of process_refund out of a monolith, and started the new module. If nothing changed overnight, resuming on Tuesday is right, and re-deriving the work would waste time.

The rule is to resume when prior context is mostly still valid.

resume versus continue

resume continue
SDK form Python resume=<session_id> TS continue: true; Python continue_conversation=True
Takes an id? Yes No
Picks up Exactly the named session Whatever was most recent in the current directory
Scenario wording "a specific investigation from earlier" "the most recent session"

With several lines of work in one project, continue may pick the wrong one.

Resuming after files change

Overnight, a teammate rewrote six files in the auth module your session analysed. When you resume, the transcript still contains Monday's contents and analysis verbatim, and nothing marks them as stale. If you say nothing, Claude reasons from Monday's files and every downstream decision inherits the error. Chapter 4 showed an unlabelled failure being read as an empty result. Here an unlabelled stale result is read as current.

When you resume, tell the agent specifically what changed. Naming the six files by path makes the problem explicit and bounded. Claude re-reads exactly those files, keeps Monday's reasoning and discards only the facts that are out of date. This is the guide's skill of "informing a resumed session about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than requiring full re-exploration."

Python

resume_prompt = """
Resuming the refund-module refactor session.
Since we last worked on this, the following files were rewritten
upstream and your prior analysis of them is stale — re-read and
re-analyze these before continuing, everything else in your prior
context still holds:

  - src/billing/auth_context.py
  - src/billing/session_guard.py
  - src/billing/token_refresh.py
  - src/billing/scopes.py
  - src/billing/middleware.py
  - src/billing/audit_hooks.py

Do not rely on your previous reading of these six files.
"""

TypeScript

const resumePrompt = `
Resuming the refund-module refactor session.
Since we last worked on this, the following files were rewritten
upstream and your prior analysis of them is stale — re-read and
re-analyze these before continuing, everything else in your prior
context still holds:

  - src/billing/auth-context.ts
  - src/billing/session-guard.ts
  - src/billing/token-refresh.ts
  - src/billing/scopes.ts
  - src/billing/middleware.ts
  - src/billing/audit-hooks.ts

Do not rely on your previous reading of these six files.
`;

A vague "Some files changed, please double-check" triggers the unbounded re-exploration you resumed to avoid.

When to start a fresh session

A research session crawled competitor pricing, a regulatory filing, and news. By the time you return, prices have updated, the filing was amended, and three links 404. Most of what the session knows is suspect, and a "here's what changed" note can't fix that.

The guide says that starting a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results. A resumed history is tool_result blocks that were true when fetched, with no signal of decay. A fresh session seeded with a summary of only facts you've just re-confirmed (the questions, the conclusions that don't depend on today's prices, the sources worth revisiting) reasons from facts you have checked. Current Agent SDK guidance agrees. Once tool results have plausibly gone stale, it says to capture what you've learned as application state and pass it into a fresh session.

Python

structured_summary = """
Prior research session (competitor pricing analysis) concluded with
these durable findings — re-verify nothing below unless noted:

  - Research questions: (1) how does competitor X price the enterprise
    tier, (2) what regulatory constraints apply in the EU market.
  - Methodology that worked: querying the vendor's public pricing page
    plus the EU filing register directly outperformed general web search.
  - Durable conclusion: competitor X's enterprise tier is seat-based,
    not usage-based — this is a structural fact unlikely to have moved.

Treat all specific prices, filing statuses, and news article contents
from the prior session as UNVERIFIED. Re-fetch before citing any figure.
"""

TypeScript

const structuredSummary = `
Prior research session (competitor pricing analysis) concluded with
these durable findings — re-verify nothing below unless noted:

  - Research questions: (1) how does competitor X price the enterprise
    tier, (2) what regulatory constraints apply in the EU market.
  - Methodology that worked: querying the vendor's public pricing page
    plus the EU filing register directly outperformed general web search.
  - Durable conclusion: competitor X's enterprise tier is seat-based,
    not usage-based — this is a structural fact unlikely to have moved.

Treat all specific prices, filing statuses, and news article contents
from the prior session as UNVERIFIED. Re-fetch before citing any figure.
`;

No threshold number decides this, so place the scenario in one of two cases:

  • A known, enumerable subset changed: resume and inform.
  • Staleness is broad or unenumerable (a wide crawl aged out, the data source rotated, too much time passed): start fresh with a summary. A patch note would be as long and uncertain as redoing the work.

Forking

fork_session is for a different situation. You have paid for a shared baseline and want to explore several paths from it without them polluting each other, and without paying for the baseline twice.

For example, Claude has mapped a service's test setup (fixtures, mocks, flaky spots). Two strategies, "migrate to contract tests" and "add property-based tests", both need that map and then diverge.

  • Both in one session: strategy A's dead ends stay in context and warp reasoning about B.
  • Two fresh sessions: no pollution, but the careful exploration is repeated or reduced to a summary.
  • fork_session: each branch inherits the full baseline once, then diverges in isolation.

The research scenario is the same: fork after the shared literature review into a regulatory branch and a pricing branch.

In code, a fork is a resume with a flag that makes it branch from the baseline id instead of continuing it.

Python

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, query

contract_tests_branch = query(
    prompt="Propose a migration to contract tests for this service.",
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline_session_id, fork_session=True),
)

incremental_branch = query(
    prompt="Propose adding property-based tests to the existing suite.",
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline_session_id, fork_session=True),
)

TypeScript

import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk";

const contractTestsBranch = query({
  prompt: "Propose a migration to contract tests for this service.",
  options: { resume: baselineSessionId, forkSession: true },
});

const incrementalBranch = query({
  prompt: "Propose adding property-based tests to the existing suite.",
  options: { resume: baselineSessionId, forkSession: true },
});

Plain --resume twice would put both prompts in one growing transcript. (Python's ClaudeSDKClient wraps resume/fork in a session-holding object, so real apps rarely pass ids by hand.)

Situation Right mechanism Why
Continuing one investigation, prior context still holds --resume <session-name> Reuses valid context at no cost
Continuing one investigation, a known subset of files changed --resume, plus an explicit list of what changed Targets re-analysis instead of trusting stale results or re-exploring everything
Continuing one investigation, most tool results are stale or unenumerable Fresh session seeded with a structured, hand-verified summary Avoids re-presenting decayed tool output as current fact
Comparing two or more approaches from one shared baseline fork_session Keeps the full baseline once, isolates each branch's exploration from the others

What the exam tests

Task 1.7 stems ask you to pick one of the four rows above.

  • A handful of files changed: resume and name the files. Traps: resume silently (stale results read as current), or discard everything (throws away valid context to fix a narrow problem).
  • Broad staleness (long gap, wide crawl, external data): fresh session with an injected summary. A targeted note isn't enough because there's no small list to give. Know the reason: resumed tool_results carry no marker of decay.
  • "Compare" / "divergent approaches" from "the same starting point": fork_session. Traps: repeated --resume into one transcript, or duplicated fresh sessions that discard the baseline.

Exercises

  1. Start a multi-file exploration with claude -n billing-audit, exit, then edit two or three of the files it read. Resume twice with claude --resume billing-audit, once saying nothing and once naming the changed files, and compare how each reasons about them.
  2. Fork that exploration into an aggressive-refactor branch and a minimal one. Confirm neither sees the other, and note what you'd lose running both as follow-ups in the original session.
  3. After a wide web-research session, write a summary of only what you'd trust unchecked. Compare a fresh session seeded with it against resuming the original. Find where the resumed one cites a fetched detail as current.

Chapter 8 — MCP

As a consumer, MCP looks like a plugin system where you add a config entry and get new tools. The exam asks about what goes in the config, who else sees it, and whether a tool should exist at all.

MCP standardises the interface between an agent and an external capability. One GitHub server works from Claude Code, an Agent SDK app or another host.

Scope of task 2.4: configuration, scoping, discovery, descriptions, build versus buy. Out of scope: transports (stdio vs network), hosting, containers, load balancing, OAuth. An answer option that relies on one of these is a distractor.

What MCP standardises

Primitive What it is Example
Tools Actions that do something or fetch a specific known thing Jira search_issues, create_issue
Resources Read-only content to browse A docs table of contents, a label taxonomy
Prompts Reusable prompt templates shipped by the server Rarely used in Claude Code workflows. Just know it exists

Resources are for catalogs; tools are for actions. A resource fixes a specific reliability problem, where an agent that doesn't know what exists guesses and calls tools speculatively.

  • Issue tracker: without a resource, the agent calls search_issues 2–3 times with guessed keywords just to learn which components and labels exist. A resource exposing the label taxonomy, component list, or open-epic summary lets it read once, then make one targeted call.
  • Document store: a resource exposing folder hierarchy and titles stops repeated list_documents calls at different prefixes.

The exam won't ask you to implement resources by hand.

Scoping: local, project, and user

Scope decides who shares the configuration. It has no effect on how the model picks tools.

Scope Where Shared? Use for
Project .mcp.json at repo root, committed Everyone who clones Team workflow tooling a new hire should have on day one
User ~/.claude.json Just you, across all projects Personal integrations (calendar, notes)
Local ~/.claude.json, keyed to this project Just you, this project only, not in git Experiments, servers you're authoring, project-specific creds you won't commit
  • The exam guide uses the two-scope model (project vs user). Local is real in current Claude Code, but assume project-vs-user unless a question names local.
  • Don't confuse local MCP scope with .claude/settings.local.json, an unrelated use of "local".
  • Set scope with claude mcp add <name> --scope local|project|user ... rather than hand-editing ~/.claude.json.
  • The my-experimental-notes-server below fits local scope better than user scope today.
// .mcp.json — project scope, committed, shared with the team
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "jira": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@some-vendor/jira-mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_API_TOKEN": "${JIRA_API_TOKEN}",
        "JIRA_BASE_URL": "https://acme.atlassian.net"
      }
    }
  }
}

// ~/.claude.json — user scope, personal, not committed anywhere
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-experimental-notes-server": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/Users/paulo/dev/notes-mcp/index.js"]
    }
  }
}

Environment variable expansion. ${JIRA_API_TOKEN} in .mcp.json is a placeholder resolved from the runner's environment at connection time. The team shares the server config while each engineer's token stays in their own shell or .env. Hardcoding a token in .mcp.json is always wrong, because committing a secret leaks it.

  • Fallbacks: ${JIRA_BASE_URL:-https://acme.atlassian.net}.
  • Expansion works in env, in command/args (stdio), and in url/headers (HTTP).

Scope is not priority. Tools from every configured server, project and user alike, are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously, in one flat inventory with the built-ins. The model picks among them per turn, just as it picks between Grep and Glob. A question where a project server "takes priority" over a user server, or hides it, describes something that doesn't happen.

There is one narrow exception, which the exam doesn't test. When two scopes define a server with the same name, Claude Code resolves the collision with a fixed precedence (local, project, user, plugin, claude.ai connector, in that order) and connects once. That is scope resolution, and tool selection still has no priority.

Why your MCP tool loses to Grep

You install a server with a better, structured search, and Claude still uses Grep or WebSearch. The cause is the Chapter 3 principle that the description is prompt text read at selection time. Grep comes with a careful paragraph and your tool has "Search Jira issues", so the model has more evidence for Grep every time.

The fix is to enhance the MCP tool's description.

Python

search_issues = {
    "name": "search_issues",
    "description": (
        "Search Jira issues by text, status, assignee, or label within the "
        "acme-platform project. Returns issue key, summary, status, assignee, "
        "labels, and the last three comments for each match — structured data "
        "pulled live from Jira, not a text search over a local checkout.\n\n"
        "Use this for any question about tickets, bugs, or work items: "
        "'what's blocking the payments epic', 'find open bugs tagged "
        "checkout', 'who is assigned OPS-4471'.\n"
        "Do NOT use Grep or a general web search for these queries — issue "
        "text lives in Jira, not in the repository, and this tool returns "
        "current status and assignment that a code search cannot see.\n"
        "If no issues match the filters, returns an empty list; this is a "
        "successful call, not an error, and usually means the filters are "
        "too narrow rather than that Jira is unreachable."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "query": {"type": "string", "description": "Free-text search, e.g. 'refund timeout'."},
            "status": {"type": "string", "description": "Optional status filter, e.g. 'In Progress'."},
        },
        "required": ["query"],
    },
}

TypeScript

const searchIssues: Anthropic.Tool = {
  name: "search_issues",
  description: [
    "Search Jira issues by text, status, assignee, or label within the",
    "acme-platform project. Returns issue key, summary, status, assignee,",
    "labels, and the last three comments for each match — structured data",
    "pulled live from Jira, not a text search over a local checkout.",
    "",
    "Use this for any question about tickets, bugs, or work items: 'what's",
    "blocking the payments epic', 'find open bugs tagged checkout', 'who is",
    "assigned OPS-4471'.",
    "Do NOT use Grep or a general web search for these queries — issue text",
    "lives in Jira, not in the repository, and this tool returns current",
    "status and assignment that a code search cannot see.",
    "If no issues match the filters, returns an empty list; this is a",
    "successful call, not an error, and usually means the filters are too",
    "narrow rather than that Jira is unreachable.",
  ].join("\n"),
  input_schema: {
    type: "object",
    properties: {
      query: { type: "string", description: "Free-text search, e.g. 'refund timeout'." },
      status: { type: "string", description: "Optional status filter, e.g. 'In Progress'." },
    },
    required: ["query"],
  },
};

The "Do NOT use Grep" line names the competing built-in, as boundary sentences name sibling tools (Chapter 3). Community servers often ship thin descriptions, so when configuring one for a team, check them and wrap or override where needed.

Build versus buy

  • Standard integrations (Jira, GitHub, Slack, Drive, common DBs): use an existing community or vendor server, configured at project scope with env-expanded tokens. Someone has already handled pagination, custom-field mapping, rate limiting, and the API edge cases that only show up after months across many installations. A home-grown server handles the cases you tested and can fail without warning on the rest.
  • Team-specific workflows: build custom. Examples: one tool wrapping three internal systems, a resource exposing your own document taxonomy, business rules such as which refund reasons need a supervisor or which labels auto-escalate. A generic server can't know your rules exist. You also then own description quality from scratch, which is one more reason not to build by default.

What the exam tests

  • Scope recall: project .mcp.json (shared) versus user ~/.claude.json (personal/experimental), plus env var expansion. The wrong answer hardcodes a token in a committed file.
  • Scope ≠ priority: with both scopes configured, every server's tools are discovered at connection time and sit together in one inventory, with no scope-based priority.
  • Resources vs tools: an agent burning calls on exploratory discovery of a content catalog (issue summaries, doc hierarchy, schema) needs a resource, not a new tool or a bigger prompt.
  • MCP tool loses to Grep: enhance its description. Don't change scope, restrict the built-in, or add a routing rule.
  • Build vs buy: standard integration means a community server. Custom is only for team-specific needs.
  • Transports, hosting, and OAuth are out of scope.

Exercises

  1. In a real repo, write a project .mcp.json entry for a community server with ${VAR} for every credential, and a personal entry in ~/.claude.json. Justify each placement in one sentence.
  2. Inspect a tool description from an MCP server you use and audit it against Chapter 3's five elements. If it's thin, rewrite it, adding a sentence naming the built-in (Grep, WebSearch) it should beat.
  3. For an internal issue tracker, split capabilities into tools (create, transition, assign) and resources (label taxonomy, components, sprint summaries), justifying each as an action or a catalog.
  4. In 2–3 sentences, argue why a "file ticket + tag per internal escalation rules + notify on-call" tool should be custom rather than assembled from Jira and Slack servers, and name the business logic a generic server couldn't know.

Chapter 9 — Configuring Claude Code

You already use CLAUDE.md. This chapter gives you the exam's vocabulary for it (task statements 3.1 and 3.3): which file wins, what "shared" means at each level, and how rules are scoped. A rule can load because of where a file sits (directory-bound) or because of what kind of file it is (type-bound, via glob). Test files interleaved across 40 packages have no directory whose boundary is "every test file", so no directory layout can scope a rule to them, but a glob in .claude/rules/ can.

Slash commands, skills, and plan mode are in Chapter 10.

The CLAUDE.md hierarchy

Level Path Shared? Scope
Managed/enterprise policy macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md; Linux/WSL /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md; Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md Org-enforced. Can't be deleted or excluded Loads first
User ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md No. Your home dir, never in git Every project you touch
Project .claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md (both valid) Yes. Committed, reaches every clone and CI job This repo
CLAUDE.local.md Project root, gitignored No This repo, just you. Loads right after project CLAUDE.md
Directory CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory Yes (committed) Only work touching that subtree

User, project, and directory are the three the exam leans on. CLAUDE.local.md suits personal-but-repo-specific preferences, like "I run this repo's tests with -k slow".

Project-level is for anything the team must follow. User-level is for your own preferences (commit verbosity, explain-before-code) and is never right for team conventions.

A common diagnostic question has a new engineer clone the repo and find that half the team's conventions don't apply for them. The conventions are in the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, written as personal habit and never promoted. The fix is always to move the content from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to the project file. More documentation or an onboarding checklist doesn't fix it.

Directory-level handles conventions for one subtree. A monorepo keeps org-wide conventions at root, DB access patterns in services/billing/CLAUDE.md, and component conventions in apps/web/CLAUDE.md. Each loads only when work touches its subtree, so it activates on location.

Current product (not tested): levels don't override one another. Claude Code concatenates every loaded CLAUDE.md from root down to the working directory, so closer files are read last, and subdirectory files load on demand. @import follows up to four hops, with relative paths resolved from the importing file.

Modular organization: @import and .claude/rules/

Two separate tools break up a monolithic CLAUDE.md.

@import pulls an external file into a CLAUDE.md by path. The package maintainer picks which standards apply:

# services/billing/CLAUDE.md

This service handles payment processing and refund issuance.

@docs/standards/python-style.md
@docs/standards/api-design.md

Refunds above $500 require the process_refund tool's manual-review path;
see the runbook in docs/refunds.md before touching that code path.

A Terraform-only package imports terraform-conventions.md instead and never loads the Python guide.

  • AGENTS.md interop: Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when no CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above. Once a CLAUDE.md exists it reads that alone, unless it imports AGENTS.md. Keep one source with @AGENTS.md inside a CLAUDE.md (or a symlink) rather than two drifting files.
  • claudeMdExcludes (settings.json, any layer, arrays merge) excludes CLAUDE.md or rules files by glob on absolute paths. Use it to stop a subpackage inheriting a rule without moving the rule file.

.claude/rules/ splits one file doing too many jobs into topic files (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md), each small enough to own and review.

.claude/
  CLAUDE.md              # thin: project overview, links to rules
  rules/
    testing.md           # pytest conventions, fixture policy
    api-conventions.md   # REST error shapes, versioning policy
    deployment.md         # rollout steps, rollback procedure

Without frontmatter these files always load, so the split is only organisational. With paths frontmatter (below), they load conditionally.

Diagnosing with /memory and /context

Instructions come from several levels, imports, and rule files, so answering "why did Claude do that?" needs tooling.

On the exam, /memory verifies which memory files are loaded and diagnoses inconsistent behaviour across sessions. That is the guide's wording for task 3.1, and /context appears nowhere in the guide.

Current Claude Code differs. /memory now lists and opens CLAUDE.md and rules locations (including ones not yet created) and toggles auto memory. The docs point to /context for what actually loaded this session. In your own work, check /context first, then use /memory to open the file and find out why (wrong level, stale @import path, non-matching glob). On the exam, answer /memory.

Path-specific rules

A .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter paths: (a list of globs) loads only when the file being edited matches.

---
paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
---

# Terraform conventions

All resources must be tagged with `team` and `cost-center`. Modules under
terraform/modules/ are versioned by git tag, not by branch — never reference
a module by branch name in a `source` argument. Run `terraform fmt` before
every commit; CI will reject unformatted plans.

Mechanics:

  • Rules are discovered recursively (.claude/rules/frontend/testing.md works) and can be symlinked in, so one rule can be shared across repos.
  • ~/.claude/rules/ applies to all your projects and loads before the project's .claude/rules/. Both load, and the project rule is read later, so it takes priority on conflict.
  • Brace expansion works (**/*.{ts,tsx}), capped at 1000 expanded patterns and 4 MiB.

That Terraform example is directory-shaped, so a directory CLAUDE.md could also express it. The case only a glob can express is file type scattered across locations, which is the exam's sample question 6:

Button.tsx sits next to Button.test.tsx, and useAuth.ts next to useAuth.test.ts, across 40 component directories. You want one test rule: use the custom render wrapper, follow arrange-act-assert comments, mock the API client uniformly.

  • Root CLAUDE.md: the rule applies to components and tests alike, written as an "if this is a test file" aside. The model has to infer scope from prose.
  • CLAUDE.md in each directory: 40 copies, no single source of truth, and the rule is still keyed to address rather than suffix.
  • Glob rule: scopes on the filename pattern (*.test.ts).
---
paths: ["**/*.test.tsx", "**/*.test.ts"]
---

# Frontend test conventions

Use `renderWithProviders` from src/test-utils, never the raw `render` export
from the testing library — our components depend on theme and auth context
that raw render does not supply. Structure test bodies as arrange, act,
assert, with a blank line between each section. Mock the API client via
`mockApiClient()` from src/test-utils; do not construct ad hoc fetch mocks.

Editing any *.test.tsx anywhere loads it.

Scoping question Right mechanism Why
"Everyone on the team needs this instruction." Project-level CLAUDE.md (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md) Committed to version control, reaches every clone.
"Only I want this instruction, on every project I touch." User-level CLAUDE.md (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) Personal, never shared, not version-controlled.
"This convention applies to one subtree and nowhere else." Directory-level CLAUDE.md Directory-bound: loads based on where the edited file lives.
"This convention applies to a file type, wherever it appears in the tree." .claude/rules/*.md with a paths glob Type-bound: loads based on what the edited file is, regardless of location.
"This file is too big; I want to pull in only the standards relevant to this package." @import inside that package's CLAUDE.md Selective inclusion driven by maintainer judgment.
"This file is too big; I want to split it by topic without changing when anything loads." Plain files under .claude/rules/ (no paths frontmatter) Organizational split; always loaded, just not monolithic.

Token economy (the second half of 3.3): conditional loading keeps Terraform rules out of context while you edit React, and the reverse. A large root CLAUDE.md carries everything on every turn, so every turn pays for rules that do not apply.

Distractors for the scattered-tests scenario:

  • "Consolidate into root CLAUDE.md with a testing section." Relies on the model inferring scope from prose. There is no mechanical match, so the advice can leak into non-test files or be missed in a long file.
  • "Put it in a skill." Skills are invoked on demand, by command or by the model's judgement. A convention that must apply automatically every time can't depend on invocation.

Choosing between subdirectory CLAUDE.md and glob rules

If the boundary is a place in the tree, use a subdirectory CLAUDE.md. If it is a kind of file that appears in many places, use a glob rule.

In practice you combine them, with a thin root CLAUDE.md for orientation and org policy, directory files for the few location-bound conventions, and glob rules for the type-bound ones (tests, migrations, generated-code markers, IaC).

Auto memory

Auto memory is written by Claude, not you. It is stored under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/, is indexed by MEMORY.md, and loads at every session start in that project. Entries are typed (user, feedback, project, reference), capped around 200 lines / 25 KB.

  • CLAUDE.md: conventions you guarantee, reviewed and versioned.
  • Auto memory: what Claude learned about how you work (terse commits, a refactor already rejected, who owns deploys).

If Claude "remembers" something never written in any CLAUDE.md, that's auto memory, not a hierarchy level you missed.

What the exam tests

  • 3.1 levels and paths: user, project, directory (plus managed above, CLAUDE.local.md below project).
  • 3.1 diagnostic: new team member missing instructions because they sit in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Fix: promote to the project file.
  • @import ≠ .claude/rules/: @import selectively pulls standards files in, chosen by the maintainer. rules/ splits a monolith into topic files.
  • /memory verifies which memory files are loaded (the guide's answer, even though current Claude Code uses /context for this).
  • 3.3 discriminator: subdirectory CLAUDE.md is directory-bound (where the file lives). paths glob rules are type-bound (what the file is). For scattered conventions (interleaved tests, migrations across services), pick the glob and reject root consolidation (inference, not matching) and skills (invocation, not automatic).
  • Secondary benefit: path scoping keeps irrelevant rules out of context and off the token budget.

Exercises

  1. Run /context in a repo you maintain. Trace each loaded file to its level and to any @import or glob rule, and explain every surprise.
  2. Split a repo's conventions (testing, API errors, deployment) into .claude/rules/ files, and give at least one a realistic paths glob (**/*.test.ts, **/*.tf, **/migrations/*.py).
  3. Write one scenario where a subdirectory CLAUDE.md is right and one where it isn't, using the location-vs-type test. Write the glob rule for the second.
  4. Put a team convention in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, confirm with /context in a fresh clone or scratch home that it's absent, then promote it to the project file and confirm it appears.

Chapter 10 — Extending Claude Code

Slash commands and skills turn a prompt into a version-controlled file the team can invoke by name (task 3.2). Plan mode decides whether a task needs a design phase before any edit (task 3.4). The exam wants the exact mechanism (file, directory, frontmatter field) and the ability to pick the right one from a task description.

Slash commands

A custom slash command is a markdown file whose body becomes the prompt, and its filename is the invocation.

Location Scope Reaches
.claude/commands/ in the repo Project Every teammate on clone or pull, via version control
~/.claude/commands/ User Only you, across all projects

If /review must run the same way for every developer on clone, the answer is .claude/commands/. Distractors:

  • Put it in CLAUDE.md. CLAUDE.md carries context and standards, not invocable actions.
  • A registration file listing commands. None is needed, because the file's presence registers the command.

Personal shorthand that shouldn't reach teammates goes in ~/.claude/commands/.

.claude/commands/review.md          # project-scoped — every teammate gets /review
~/.claude/commands/my-triage.md     # user-scoped — only you get /my-triage

Skills

A skill is a command plus frontmatter that Claude Code enforces around the invocation. Current Claude Code treats them as one mechanism: .claude/commands/foo.md and .claude/skills/foo/SKILL.md both give /foo, and a skill is the superset.

Locations and precedence:

  • Enterprise/managed: org-controlled, applies to everyone.
  • Personal: ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md.
  • Project: .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, shared via git.
  • Plugin: <plugin>/skills/, invoked as plugin:skill to avoid name collisions.
  • Nested project dirs: apps/web/.claude/skills/deploy/ is invoked as /apps/web:deploy, so frontend and backend deploy skills can coexist in a monorepo.

Frontmatter fields the exam tests:

Field Does Use when
argument-hint Prompts the developer for a missing argument when invoked bare The skill can't work without, e.g., a service name or ticket. Otherwise it guesses or fails silently
allowed-tools Restricts tools during skill execution (the guide's framing) The skill must not be able to delete or run arbitrary shell. E.g. release notes: read plus file-write only
context: fork Runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context. Only the result returns to your conversation The skill is verbose (reads dozens of files for a 3-paragraph summary) or exploratory (brainstorming whose discarded options would bias later turns)
  • In current docs, outside the exam, allowed-tools lists tools usable without asking permission. That pre-approves them but doesn't block other tools. The field that removes tools is disallowed-tools. On the exam, allowed-tools restricts tools. In your repos, use disallowed-tools for the guarantee.
---
name: analyze-refund-patterns
description: Scans recent process_refund calls for anomalies and reports a summary.
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob
argument-hint: "[date-range, e.g. 2026-08-01..2026-08-31]"
---

The body after the frontmatter is plain markdown.

Who may invoke a skill:

  • disable-model-invocation: only a human can trigger it, never the model on its own judgement. Use it for side effects like /deploy.
  • user-invocable: false: hidden from the command list, so the model invokes it automatically. Use it for background-knowledge skills.
  • paths frontmatter: same glob scoping as .claude/rules/. The skill is considered for auto-invocation only when the current file matches.

Other frontmatter exists and isn't tested: when_to_use, arguments/$name, model, effort, background, agent, hooks, shell, metadata, license, compatibility.

Bundled skills (/doctor, /code-review, /run, /verify, /loop, /debug, …) ship out of the box. disableBundledSkills and skillOverrides turn them off or replace them.

Personal variants of a shared skill

To get different behaviour from a shared skill, create a second skill under a different name in ~/.claude/skills/. The project has .claude/skills/extract-invoice/SKILL.md, and you want currency normalisation too, so create ~/.claude/skills/extract-invoice-mine/SKILL.md. The shared skill is untouched and teammates are unaffected.

Skills versus CLAUDE.md

Choose by whether the content applies to every interaction or only to one nameable task, regardless of how important it is:

  • CLAUDE.md: universal standards loaded every turn, e.g. the commit message convention.
  • Skill: an on-demand, task-specific workflow, e.g. auditing process_refund call sites for compliance. Loading it every turn would waste context.

Plan mode versus direct execution

Decide from the task description, before any exploration, whether plan mode is needed.

Plan mode gives safe exploration plus a human-reviewed design before any file changes. It prevents rework from committing to the wrong design. Use it when there are several legitimate approaches and a wide blast radius. Typical cases:

  • Monolith to microservices.
  • Migrating 45 files to a new library version.
  • Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements.

Direct execution fits tasks with one reasonable shape: a single-file fix where the stack trace names the line, or adding one validation conditional. Planning those produces a plan that says "add the null check", which adds friction with no safety gain.

People often get the timing backwards. The complexity is stated in the request, and "Restructure into microservices" announces it in the first sentence. A common distractor starts in direct execution "to see how far you get" and switches to plan mode once things get messy. By then you've made hard-to-undo choices across many files, so choose plan mode at the outset.

Plan mode Direct execution
Number of legitimate approaches Several, actively competing One, or near enough that debate is wasted motion
What you're protecting against Costly rework from committing to the wrong design early Nothing unusual, only normal execution risk
Cost of using it anyway on the wrong case Ceremony and delay with no safety payoff Irreversible missteps across many files before anyone notices

Combine them. Plan the migration once (target API, order, special-case call sites), then directly execute the 45 edits. The plan is a durable spec the execution phase consumes. Treating plan mode and direct execution as one either/or choice for the whole task is a common wrong answer.

The Explore subagent

Investigation can consume the context budget the rest of the task needs: mapping 45 call sites, surveying service boundaries, dead ends. The Explore subagent does the verbose discovery in its own isolated context and returns a summary. It works the same way as context: fork (Chapter 5 covers subagent mechanics). Use it in the investigation phase of a multi-phase task so exploration doesn't exhaust context before you act. A plan that had to read all 45 files in-session leaves no room to discuss it.

What the exam tests

  • 3.2 placement: command or skill for every developer on clone goes in .claude/commands/ or .claude/skills/ (in git). A personal variant goes in ~/ under a new name, never as an edit to the shared file.
  • Frontmatter by scenario: noisy analysis or brainstorming means context: fork. Must not destroy anything means scoped allowed-tools. Invoked with no parameters means argument-hint.
  • Skill vs CLAUDE.md: always-loaded standards go in CLAUDE.md, on-demand workflows in a skill, regardless of importance.
  • 3.4: complexity stated up front (microservices, 45-file migration, integration choice) means plan mode at the outset, not midway. Single-file fix or one conditional means direct execution.
  • Combined: plan for investigation, direct execution for implementation. The Explore subagent keeps verbose discovery from exhausting context.

Exercises

  1. Write .claude/skills/audit-refund-flow/SKILL.md (checks process_refund call sites for missing identity verification) with context: fork and read-only allowed-tools. Then make a date-range version with argument-hint. Confirm the forked exploration never appears in your transcript.
  2. Before starting a real refactor, write one sentence on whether its complexity is declared up front. If it is, plan first and compare the plan with what direct execution would have done for the first few files.
  3. Copy a team skill under a new name into ~/.claude/skills/ and modify it. Confirm the original still behaves as teammates expect.
  4. On a small multi-call-site change, plan across all call sites, then execute. Note where the plan was wrong and whether an Explore pass first would have caught it.

Chapter 11 — Claude Code in CI

Interactive Claude Code waits for you when it's stuck or needs permission. In a pipeline nobody answers, so the job hangs until the runner times out. This chapter (task statement 3.6) covers what makes Claude Code a CI participant: a flag that never waits for input, flags for machine-parseable output, and CLAUDE.md as the way to tell an unattended instance what "good" looks like.

Running example: a PR review bot that checks a diff against team standards and posts inline comments. Secondary example: test generation for changed code.

The -p flag

-p / --print runs Claude Code non-interactively in a single shot. It takes the prompt, does the work, writes to stdout, and exits, without asking follow-up questions or blocking on stdin. Sample question 10 asks what fixes a CI job that hangs waiting for interactive input.

claude -p "Review the diff between origin/main and HEAD for correctness issues, \
security concerns, and violations of the standards in CLAUDE.md" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$(cat ./ci/review-schema.json)"

Wrong answers to reject by name:

  • CLAUDE_HEADLESS: doesn't exist.
  • --batch: doesn't exist.
  • < /dev/null: a generic Unix trick. It doesn't use Claude Code's non-interactive contract (write stdout, exit).

For GitHub Actions specifically, the official anthropics/claude-code-action wraps headless claude -p. It takes claude_args (e.g. --json-schema) and exposes structured_output as an Actions output. It is more idiomatic than hand-rolled subprocess calls. The code below does the same thing by hand.

Structured findings: --output-format json and --json-schema

The consumer is a script that posts inline comments at file and line, or decides pass/fail. Parsing prose breaks as soon as a word changes.

  • --output-format json: output is JSON.
  • --json-schema: constrains that JSON to your schema (fields, types, required), so the bot can deserialise into a known type.

Use them together. An option naming --output-format json alone, or regex-parsing prose, is incomplete.

Two mechanical gotchas the CLI enforces (the guide doesn't mention them):

  1. --json-schema takes the schema inline as a JSON string, not a file path. --json-schema ./ci/review-schema.json fails with --json-schema is not valid JSON. Keep the file in git, but pass its contents: "$(cat ./ci/review-schema.json)".
  2. --output-format json returns a single JSON object (result, session_id, usage, total_cost_usd, and structured_output when a schema is passed). Read json.loads(stdout)["structured_output"]. The array of events (system/assistant/user/result) belongs to --output-format stream-json, a newline-delimited stream for live progress (token-level needs --verbose --include-partial-messages). Treating the json output as an array gives a TypeError.

Finding schema:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "findings": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "file": { "type": "string" },
          "line": { "type": "integer" },
          "severity": { "type": "string", "enum": ["blocking", "warning", "nit"] },
          "message": { "type": "string" },
          "issueId": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["file", "line", "severity", "message", "issueId"]
      }
    }
  },
  "required": ["findings"]
}

Build in issueId from the start, because it's what makes duplicate-free re-review possible (below). Chapter 13 covers schema design in general.

Python

import json
import subprocess

def claude_structured(prompt: str, schema_path: str) -> dict:
    """Run Claude Code non-interactively and return the structured payload."""
    schema = open(schema_path).read()
    completed = subprocess.run(
        ["claude", "-p", prompt, "--output-format", "json", "--json-schema", schema],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True,
    )
    return json.loads(completed.stdout)["structured_output"]

def run_review(schema_path: str, base_ref: str = "origin/main") -> dict:
    return claude_structured(
        f"Review the diff between {base_ref} and HEAD against the standards "
        "in CLAUDE.md. Report only issues you are confident about.",
        schema_path,
    )

def post_inline_comments(findings: dict, pr_number: int) -> None:
    for finding in findings["findings"]:
        github_client.create_review_comment(
            pr_number,
            path=finding["file"],
            line=finding["line"],
            body=f"**{finding['severity']}**: {finding['message']}",
        )

TypeScript

import { execFile } from "node:child_process";
import { promises as fs } from "node:fs";
import { promisify } from "node:util";

const execFileAsync = promisify(execFile);

async function claudeStructured<T>(prompt: string, schemaPath: string): Promise<T> {
  const schema = await fs.readFile(schemaPath, "utf-8");
  const { stdout } = await execFileAsync("claude", [
    "-p", prompt, "--output-format", "json", "--json-schema", schema,
  ]);
  const response = JSON.parse(stdout) as { structured_output: T };
  return response.structured_output;
}

interface Finding {
  file: string;
  line: number;
  severity: "blocking" | "warning" | "nit";
  message: string;
  issueId: string;
}

async function runReview(schemaPath: string, baseRef = "origin/main"): Promise<{ findings: Finding[] }> {
  return claudeStructured(
    `Review the diff between ${baseRef} and HEAD against the standards in CLAUDE.md. ` +
      "Report only issues you are confident about.",
    schemaPath,
  );
}

async function postInlineComments(findings: { findings: Finding[] }, prNumber: number) {
  for (const finding of findings.findings) {
    await githubClient.createReviewComment(prNumber, {
      path: finding.file,
      line: finding.line,
      body: `**${finding.severity}**: ${finding.message}`,
    });
  }
}

The prompt line about confidence states the goal of minimising false positives, which matters because a bot that comments on every quibble gets muted within a week. It is a weak way to meet that goal, though. Chapter 12 explains why a vague appeal to confidence fails and why explicit report/skip categories in CLAUDE.md work better. The schema constrains the shape; the prompt and CLAUDE.md constrain which findings get posted.

Non-interactive execution

  • --bare is recommended for CI and scripting. It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, CLAUDE.md, and auto memory, for determinism across runners. The cost is that CLAUDE.md doesn't load either. If you need both reproducibility and team standards, supply them explicitly, e.g. --append-system-prompt-file.

  • Permission prompts stall a pipeline like unanswered stdin. Settle them up front:

    • --allowedTools pre-approves specific tools without restricting the rest. --tools restricts which tools exist, and --disallowedTools removes one.
    • --permission-mode (auto, dontAsk, acceptEdits) sets the default for everything else.

    A read-only review bot needs little. A test-generation pass must have the write tool pre-approved.

CLAUDE.md as the CI context mechanism

A CI instance has no memory of your interactive sessions. It doesn't know "no magic numbers" or "use Fixtures.customer()". CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for supplying testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria, loaded the same as in interactive sessions (without --bare).

Write specific rules. "Follow best practices" adds nothing, while "Flag any process_refund call without an idempotency key" encodes something you've been burned by.

Test generation: documenting what a valuable test looks like

Asking for "tests for this" produces lots of low-value tests: restating the type checker, testing getters. The fix in the Code Generation scenario is to document testing standards, valuable-test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md. For example:

  • One test per distinct business rule, not per code path.
  • Constructor and trivial-getter tests aren't valuable.
  • Use the Fixtures module, not inline literals.
  • Refund-window and partial-refund edge cases are always worth covering. Description-field formatting variants are not.

The second lever is to include existing test files in context as well as the changed source. Otherwise the pass can't know test_refund_after_window_closed exists and will propose a near-duplicate.

Python

def generate_tests_for_pr(changed_file: str, existing_test_file: str, schema_path: str) -> dict:
    existing_tests = open(existing_test_file).read()
    return claude_structured(
        f"Generate tests for the changes in {changed_file}. "
        "Testing standards and valuable-test criteria are in CLAUDE.md. "
        "Here are the existing tests for this module — do not propose scenarios "
        f"already covered:\n\n{existing_tests}",
        schema_path,
    )

TypeScript

async function generateTestsForPr(
  changedFile: string, existingTestFile: string, schemaPath: string,
): Promise<{ tests: unknown[] }> {
  const existingTests = await fs.readFile(existingTestFile, "utf-8");
  return claudeStructured(
    `Generate tests for the changes in ${changedFile}. ` +
      "Testing standards and valuable-test criteria are in CLAUDE.md. " +
      "Here are the existing tests for this module — do not propose scenarios " +
      `already covered:\n\n${existingTests}`,
    schemaPath,
  );
}

Why the session that wrote the code is a poor judge of it

Having the session that just wrote the code review it seems efficient, but it works worse than an independent instance, for these reasons:

  • While writing, the session made many small calls (skip this unlikely edge case, this name is close enough, this shortcut is fine), each reasonable in context.
  • Reviewing its own work, it grades decisions it just rationalised. Its context carries momentum toward "this is fine", and self-consistency makes it stick with earlier judgements rather than reopen them.
  • A fresh claude -p reads the diff against CLAUDE.md with no prior context and no investment in those choices, so it is better placed to catch the skipped null check or the misused fixture.

The CI pipeline should run a separate review step.

Avoiding duplicate comments across re-reviews

A bot that re-runs on every push reposts the same comments, because a fresh claude -p has no memory of the last run. The fix is to pass the prior findings in the prompt and instruct it to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. The bot's own state (a file, the comment thread, a DB row) holds the last run's issueIds.

Python

def run_incremental_review(schema_path: str, prior_findings: list[dict], base_ref: str) -> dict:
    prior_summary = json.dumps(prior_findings)
    return claude_structured(
        f"Review the diff between {base_ref} and HEAD against CLAUDE.md standards. "
        f"Here are findings from the previous review of this PR: {prior_summary}. "
        "Report only issues that are new since that review, or that were previously "
        "flagged and remain unaddressed in the current diff. Reuse the same issueId "
        "for a still-unaddressed issue rather than minting a new one.",
        schema_path,
    )

TypeScript

async function runIncrementalReview(
  schemaPath: string, priorFindings: Finding[], baseRef: string,
): Promise<{ findings: Finding[] }> {
  return claudeStructured(
    `Review the diff between ${baseRef} and HEAD against CLAUDE.md standards. ` +
      `Here are findings from the previous review of this PR: ${JSON.stringify(priorFindings)}. ` +
      "Report only issues that are new since that review, or that were previously " +
      "flagged and remain unaddressed in the current diff. Reuse the same issueId " +
      "for a still-unaddressed issue rather than minting a new one.",
    schemaPath,
  );
}

Rejected alternatives:

  • Don't re-run after new commits. You lose the safety net exactly when a fix introduces a new problem.
  • Diff raw comment text to suppress repeats. This is fragile, because slight rewording breaks the match.

What the exam tests

  • -p / --print is the only fix for a CI hang on interactive input. CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch are invented. /dev/null doesn't address the command contract. This is sample question 10.
  • --output-format json + --json-schema together give structured findings for inline PR comments. The payload is one object with structured_output. The event array is stream-json.
  • CLAUDE.md supplies testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria to CI runs. --bare skips its auto-loading, so "reproducible and must follow CLAUDE.md" means supplying it explicitly.
  • --permission-mode / --allowedTools pre-clear actions so the pipeline doesn't stall on a permission prompt.
  • Independent review instance beats self-review. Be able to explain why, in terms of momentum and self-consistency.
  • Avoid duplicate work, as a pair: prior findings plus "report only new or unaddressed" for re-review; existing test files in context for generation.

Exercises

  1. Add a claude -p review step to a GitHub Actions workflow on every PR, with --output-format json and your own --json-schema, posting each finding inline via the GitHub API. Confirm no hang on a large diff.
  2. Write a specific CLAUDE.md review and testing section (real fixture names, real "not worth flagging" examples). Run the same diff with and without it and compare, including false positives that disappeared.
  3. Run the bot, capture issueIds, fix one issue and leave one, push, and re-run with prior findings. The fixed one should drop off and the other persist with the same id.
  4. Have a session review its own nontrivial change to process_refund or extract_invoice, then run a fresh claude -p review of the same diff. Compare.

Chapter 12 — Prompt engineering

Every CLAUDE.md line you tightened because Claude kept getting it wrong was prompt engineering. The exam asks you to diagnose a prompt's failure and pick the matching fix.

Tasks 4.1 and 4.2 turn on one distinction. Explicit criteria fix a rule that was never written down. Few-shot examples fix a rule that is written down but applied inconsistently.

Task 3.5 (iterative refinement) is separate. It covers the process you run with Claude Code to converge on a working prompt or implementation, not what the prompt contains.

Running example

A review bot (the Code Generation scenario) has run on every PR for a month. About one comment in three is noise: style nits labelled "medium", or false alarms on patterns standard in this codebase. Developers stop reading it, including the comment that would have caught a real bug.

False positives in one category erode trust in every category, because readers don't track trust per category.

The instinctive fix is "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings", which is a named trap. General appeals to caution don't improve precision compared with specific categorical criteria. The model was already guessing at an undefined boundary. "Be conservative" makes it guess less often, in both directions, in a ratio you didn't choose.

4.1 When the rule does not exist

Write the rule down, as in this pair:

  • Vague: "Check that comments are accurate." This is a fuzzy standard that gets judged differently on Monday and Friday.
  • Explicit: "Flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior." This is an operational test. You read the claim, read the code, and check whether they contradict.

The general skill is to state which categories to report and which to skip, not to filter by confidence. Confidence is the model's self-assessment of an undefined question, and it is no more reliable than the question. Put bugs and security in scope, minor style and locally idiomatic patterns out, stated as rules about the code.

Python

REVIEW_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are reviewing a pull request diff for get_customer, lookup_order, and
process_refund. Report an issue only if it falls into one of these categories:

- BUG: the code will produce an incorrect result or crash on some input that
  the diff's tests do not cover. Do not report a bug for behavior that matches
  the existing tests, even if you would have designed it differently.
- SECURITY: the change introduces an injection risk, a missing authorization
  check on a path that mutates customer data, or logs a secret or PII field.
- COMMENT_MISMATCH: a comment or docstring makes a factual claim about
  behavior that contradicts what the code actually does. Do not report a
  comment merely because it is vague, outdated in tone, or could be phrased
  better — only contradiction counts.

Do NOT report: formatting, naming conventions, import order, or any pattern
that already appears elsewhere in this file. If a pattern is already in the
codebase, it is a local convention, not a bug, even if you would write it
differently.
"""

TypeScript

const REVIEW_SYSTEM_PROMPT = `
You are reviewing a pull request diff for getCustomer, lookupOrder, and
processRefund. Report an issue only if it falls into one of these categories:

- BUG: the code will produce an incorrect result or crash on some input that
  the diff's tests do not cover. Do not report a bug for behavior that matches
  the existing tests, even if you would have designed it differently.
- SECURITY: the change introduces an injection risk, a missing authorization
  check on a path that mutates customer data, or logs a secret or PII field.
- COMMENT_MISMATCH: a comment or docstring makes a factual claim about
  behavior that contradicts what the code actually does. Do not report a
  comment merely because it is vague, outdated in tone, or could be phrased
  better -- only contradiction counts.

Do NOT report: formatting, naming conventions, import order, or any pattern
that already appears elsewhere in this file. If a pattern is already in the
codebase, it is a local convention, not a bug, even if you would write it
differently.
`;

Severity: if labels vary with no anchor, define each level with a concrete code example. "High: an unauthenticated endpoint returning another customer's order history, like lookup_order(order_id) with no ownership check" can be pattern-matched. "High: something important" can't.

Disable a collapsing category. When one category's false positives are destroying trust and you haven't found the right criteria yet, turn it off. Ship BUG + SECURITY only, disable COMMENT_MISMATCH, fix its prompt offline against a sample set, and re-enable it once its precision is defensible.

4.2 When the rule exists but bends on hard cases

The criteria are in place and good, and the bot gets the obvious cases right, but it is inconsistent near the boundary. process_refund catches a broad exception and logs without re-raising, which could be a bug or deliberate degradation. It's flagged on some runs and not others. The rule is defined but applied inconsistently where judgement is needed, which calls for few-shot examples.

Few-shot means 2–4 fully worked examples in the prompt: input, reasoning, output. It works best for consistent, actionable output when prose keeps producing variation, because an example demonstrates the reasoning behind an ambiguous call, and the model can generalise that reasoning to novel cases. The examples don't need to cover every pattern, because they show how to weigh competing considerations.

Include the reasoning with each verdict.

  • "diff X → no finding" teaches one answer.
  • "diff X → broad catch swallows the exception without logging the customer-facing error path, no upstream handler visible, so a bug, not deliberate degradation → BUG, medium" teaches the test to run next time.

Python

FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES = """
Example 1 — ambiguous exception handling
Diff: process_refund catches `PaymentGatewayError` broadly, logs the message
at INFO level, and returns a generic success response to the caller.
Reasoning: swallowing a payment failure and reporting success to the caller
means a failed refund looks successful to the customer-facing code. This is
not a deliberate degrade-gracefully pattern (there's no fallback path here,
just silence), and the customer-facing consequence is a real correctness
issue, not a style choice.
Output: {"location": "process_refund:47", "issue": "Payment failure is
caught and logged but reported to the caller as success", "severity": "high",
"suggested_fix": "Return an error result when the gateway call fails instead
of a generic success payload"}

Example 2 — a broad catch that IS acceptable
Diff: lookup_order catches `Exception` around a metrics-emission call, logs
at DEBUG, and continues; the function's real return value is computed before
the try block and is unaffected either way.
Reasoning: the broad catch only protects a non-critical side effect
(metrics), and its failure cannot alter the function's actual return value.
This matches the existing pattern used around every other metrics call in
this file, so it's a local convention, not a bug.
Output: no finding.
"""

TypeScript

const FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES = `
Example 1 -- ambiguous exception handling
Diff: processRefund catches PaymentGatewayError broadly, logs the message at
INFO level, and returns a generic success response to the caller.
Reasoning: swallowing a payment failure and reporting success to the caller
means a failed refund looks successful to the customer-facing code. This is
not a deliberate degrade-gracefully pattern (there's no fallback path here,
just silence), and the customer-facing consequence is a real correctness
issue, not a style choice.
Output: {"location": "processRefund:47", "issue": "Payment failure is caught
and logged but reported to the caller as success", "severity": "high",
"suggestedFix": "Return an error result when the gateway call fails instead
of a generic success payload"}

Example 2 -- a broad catch that IS acceptable
Diff: lookupOrder catches a generic error around a metrics-emission call,
logs at DEBUG, and continues; the function's real return value is computed
before the try block and is unaffected either way.
Reasoning: the broad catch only protects a non-critical side effect
(metrics), and its failure cannot alter the function's actual return value.
This matches the existing pattern used around every other metrics call in
this file, so it's a local convention, not a bug.
Output: no finding.
`;

Named uses of few-shot:

  1. Ambiguous cases, shown with reasoning (above). The guide's examples: tool selection for ambiguous requests (below) and branch-level test coverage gaps (is an untested else branch worth flagging?).
  2. Distinguishing acceptable patterns from real issues. The pair above deliberately shows one real issue and one lookalike that's fine. Positives alone teach surface matching ("broad catch = flag").
  3. Output format. Location, issue, severity, fix, in order. The model copies a shown structure far more reliably than it follows a described one.
  4. Reducing hallucination in extraction from informal measurements and varied document structures. extract_invoice will fabricate total_amount when the total appears only as "call it forty-five hundred, even" in a footnote, unless it has seen that handled. Give 2–3 worked extractions covering real variants (line-item table with a totals block, total only in prose, implied discount), including absent field returns null, don't invent. The same applies to inline citations vs a bibliography, or methodology up front vs embedded in results.

Tool selection works the same way. "Where's my package" is clearly lookup_order. "Third time my order's been late, I want someone to look at my account" splits between lookup_order and escalate_to_human. An example reasoning that the repeated history and the word "someone" point to escalation, and that a lookup first only delays a human, teaches the weighing so it transfers to different wording.

Telling 4.1 and 4.2 apart

Few-shot is the wrong fix when no one has written down what counts, because there is no correct behaviour to demonstrate yet. Rewording the criteria is the wrong fix when they are agreed and the trouble is on judgement calls.

Symptom Diagnosis Fix
No stated rule for what counts as a bug vs. a nit Undefined decision boundary Explicit categorical criteria (4.1)
Severity labels vary reviewer to reviewer, no anchor Undefined severity scale Severity criteria with concrete examples per level (4.1)
One category has terrible precision, trust is collapsing Undefined or poorly-tuned rule for that category Disable the category temporarily, fix its prompt offline (4.1)
Rule is written down, edge cases still go wrong Defined boundary, inconsistent application 2 to 4 few-shot examples with reasoning (4.2)
Output format drifts run to run despite instructions Defined intent, inconsistent formatting Examples showing the literal output shape (4.2)
Extraction returns null or fabricates values on unusual documents Defined schema, inconsistent handling of varied structure Examples spanning the structural variants (4.2)

"Be conservative" is neither a criterion nor an example, so it fixes neither 4.1 nor 4.2.

3.5 Iterative refinement

Task 3.5 covers how you converge on a result with Claude Code, turn by turn, using four techniques:

  1. Concrete input/output examples when prose fails. "Normalise dates, handling the three legacy formats" gets read inconsistently. 2–3 exact input/output pairs pin it down. It's the same mechanism as few-shot, used to communicate a spec during development. The guide's named case is data-migration edge cases. Instead of "handle nulls sensibly", give customer_id: null, order_total: 45.00 → route to the quarantine table, don't insert with a fabricated ID.
  2. Test-driven iteration. Write tests first (expected behaviour, edge cases, performance requirements), then iterate by feeding Claude Code the test failures. A failing test is a precise, falsifiable statement of the gap, and every red test replaces a round of "no, I meant…".
  3. The interview pattern. Have Claude Code ask you questions first, as a competent engineer would before coding. It is most valuable in unfamiliar domains, where it brings up things you wouldn't think to specify: cache invalidation strategy for a caching layer, failure modes of a job queue you've never run. It's the clarifying question in plan mode, invoked deliberately and up front.
  4. Single message vs sequential, depending on whether the problems interact:
    • Independent (a typo here, an unrelated off-by-one there): fix sequentially. Bundling adds nothing and makes each fix harder to verify.
    • Interacting (a caching bug plus an invalidation-ordering bug that only makes sense given the first): one detailed message. Fixed separately, the first fix can invalidate your description of the second or make it worse. For example, a migration's null-handling fix depends on where the transaction boundary is placed.

Context awareness

On Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, and Haiku 4.5, Claude automatically receives <budget:token_budget> and <system_warning>Token usage: X/Y remaining</system_warning> as a conversation runs. So "as you approach your budget, stop exploring and write up what you have" now works without you computing the number.

It does not replace Chapter 14's case-facts block or manifest. Budget awareness paces work against a shrinking window. Those patterns decide which exact numbers and conclusions must survive compaction. A model that wraps up gracefully at 90% can still lose a dollar amount to summarisation.

Models older than Opus 4.7 don't get this automatically. They need an explicit task budget via a beta flag, stated in the prompt.

What the exam tests

  • 4.1/4.2 as a diagnostic pair. A frequent trap is "be more conservative" or "raise the confidence threshold". Treat any general appeal to caution as wrong.
  • Missing boundary (4.1): write criteria, define severity with concrete examples, or temporarily disable a collapsing category.
  • Shaky on ambiguous cases (4.2): 2–4 few-shot examples showing reasoning, distinguishing acceptable from real issues, demonstrating output format.
  • Extraction under 4.2: varied document structure and null-field fabrication are few-shot problems once the schema is correct. Schema problems are Chapter 13.
  • 3.5: concrete I/O examples after prose has failed; test-first with failures as feedback; interview pattern for unfamiliar domains; single message vs sequential depends on interaction.

Exercises

  1. Write a vague review prompt ("check for bugs and be careful about false positives"). Run it on a diff with one real bug and two borderline patterns. Rewrite it with explicit report/skip categories and confirm the borderline verdicts moved (the 4.1 effect).
  2. Add two reasoning-bearing few-shot examples (one flag, one not). Test on a third, unseen borderline pattern and check that the model generalises the reasoning (the 4.2 effect).
  3. Run an ambiguous transformation (real-world dates, or mapping requests to lookup_order/escalate_to_human) three times from prose alone, then three times with 2–3 I/O examples. Compare the variance.
  4. Build interacting problems: a rate limiter with a counter race plus a window off-by-one, where fixing the boundary moves the race. Report both in one message, then sequentially in a fresh session. If the sequential first fix has to be partly undone, you've reproduced the 3.5 failure.

Chapter 13 — Structured output

When output goes to a program rather than a person, a careful prompt that asks for JSON isn't enough. The running example is extract_invoice, which returns vendor, line items, taxes, and total for an accounts-payable pipeline.

It fails in two different ways, with different fixes:

  • Syntax: malformed JSON (dangling comma, unescaped quote in "Smith & Sons"). Fixed by schema and tool use.
  • Semantics: well-formed JSON that is wrong (line items sum to $412.50, total says $391.00). Fixed by validation.

Using a stricter schema for a semantic error, or validation for a syntax error, is a misdiagnosis.

Tool use as the extraction mechanism

A tool_use block's input conforms to the tool's input_schema. For extraction, the "tool" does nothing and extract_invoice touches no database. Its schema is the contract, and tool_use.input arrives as a parsed object.

Tool use is a reliable way to get schema-compliant output. Asking for JSON in prose means validating a string after the fact, and a dropped brace shows up at json.loads, far from the cause. With tool use there's no string to parse, so malformed JSON is structurally impossible, which is a guarantee and not only a lower error rate.

Python

extract_invoice = {
    "name": "extract_invoice",
    "description": (
        "Extract structured data from an invoice document: vendor identity, "
        "line items, tax, and totals. Use this on any invoice, receipt, or "
        "billing statement provided as text or an attached document. Do not "
        "use this on purchase orders or shipping manifests, which have no "
        "total to reconcile."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "vendor_name": {"type": "string"},
            "invoice_number": {"type": ["string", "null"]},
            "invoice_date": {
                "type": ["string", "null"],
                "description": "ISO 8601 date, e.g. 2026-03-14. Null if unreadable.",
            },
            "line_items": {
                "type": "array",
                "items": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "description": {"type": "string"},
                        "quantity": {"type": "number"},
                        "unit_price": {"type": "number"},
                        "line_total": {"type": "number"},
                    },
                    "required": ["description", "quantity", "unit_price", "line_total"],
                },
            },
            "tax_amount": {"type": ["number", "null"]},
            "stated_total": {
                "type": "number",
                "description": "The total as printed on the invoice.",
            },
            "calculated_total": {
                "type": "number",
                "description": (
                    "Sum of line_total across line_items, plus tax_amount. "
                    "Compute this yourself; do not copy stated_total."
                ),
            },
            "conflict_detected": {
                "type": "boolean",
                "description": "True if calculated_total and stated_total differ by more than $0.01.",
            },
            "category": {
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["goods", "services", "subscription", "other"],
            },
            "category_detail": {
                "type": ["string", "null"],
                "description": "Required when category is 'other'; free-text description.",
            },
        },
        "required": [
            "vendor_name", "line_items", "stated_total",
            "calculated_total", "conflict_detected", "category",
        ],
    },
}

TypeScript
