Reading the result:

Python

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=[extract_invoice],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice_text}],
)
invoice_block = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
invoice_data = invoice_block.input  # already a parsed dict, schema-shaped

TypeScript

const response = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-sonnet-5",
  max_tokens: 1024,
  tools: [extractInvoice],
  tool_choice: { type: "tool", name: "extract_invoice" },
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: invoiceText }],
});
const invoiceBlock = response.content.find(
  (b): b is Anthropic.ToolUseBlock => b.type === "tool_use",
);
const invoiceData = invoiceBlock!.input; // already parsed, schema-shaped

output_config.format and strict tool use

  • output_config.format with {"type": "json_schema", "schema": {...}} is dedicated structured output with no tools involved. Constrained decoding guarantees a match, and the JSON arrives in a plain text block. It is the more direct fit when there's no natural "tool", e.g. classifying a ticket into fixed fields.
  • strict: true on a tool definition. tool_choice forcing guarantees that a call happens, but without strict the arguments are only reliable, not guaranteed. strict applies constrained decoding to the arguments, so extract_invoice should carry it.

The two are independent. output_config.format shapes the answer and strict shapes tool calls, so one request can use both (e.g. lookup-then-report).

Python

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice_text}],
    output_config={
        "format": {
            "type": "json_schema",
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "vendor_name": {"type": "string"},
                    "stated_total": {"type": "number"},
                },
                "required": ["vendor_name", "stated_total"],
                "additionalProperties": False,
            },
        }
    },
)
invoice_data = json.loads(response.content[0].text)

TypeScript

const response = await client.messages.create({
  model: "claude-sonnet-5",
  max_tokens: 1024,
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: invoiceText }],
  output_config: {
    format: {
      type: "json_schema",
      schema: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          vendor_name: { type: "string" },
          stated_total: { type: "number" },
        },
        required: ["vendor_name", "stated_total"],
        additionalProperties: false,
      },
    },
  },
});
const invoiceData = JSON.parse(response.content[0].text);

Supported JSON Schema subset (both mechanisms):

  • No numeric bounds (minimum, maximum, multipleOf).
  • No string length bounds.
  • additionalProperties must be false.
  • No recursive schemas.
  • Only a limited regex dialect for pattern.

Nullable ["string", "null"] and enum-plus-detail (below) still work. Move range and length checks into your own code.

The first call with a schema pays grammar compilation latency. The grammar is cached for 24 h from last use. Changing the schema invalidates both the cached grammar and the prompt cache, so keep the schema fixed and put per-request variation in the prompt text.

Choosing how the tool gets called

Setting Guarantees Invoice-pipeline use
{"type": "auto"} Nothing. Claude may answer in text Wrong default for extraction
{"type": "any"} Some tool is called Mixed document stream, schema unknown until Claude looks
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} That specific tool is called Document type known, or extraction must precede enrichment
  • "any": a mixed stream (invoices, POs, manifests). Claude must pick some extraction tool, classifying implicitly.
  • Forced: force extract_invoice first when enrich_vendor_record needs vendor_name, or flag_for_review needs conflict_detected. Then return to "auto".

Current product (not tested): forced tool_choice returns a 400 on Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1; see Chapter 2. On those models use strict: true or output_config.format.

Schema design decisions

  • Required fields invite fabrication. Require invoice_number and a receipt that lacks one will sometimes get an invented value. Make it nullable (["string", "null"]). An honest null trips your validation, but a fabricated value passes it.
  • Enum with an escape hatch. category ∈ "goods", "services", "subscription", "other", plus category_detail, required when "other". You get clean aggregation on the common cases and an accurate description of the rest.
  • "unclear" for judgement enums (paid/unpaid/disputed), so an ambiguous case has a legitimate answer and the model isn't forced into a wrong guess.
  • Format normalisation goes in the prompt, not the schema. A string field accepts 03/14/2026, 14 Mar 2026, and 2026-03-14 alike. "Return dates as ISO 8601; if ambiguous, infer the most likely reading" does what no pattern can.

Syntax versus semantics

Schema compliance tells you the output parses, not that it's correct. The $412.50 vs $391.00 invoice is fully schema-valid. Structure says nothing about arithmetic, provenance, or internal consistency.

The worked example has the model do the arithmetic in a checkable field.

  • stated_total: the number printed on the document.
  • calculated_total: "sum of line_total across line_items, plus tax_amount. Compute this yourself; do not copy stated_total."

The model has to add up the lines instead of copying the printed total, and your code diffs the two. A difference of more than a cent goes to a human before AP.

conflict_detected is a boolean the model sets when the document is internally inconsistent (totals that disagree, two dates for one event, a name spelled two ways). Because it is a field, the pipeline can check it on every document.

Failure Fixed by
Malformed / unparseable JSON Schema + tool use (eliminated structurally)
Required field omitted Tool use catches and refuses it. Whether retry helps is the next section
Valid JSON, wrong values (don't reconcile, wrong field, fabrication) Validation logic, not a stricter schema

Validation, retry, and feedback loops

Retry only fixes some failures:

  • Retriable: the information is in the document and the first pass got it wrong (an omitted field, a dropped line item, a miscalculated total).
  • Not retriable: the information isn't in the source (e.g. a PO in a system you never provided). Attempt five has no more access than attempt one, and an unguarded loop burns requests forever. Route to a human, or to a step that fetches the missing document.

Classify the failure before retrying. When you retry, send the original document + the failed extraction + the specific validation error, so the model fixes a named mistake.

Python

def retry_extraction(client, document_text, failed_extraction, validation_error):
    retry_prompt = (
        f"The previous extraction of this invoice failed validation:\n\n"
        f"{validation_error}\n\n"
        f"Previous extraction:\n{json.dumps(failed_extraction, indent=2)}\n\n"
        f"Original invoice:\n{document_text}\n\n"
        f"Re-extract, correcting the specific issue above. Recompute "
        f"calculated_total from line_items rather than reusing the prior value."
    )
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=[extract_invoice],
        tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": retry_prompt}],
    )
    return next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use").input

TypeScript

async function retryExtraction(
  client: Anthropic,
  documentText: string,
  failedExtraction: unknown,
  validationError: string,
): Promise<unknown> {
  const retryPrompt = [
    `The previous extraction of this invoice failed validation:`,
    ``,
    validationError,
    ``,
    `Previous extraction:`,
    JSON.stringify(failedExtraction, null, 2),
    ``,
    `Original invoice:`,
    documentText,
    ``,
    `Re-extract, correcting the specific issue above. Recompute`,
    `calculated_total from line_items rather than reusing the prior value.`,
  ].join("\n");

  const response = await client.messages.create({
    model: "claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens: 1024,
    tools: [extractInvoice],
    tool_choice: { type: "tool", name: "extract_invoice" },
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: retryPrompt }],
  });
  const block = response.content.find(
    (b): b is Anthropic.ToolUseBlock => b.type === "tool_use",
  );
  return block!.input;
}

For code-scanning agents, detected_pattern is a field naming the construct that triggered each finding. When developers dismiss findings, group the dismissals by detected_pattern to see which construct over-triggers. Like calculated_total, it turns part of the model's reasoning into a field you can query.

Designing for batch volume

Message Batches API (task 4.5):

  • 50% cheaper, flat, not volume-tiered.
  • Processed within up to 24 hours, with no SLA for anything faster. Design for the slow case.
  • Not for multi-turn tool calling (see below).
  • Every request carries a custom_id.

The deciding question is latency tolerance, not cost, meaning whether anyone is blocked waiting for the result.

  • Fits: overnight tech-debt report, weekly compliance audit, nightly test generation, nightly invoice reconciliation. The consumer checks a dashboard tomorrow.
  • Doesn't fit: a pre-merge check. A developer can't wait an unknown 20 minutes to 24 hours.

The SLA arithmetic

Suppose the commitment is a 30-hour SLA and you batch on a fixed schedule.

  • Worst case = wait until the next submission + up to 24 h of processing.
  • 30 − 24 = 6 h of budget for the wait.
  • Every 6 h gives a 30 h worst case, exactly at the ceiling with no margin.
  • Every 4 h gives a 28 h worst case and a 2 h buffer, which makes it the correct answer.

In general, subtract the window from the SLA, then choose an interval comfortably inside the remainder, not at the boundary.

Batch requests

A batch is a list of ordinary Messages requests, each with your custom_id. You submit it, poll, and read the results. They come back in any order, so match on custom_id, never on position.

Python

from anthropic.types.message_create_params import MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming
from anthropic.types.messages.batch_create_params import Request

batch_requests = [
    Request(
        custom_id=f"invoice-{invoice['id']}",
        params=MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming(
            model="claude-sonnet-5",
            max_tokens=1024,
            tools=[extract_invoice],
            tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": invoice["text"]}],
        ),
    )
    for invoice in todays_invoices
]

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=batch_requests)

# Later, after polling batch.processing_status until "ended":
for result in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if result.result.type == "succeeded":
        block = next(b for b in result.result.message.content if b.type == "tool_use")
        store_invoice(custom_id=result.custom_id, data=block.input)
    else:
        queue_for_resubmission(custom_id=result.custom_id, failure=result.result)

TypeScript

const batchRequests = todaysInvoices.map((invoice) => ({
  custom_id: `invoice-${invoice.id}`,
  params: {
    model: "claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens: 1024,
    tools: [extractInvoice],
    tool_choice: { type: "tool" as const, name: "extract_invoice" },
    messages: [{ role: "user" as const, content: invoice.text }],
  },
}));

const batch = await client.messages.batches.create({ requests: batchRequests });

// Later, after polling batch.processing_status until "ended":
for await (const result of client.messages.batches.results(batch.id)) {
  if (result.result.type === "succeeded") {
    const block = result.result.message.content.find(
      (b): b is Anthropic.ToolUseBlock => b.type === "tool_use",
    );
    storeInvoice(result.custom_id, block!.input);
  } else {
    queueForResubmission(result.custom_id, result.result);
  }
}

A batch request does not support multi-turn tool calling. Each entry is one call. It can return tool_use, but nothing executes the tool and feeds the result back, and no error tells you so.

  • Fits: invoice extraction, because extract_invoice is never executed. The tool block is just the vehicle for structured output.
  • Doesn't fit: look up a vendor mid-extraction, decide whether to flag, then extract. That loop needs multi-turn execution. Run it synchronously, or split it into a batch-friendly first pass plus a later step.

Handling batch failures

  • Results come back errored, canceled, or expired for some fraction. Resubmit only the failed custom_ids, never the whole batch.
  • If failures share a cause, such as oversized scans exceeding context, fix the cause before resending, for example by chunking those documents.
  • Before batching the full volume, run 50–100 invoices synchronously and iterate until first-pass success is high. Discovering a date-format gap after a day-long batch costs the day plus the redo.

What the exam tests

  • 4.3: guaranteed-parseable output needs tool_use + JSON schema, which eliminates syntax errors as a category. tool_choice: "any" when the doc type is unknown, forced when it's known or must precede enrichment.
  • 4.4: syntax vs semantics. Malformed is a schema problem. Well-formed but inconsistent is a validation problem. Be able to reproduce calculated_total vs stated_total + conflict_detected from memory.
  • 4.4 retry classification: format and arithmetic errors are retriable. Information absent from the source is not, so route to a human.
  • 4.5 arithmetic: SLA minus 24 h window, then an interval comfortably inside the remainder (30 h gives every 4 h).
  • 4.5: "call a tool, see the result, decide next" can't run in a batch request. Resubmit only failed custom_ids.

Exercises

  1. Build extract_invoice. Run five invoices with inconsistent totals and confirm conflict_detected flags all five. Then simulate raw-text JSON corruption and note that tool use eliminates it.
  2. Write a retry harness sending document + failed extraction + specific error. Test an arithmetic slip (fixable) and a field that is absent from the document (not fixable, whatever the attempt count).
  3. Redo the SLA arithmetic for a 20-hour SLA with a 24 h window. Can any cadence satisfy it? Explain why not once the SLA is shorter than the window.
  4. Batch ten invoices including one malformed document. Poll, iterate by custom_id, and resubmit only the failure.

Chapter 14 — Context engineering

Two hours into a session, answers soften ("typically follows the pattern used elsewhere") and after /compact a decision from 20 minutes ago has to be repeated. Both have the same cause. The messages array is finite, it holds everything the agent knows, and neither growth nor compression is free.

Task 5.1 Task 5.4
Problem Keep critical facts alive in one long conversation Coordinate context across an exploration too big for one conversation
Example A two-hour, three-issue support case where a dollar amount must survive exactly A multi-phase codebase investigation across subagents
Key fixes Case-facts block, trim tool output Subagents, scratchpads, phase summaries, manifests

5.1 Preserving facts inside one long conversation

  1. Progressive summarisation destroys specifics. Paraphrase keeps the gist and loses numbers. "Customer disputed a charge and we discussed a refund" is a faithful summary of "disputed a $284.17 charge on SO-88213, promised a refund by the 15th, second contact". The amount, order ID, and date are gone. Summarisation is working as designed when it does this.
  2. Lost in the middle. Models attend reliably to the start and end of long input and worse to the middle. A fact stated once mid-conversation is at higher risk of being ignored. It comes from how models read long input, so a model upgrade won't remove it.
  3. Tool results cost tokens by size, not relevance. A realistic lookup_order returns 40+ fields (SKUs, routing codes, tax flags, three address blocks). A return needs five: order id, item, amount, ship date, status. Nothing removes an appended result, so three lookups bury the signal under a hundred-plus irrelevant fields, reprocessed every turn.

The API is stateless, so you must pass the complete history with every request. If you drop earlier turns to save tokens, the model knows nothing about them.

On Claude 4.5+, running out of room mid-generation gives stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded" (older models reject the request outright). Handle it separately from max_tokens, which looks similar but has a different cause.

The case-facts block

The fix is to extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses, customer-stated expectations) into a structured block that you include in full in every prompt, outside summarised history. It is the per-conversation equivalent of CLAUDE.md sitting in system rather than messages.

Python

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class CaseFacts:
    """Durable, non-summarizable facts for one support case."""
    customer_id: Optional[str] = None
    tier: Optional[str] = None
    issues: list[dict] = field(default_factory=list)
    # each issue: {order_id, amount_cents, status, promised_date, stated_by_customer}

    def render(self) -> str:
        lines = [f"CASE FACTS (verified, do not paraphrase):",
                  f"customer_id={self.customer_id} tier={self.tier}"]
        for i, issue in enumerate(self.issues, start=1):
            lines.append(
                f"  issue {i}: order={issue['order_id']} "
                f"amount=${issue['amount_cents']/100:.2f} "
                f"status={issue['status']} "
                f"promised_by={issue.get('promised_date', 'n/a')}"
            )
        return "\n".join(lines)


def build_request(case_facts: CaseFacts, messages: list, user_turn: str) -> dict:
    # The facts block rides in `system`, alongside the persistent instructions,
    # so /compact and any summarization pass over `messages` never touch it.
    return {
        "model": "claude-sonnet-5",
        "system": f"{SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\n{case_facts.render()}",
        "messages": messages + [{"role": "user", "content": user_turn}],
    }

TypeScript

interface Issue {
  orderId: string;
  amountCents: number;
  status: string;
  promisedDate?: string;
}

interface CaseFacts {
  customerId?: string;
  tier?: string;
  issues: Issue[];
}

function renderCaseFacts(facts: CaseFacts): string {
  const lines = [
    "CASE FACTS (verified, do not paraphrase):",
    `customer_id=${facts.customerId} tier=${facts.tier}`,
  ];
  facts.issues.forEach((issue, i) => {
    lines.push(
      `  issue ${i + 1}: order=${issue.orderId} ` +
        `amount=$${(issue.amountCents / 100).toFixed(2)} ` +
        `status=${issue.status} promised_by=${issue.promisedDate ?? "n/a"}`,
    );
  });
  return lines.join("\n");
}

function buildRequest(facts: CaseFacts, messages: Anthropic.MessageParam[], userTurn: string) {
  return {
    model: "claude-sonnet-5",
    system: `${SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT}\n\n${renderCaseFacts(facts)}`,
    messages: [...messages, { role: "user" as const, content: userTurn }],
  };
}
  • Rebuilt each request from your application state, not produced by asking the model to summarise itself, so it never passes through lossy compression.
  • A separate layer per issue in multi-issue sessions. A billing dispute plus a later shipping complaint each keep their own order id, amount, and status. If both are written in one paragraph, the second issue can end up with the first one's amount. Structured issue data lets the agent answer "status of the shipping issue?" without wading through the billing discussion.

Trimming tool output at the source

The case-facts block protects facts after extraction. Tool bloat happens earlier, when lookup_order returns. Trim before appending. You design the tool boundary, so make the function the agent calls project the full record down to what the task needs.

Python

RETURN_RELEVANT_FIELDS = {"order_id", "item", "amount_cents", "ship_date", "status"}

def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    full_record = fulfillment_backend.get_order(order_id)  # 40+ fields
    return {k: v for k, v in full_record.items() if k in RETURN_RELEVANT_FIELDS}

TypeScript

const RETURN_RELEVANT_FIELDS = new Set([
  "orderId", "item", "amountCents", "shipDate", "status",
]);

async function lookupOrder(orderId: string): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
  const fullRecord = await fulfillmentBackend.getOrder(orderId); // 40+ fields
  return Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(fullRecord).filter(([key]) => RETURN_RELEVANT_FIELDS.has(key)),
  );
}

Once fields are in several tool_results, only a destructive rewrite removes them, and that rewrite is the summarisation that damages numbers.

When you don't own the tool (a third-party MCP server), use the context editing API (beta context-management-2025-06-27) as a fallback:

  • context_management: {"edits": [{"type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919", ...}]} clears old tool results by rule.
  • Knobs: trigger (when), keep (recent results to leave), clear_at_least (minimum to reclaim), exclude_tools (never clear), clear_tool_inputs (also strip the call arguments).
  • clear_thinking_20251015 does the same for old thinking blocks.

Ordering bundled results

When bundling several tool results plus a question, put the key findings summary first, then supporting detail under explicit section headers, so the model has anchors in the middle of the input. It costs nothing, and it matters most when results are long and you're tempted to concatenate them in call order.

KEY FINDINGS
- Order SO-88213: shipped 19 days ago, within 30-day return window.
- Customer has one prior return on this account (SO-77410, approved).
- Policy: standard return, no manager approval required.

## Order Detail
...

## Account History
...

## Applicable Policy Section
...

Requiring metadata and structure from subagents

A subagent returning verbose prose with no provenance leaves the consumer unable to tell which claim came from where, when, or how confident, and it wastes context re-deriving structure. Put a contract on the output shape:

  • Every result carries dates, source locations, and methodological context.
  • When the consumer's budget is limited (normal in multi-agent pipelines), return key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of verbose content and reasoning chains.

Python

@dataclass
class SubagentFinding:
    claim: str
    source: str          # file path, ticket id, or document name
    as_of_date: str       # when this fact was true / last verified
    relevance: float      # 0-1, how directly this bears on the question asked
    # deliberately no "reasoning" field — the coordinator needs the conclusion,
    # not the chain that produced it

TypeScript

interface SubagentFinding {
  claim: string;
  source: string;      // file path, ticket id, or document name
  asOfDate: string;     // when this fact was true / last verified
  relevance: number;    // 0-1, how directly this bears on the question asked
  // deliberately no `reasoning` field — the coordinator needs the conclusion,
  // not the chain that produced it
}

The reasoning chain was necessary for the subagent and is nearly worthless to the coordinator. Its token cost grows with thoroughness, which is the wrong way round for a limited budget. Five paragraphs compress to one line that can sit beside four other subagents' findings.

5.4 Context across a large codebase exploration

Here the task never fit in one window, so it's split across phases and subagents from the start. The named symptom is an agent that, asked about retries an hour in, says "this typically follows a standard retry pattern with exponential backoff" instead of naming RetryableOrderProcessor at services/orders/retry.py:142, which it read 40 tool calls ago. It is reconstructing a generic answer because the specific one has degraded out of reach. The fact may still be in context, but the signal-to-noise ratio has collapsed. This is context degradation, not a reasoning failure a better prompt fixes.

Subagent delegation for verbose exploration

For "find every file touching the refund flow" or "trace what calls process_refund", spawn a subagent. Its context absorbs the dead ends and the coordinator's doesn't. It returns a short structured list, ideally in the metadata shape above.

The coordinator keeps to its Chapter 5 role of deciding what to investigate, dispatching and reconciling. Reading files directly "just this once" pollutes the context that delegation is meant to protect.

Scratchpad files

Delegation protects the coordinator, but a long subagent trace can degrade too. A scratchpad file records key findings on disk as they're found, and the agent re-reads it rather than re-deriving. Write "refund cancellation → RefundCanceller.revert at services/orders/cancel.py:88, called from services/webhooks/stripe.py:210" the moment it's found, and read it back when needed.

# scratchpad: refund-flow-trace.md

## Confirmed call chain
- entry: `services/webhooks/stripe.py:210` (webhook handler)
- calls: `RefundCanceller.revert` at `services/orders/cancel.py:88`
- calls: `LedgerAdjustment.apply` at `services/ledger/adjust.py:41`

## Open questions
- Does `LedgerAdjustment.apply` retry on ledger-service timeout? Not yet checked.

## Files ruled out
- `services/orders/refund.py` — handles issuance, not cancellation. Not relevant here.

It's a curated record of conclusions, not a log (the transcript is already the log).

The memory tool ({"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}) is the supported version. It is client-executed and gives a persistent /memories directory across sessions with view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, and rename. Anthropic's "multisession software development" pattern (a progress log plus a feature checklist, read back on resume) is this chapter's scratchpad-plus-manifest. Build it yourself when you need a bespoke format or location.

Phase summaries before the next round of subagents

In a multi-phase exploration (map refund code paths, then audit each for a bug pattern), summarise phase one and inject that summary into each phase-two subagent's initial prompt. Phase two then starts with what phase one learned and doesn't re-explore it.

Manifests for crash recovery

Sessions get interrupted when the process dies or when context fills and needs a fresh start. Each agent exports its state to a known location as it works (conclusions, open items, scratchpad references). On resume, the coordinator loads a manifest (an index of what state exists where) and injects the relevant parts into fresh agents' prompts.

{
  "exploration_id": "refund-flow-audit-2026-09-03",
  "phase": 2,
  "phase_1_summary": "scratchpad/refund-flow-trace.md",
  "subagents_completed": ["trace-webhook-path", "trace-ledger-path"],
  "subagents_pending": ["audit-retry-behavior", "audit-idempotency"],
  "open_questions": [
    "Does LedgerAdjustment.apply retry on ledger-service timeout?"
  ]
}

A crash then costs minutes, not a rerun of phase one.

/compact inside an exploration

/compact is a legitimate way to reclaim room filled with exploratory noise, as long as you get the sequence right. Compact after the phase summary is written and the scratchpad is current, so durable findings are already safe and only noise gets compressed. Compact before and you may lose the fact the summary was meant to capture.

Server-side compaction (beta compact-2026-01-12, context_management: {"edits": [{"type": "compact_20260112", "instructions": "..."}]}):

  • instructions replaces the default summarisation prompt, e.g. "preserve all dollar amounts, order numbers, and dates verbatim". It complements the case-facts block and doesn't replace it, and it's only as good as your knowledge of what's at risk.
  • pause_after_compaction stops after compacting so you can check what survived before the agent continues.

What the exam tests

  • 5.1 stem: an amount, date, or order number goes vague after several turns. Diagnosis: progressive summarisation; the fix is a persistent case-facts block. Distractors: "summarise more carefully", "ask the model to double-check".
  • 40-field tool result: trim at the source, before it enters context.
  • Where the block goes: the guide says "included in each prompt, outside summarized history". Any answer that keeps the facts inside summarised history is wrong.
  • 5.4 symptom: "typical patterns" instead of the specific class means context degradation, not something a better prompt fixes.
  • Subagent for an isolated question, rather than the coordinator exploring directly.
  • Manifest is for crash recovery. Scratchpad is for degradation within an ongoing session.
  • /compact is legitimate. The tested judgement is compacting after findings are externalised.

Exercises

  1. In a long Claude Code session, ask about something found 30+ tool calls ago (function name, path, config value). Note any hedged answer and its phrasing (look for "typically").
  2. Design a case-facts block for one customer with two disputed charges and one shipping complaint. Decide what's persistent versus conversational, and write the block after all three are raised.
  3. Take a tool returning a large record and write the trimmed projection for one task. Compare field counts and estimate the token difference over 20 turns.
  4. Design a manifest for a three-phase audit (dependencies, dead code, coverage): what each phase writes, what the coordinator reads on resume, and what a phase-three subagent gets if the crash hit mid-phase-two.

Chapter 15 — Escalation, review, and provenance

This chapter covers four tasks: who checks a result (4.6), when the system should hand a case to a human (5.2), how humans review at scale (5.5), and how citations survive synthesis (5.6). A final section reconciles two rules about confidence scores that appear to contradict each other.

Review architecture

"Review the diff you just wrote" sometimes catches a typo but rarely questions a decision, because a model reviewing its own output in the same session keeps the reasoning context from generation. It re-reads the code alongside its own justification and stays biased toward it.

Extended thinking doesn't fix this. More reasoning helps generation, but the bias comes from reasoning that already happened and now anchors the review, so more effort doesn't remove it.

The fix is an independent instance whose context holds only the artifact (diff, extraction, plan) and none of the generator's reasoning. It catches subtle issues that both self-review instructions and extended thinking miss.

Python

async def generate_and_review(task_description: str) -> dict:
    generation = await claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": task_description}],
    )
    code = extract_code(generation)

    # A fresh instance: no system prompt overlap with generation, no shared
    # conversation history, nothing but the artifact and a review brief.
    review = await claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                "Review the following code for correctness bugs, edge cases, "
                "and unstated assumptions. You have no knowledge of why any "
                "decision was made; judge only what is written.\n\n" + code
            ),
        }],
    )
    return {"code": code, "review": extract_text(review)}

TypeScript

async function generateAndReview(taskDescription: string) {
  const generation = await claude.messages.create({
    model: "claude-sonnet-5",
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: taskDescription }],
  });
  const code = extractCode(generation);

  const review = await claude.messages.create({
    model: "claude-sonnet-5",
    messages: [{
      role: "user",
      content:
        "Review the following code for correctness bugs, edge cases, and " +
        "unstated assumptions. You have no knowledge of why any decision " +
        "was made; judge only what is written.\n\n" + code,
    }],
  });
  return { code, review: extractText(review) };
}

Two further techniques help with large artifacts:

  • Multi-pass review against attention dilution. One pass over 10 files spreads attention thin, and cross-file and single-file issues tangle into contradictory findings. Instead, do a per-file local pass for internal correctness plus a separate cross-file integration pass for data flow (does a return value match what callers assume, is a schema change honoured everywhere).
  • Per-finding self-reported confidence as a routing signal. High confidence ("missing null check, throws on documented empty list") goes to the human first. Low ("might be a race depending on scheduling") goes to a follow-up pass or lower priority. The score prioritises human attention but does not decide correctness or block merges on its own (see the final section).

Escalation and ambiguity resolution

The exam's answer is a closed list of three valid triggers:

  1. The customer explicitly asks for a human.
  2. Policy has a gap the agent lacks authority to resolve.
  3. The agent can't make meaningful progress after a real attempt.

Anything else ("felt hard", "seemed upset", "wasn't sure") misfires in both directions. It escalates easy cases that looked complex and keeps working on hard cases where the model was confidently wrong.

Trigger 1, explicit request.

  • Explicit request: escalate immediately. Don't say "let me just check one thing first", because investigating anyway treats the stated preference as an obstacle.
  • Frustrated but no request: not a trigger. Acknowledge the frustration, offer to resolve if it's within capability, and escalate only if they reiterate. What counts is what they asked for, not what tone implied.

Trigger 2, policy gap. The policy covers price drops on your own site and says nothing about competitor price matching. "Policy doesn't forbid it" invents unapproved policy. "Not covered, so no" denies something the business might want. Both are wrong because the agent lacks authority either way, so the policy's silence is itself the trigger.

Trigger 3, no progress. It is measured by outcome (tools and reasonable alternatives tried and exhausted), not by a forecast before trying.

The exam names two invalid proxies:

  • Sentiment. It doesn't correlate with complexity. An angry customer can have a trivial issue, and a calm one a case the agent shouldn't handle alone.
  • Self-reported confidence. A model wrong about a hard case is often wrong about being wrong. The limitations that made the case hard also corrupt its self-assessment, so it says "confident" on exactly the cases it's likely to get wrong.

The fix is explicit escalation criteria in the system prompt, plus few-shot examples in both directions: a case that looks complex but resolves cleanly, and one that looks simple but hits a policy gap.

Python

ESCALATION_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
Escalate to a human agent only when one of the following is true:
1. The customer explicitly asks to speak with a human agent.
2. The applicable policy is silent or ambiguous on the customer's specific
   request (not merely complex to apply).
3. You have attempted a resolution using the tools available and cannot
   make further progress.

Do not escalate based on how difficult the case seems, how frustrated the
customer sounds, or how confident you feel. Frustration without an explicit
request for a human should be met with acknowledgment and an offer to
resolve; escalate only if the customer repeats the request for a person.

Example — escalate:
  Customer: "I want a price match against a competitor's listing."
  Policy covers only same-site price drops. -> Escalate: policy gap.

Example — do not escalate:
  Customer (frustrated): "This is the third time I've had to explain this,
  just fix it!"
  Issue: a standard, in-policy refund. -> Acknowledge frustration, resolve
  the refund, do not escalate.
"""

TypeScript

const ESCALATION_SYSTEM_PROMPT = `
Escalate to a human agent only when one of the following is true:
1. The customer explicitly asks to speak with a human agent.
2. The applicable policy is silent or ambiguous on the customer's specific
   request (not merely complex to apply).
3. You have attempted a resolution using the tools available and cannot
   make further progress.

Do not escalate based on how difficult the case seems, how frustrated the
customer sounds, or how confident you feel. Frustration without an explicit
request for a human should be met with acknowledgment and an offer to
resolve; escalate only if the customer repeats the request for a person.

Example -- escalate:
  Customer: "I want a price match against a competitor's listing."
  Policy covers only same-site price drops. -> Escalate: policy gap.

Example -- do not escalate:
  Customer (frustrated): "This is the third time I've had to explain this,
  just fix it!"

`;

Multiple matches from get_customer: don't use a heuristic (most recent, closest name). It can silently act on the wrong customer's data, and near process_refund that causes real harm. Ask for an additional identifier (order number, billing zip) and disambiguate deterministically.

Human review workflows and confidence calibration

The aggregate-accuracy trap. "97% accurate" invites cutting human review. But 97% overall is consistent with 99.5% on the dominant invoice type and 60% on a rare type or a hard field (foreign-currency total, handwritten date, vendor-specific field). Automate on the aggregate and you remove oversight exactly where it's needed. Validate accuracy by document type and by field, and confirm it holds in every segment before reducing review on any.

Two mechanisms need to run continuously:

  • Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions, the ones that would otherwise go unseen. That's how you measure the true error rate on the bucket you aren't otherwise checking, and catch new error patterns early.
  • Field-level confidence, calibrated on a labelled validation set. Per-field scores are checked against ground truth, and 0.9 should mean right about 90% of the time, not 65%. Once calibrated, route low-confidence fields and documents with contradictory sources to humans first, so limited reviewer time goes where errors are most likely.

Python

def route_for_review(extraction: dict, calibration: dict) -> str:
    """calibration maps confidence buckets to measured accuracy from a
    labeled validation set -- e.g. {0.9: 0.97, 0.8: 0.88, 0.7: 0.61}."""
    field_conf = extraction["fieldConfidence"]  # per-field raw score
    lowest = min(field_conf.values())
    measured_accuracy = calibration_lookup(calibration, lowest)

    if extraction.get("sourceContradictory"):
        return "human_review"          # contradictory source, regardless of score
    if measured_accuracy < 0.90:
        return "human_review"          # calibrated accuracy below threshold
    if is_in_stratified_sample(extraction["documentId"]):
        return "human_review"          # sampled even though it looks safe
    return "auto_accept"

TypeScript

function routeForReview(
  extraction: Extraction,
  calibration: Map<number, number>,
): "human_review" | "auto_accept" {
  const fieldConf = extraction.fieldConfidence;
  const lowest = Math.min(...Object.values(fieldConf));
  const measuredAccuracy = calibrationLookup(calibration, lowest);

  if (extraction.sourceContradictory) return "human_review";
  if (measuredAccuracy < 0.90) return "human_review";
  if (isInStratifiedSample(extraction.documentId)) return "human_review";
  return "auto_accept";
}

This confidence number is trustworthy where the escalation one wasn't, because it has been checked against labelled data (see the final section).

Provenance in multi-source synthesis

Subagents gather from different sources and synthesis combines them. The failure is easy to miss, because the result is a right answer that can't say where it came from.

Attribution gets lost because summarisation's job is to compress, and a citation looks like a detail that is safe to drop, since the claim survives without it. After two or three passes, the report is full of confident, unattributed claims indistinguishable from verified ones.

The structural fix is that every subagent outputs claim-source mappings (claim + source URL or document name + supporting excerpt), and every downstream step, including synthesis, preserves and merges them. "Summarize these findings" invites loss. "Merge these findings; every claim must carry the source mapping it arrived with" makes a dropped citation a visible, checkable defect.

Python

class ClaimSource(TypedDict):
    claim: str
    sourceUrl: str
    excerpt: str
    publicationDate: str | None   # required when available -- see below

class SubagentFinding(TypedDict):
    topic: str
    claims: list[ClaimSource]

def synthesize(findings: list[SubagentFinding]) -> dict:
    # Merge, don't summarize away, the claim-source pairs.
    all_claims = [c for f in findings for c in f["claims"]]
    conflicts = detect_conflicting_values(all_claims)
    contested_claims = {c["claim"] for c in conflicts}
    return {
        "wellEstablished": [c for c in all_claims if c["claim"] not in contested_claims],
        "contested": conflicts,   # annotated, not resolved by picking one
        "allSources": all_claims,
    }

TypeScript

interface ClaimSource {
  claim: string;
  sourceUrl: string;
  excerpt: string;
  publicationDate?: string;
}

interface SubagentFinding {
  topic: string;
  claims: ClaimSource[];
}

function synthesize(findings: SubagentFinding[]) {
  const allClaims = findings.flatMap((f) => f.claims);
  const conflicts = detectConflictingValues(allClaims);
  const contestedClaims = new Set(conflicts.map((c) => c.claim));
  return {
    wellEstablished: allClaims.filter((c) => !contestedClaims.has(c.claim)),
    contested: conflicts,
    allSources: allClaims,
  };
}

Built-in citations cover a different case. When Claude reads a source directly via a document content block with citations: {"enabled": true}, the API returns citation blocks automatically (cited text, document, location). Anthropic reports up to 15% better recall than prompt-based citation. Use it when Claude is reading the document. Keep ClaimSource for subagent handoffs, where what's passed is a prior finding with no document to cite into.

Conflicts: annotate, don't resolve. One source says 12% growth, another 9%. Both may be credible, measuring slightly different things or different times. Report both values with sources rather than picking the more reputable-sounding one. A labelled contested finding is useful, while a confident one that settled a disagreement without saying so hides a judgement call (compare Chapter 4's coverage gaps). Upstream document analysis should do the same: complete the analysis with both values marked as conflicting and pass them up, because the coordinator holds the full picture.

Figures that look contradictory may be temporal differences, measurements taken on different dates. Drop the dates and a normal trend reads as inconsistency. Require a publication or data-collection date on every claim (publicationDate) so synthesis can tell "sources disagree" from "the world changed". Structure the report with sections separating well-established from contested findings.

Render content types natively: financial figures as tables, news as prose, multi-part technical findings as lists. Keep the source's characterisation and methodology (survey, regulatory filing, estimate). It is part of the claim.

Reconciling the confidence-score rules

The chapter appears to contradict itself:

  • Self-reported confidence is not a valid escalation trigger (5.2).

  • Yet field-level confidence drives review routing (5.5), and having review passes self-report confidence is good design (4.6).

  • Uncalibrated self-report is the model's guess about itself, made by the system whose competence is in question. It is least reliable on exactly the cases where the model is wrong, since the same limitation affects both.

  • A calibrated score is computed the same way, but it is checked against a labelled validation set and shown to track the true error rate (0.9 ≈ 90% correct on ground truth). At that point it is a measurement, like any instrument verified before use.

Never let a raw, unchecked self-report make an autonomous decision to escalate or to call code correct. Once calibrated against ground truth, a score is a legitimate routing input for human review.

What the exam tests

  • 4.6: independent instances beat self-review because retained reasoning context biases the generator, not because of effort. Extended thinking is no substitute. Multi-pass review is per-file plus cross-file integration.
  • 5.2: the three triggers are a closed set. Sentiment and self-reported confidence are the plausible wrong answers. Explicit request (immediate) vs frustration (acknowledge, offer resolution). A silent policy means escalate the gap. Multiple matches means ask for another identifier.
  • 5.5: aggregate accuracy masks segment failures. Validate per type and field, use stratified sampling of high-confidence items, and route on calibrated field-level confidence.
  • 5.6: claim-source mappings survive synthesis. Conflicts are annotated, not resolved. Publication dates are required. Sections separate established from contested. Format matches content type.
  • Confidence scores: self-reported confidence is invalid as an autonomous trigger but valid as a calibrated routing input.

Exercises

  1. Take code from one Claude Code session and have a fresh session with no shared history review it. Compare with the original session reviewing itself, and find one issue only the fresh instance caught.
  2. Draft an escalation prompt for process_refund/escalate_to_human with few-shot examples for all three triggers plus negative examples (sentiment, confidence). Test an angry customer with a simple in-policy request and a calm one asking about something the policy never covers.
  3. Build extract_invoice with per-field confidence and a 20-document labelled set. Compute accuracy per confidence bucket, decide whether the raw scores are calibrated, and choose a routing threshold.
  4. Run a three-subagent research task with likely disagreement. Require claim-source mappings with dates, and have synthesis produce wellEstablished and contested sections. Rerun with "summarize the findings" and compare what survives.

Study with Claude

Unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice scores but cut later unaided exam scores by 17% once the tool was removed, and students did not notice (Bastani et al., PNAS 2025). A tutor limited to hints caused no such drop. A structured AI tutor beat in-class active learning in a Harvard physics RCT (Kestin et al., Sci Reports 2025). In both studies the tutor withheld the answer and the learner did the retrieval.

Run every prompt below in Claude Code from the repo root.

Rules

  1. Attempt first. Write your answer and your reason before Claude says anything. Never let Claude solve an item before you do.
  2. Ground it. Generation and grading use only the exam guide PDF and study-guide/. Tell Claude to cite file and section, and to refuse when the sources do not support an answer.
  3. Check every generated item for flaws. One study found 49% of ChatGPT-written MCQs had item-writing flaws and 22% had factual or conceptual errors. Expect to fix or drop a good share.
  4. Verify answer-deciding facts against the PDF. Parameters, flags and file names that decide an answer must trace to it or to current docs. If Claude, the study guide and the PDF disagree, the PDF wins, then current docs, then the study guide, then Claude's memory of its own product.
  5. Calibrate on the official items. The 12 official samples are the only items with the real exam's style. Re-do your misses without notes.
  6. Stop generating new items in the last 24 hours. Review your error log and the guide instead.

8. Scenario walk-through

When: you can answer single items but lose points when several choices interact.

Play the lead engineer of the "[scenario name]" scenario from the exam guide. Describe the system in four sentences, then raise one design problem at a time. After each problem, wait for my design choice and reason. Challenge it with a realistic constraint, then say which task statement it exercised. After five problems, grade my choices against the PDF and list which task statements I should drill next. Do not reveal the intended answer before I commit.

What not to do

  • Asking Claude to summarise chapters. A summary is easy to read and gives you no retrieval practice. Have it quiz you, and read the chapter yourself.
  • Judging progress by sessions that went well. Count only unaided Drill results, because a session full of hints feels productive without showing what you can recall.
  • Treating generated items as the exam. They check recall of the guide. Difficulty and style come from the 12 official samples.

Practice Questions

Sixty original scenario questions, a full-length mock, written against the v1.0 task statements and in the style of the exam guide's own samples, split D1 ×15, D2 ×11, D3 ×12, D4 ×11, D5 ×11. Eight items are multiple-response (Q11, Q34, Q46, Q48, Q50, Q53, Q55, Q58), as v1.0 says to expect.

These are not Anthropic's questions. The twelve official sample questions are in §9 of the exam guide PDF; do those too, because their answer explanations show best how the exam chooses between options.

Answers and explanations follow all the questions, at the end of the page.

This page is the printable version. For practice, use the Drill page, which shuffles the options, asks for your confidence, explains every option, and brings back your misses.

Domain 1 — Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

Q1. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) Your agentic loop terminates as soon as the assistant response contains any text, on the theory that Claude only writes prose when it has a final answer. Support engineers report the agent frequently replies "Let me look that up for you" and then stops. What is the correct fix?

A. Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude not to narrate before calling tools. B. Continue while stop_reason is "tool_use"; terminate only on "end_turn". C. Set a minimum of three iterations before the loop is allowed to exit, whatever the stop reason. D. Strip text content blocks from the response before evaluating the termination condition.

Q2. (Multi-Agent Research System) Your coordinator delegates to a web search subagent and then a synthesis subagent. The synthesis subagent's prompt is "Synthesize the research findings into a report." Its output is generic and cites nothing. What is the root cause?

A. The synthesis subagent's model is too small for synthesis work, so it falls back on generic summaries. B. The synthesis subagent needs the WebSearch tool so it can gather its own material. C. The coordinator left prior findings out of the synthesis prompt; subagents do not inherit context. D. The coordinator should invoke synthesis in the same turn as web search so that both share context.

Q3. (Multi-Agent Research System) You want four subagents to run concurrently rather than one after another. How does the coordinator achieve this?

A. Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response. B. Set parallel: true in each AgentDefinition. C. Issue one Task call per turn and rely on the SDK to overlap them. D. Set disable_parallel_tool_use to false on the coordinator's requests.

Q4. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) Company policy is that refunds above $500 require human approval. Your system prompt says so clearly. Over three months, four refunds above $500 were processed autonomously. Choose the most appropriate remediation.

A. Restate the rule at both the beginning and end of the system prompt for position emphasis. B. Add few-shot examples showing the agent escalating a $600 refund. C. Intercept outgoing process_refund calls and block any exceeding $500, redirecting to escalation. D. Add a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that flags refunds above $500 for after-the-fact audit.

Q5. (Developer Productivity with Claude) Different MCP servers return timestamps as Unix epochs, ISO 8601 strings, and human-readable dates. The agent frequently miscompares dates. What is the cleanest fix?

A. A PostToolUse hook that normalizes timestamp formats before the model reads the results. B. A system prompt section explaining all three formats and how to convert between them. C. Rewrite each MCP server so that it emits ISO 8601 timestamps. D. A tool-call interception hook that rejects calls to tools known to return non-ISO timestamps.

Q6. (Code Generation with Claude Code) You analyzed a codebase in a session two days ago. Since then, six files in the authentication module were rewritten. You want to continue the investigation. What is the best approach?

A. Resume the session with --resume and say nothing; Claude will re-read any files it needs as it goes. B. Resume with --resume and name the changed files so it re-analyzes those targets. C. Fork the session so the original analysis is preserved and the work continues on a branch. D. Always start fresh; resumed sessions cannot be trusted after code changes.

Q7. (Developer Productivity with Claude) You want to compare two refactoring strategies, both starting from the same completed codebase analysis, and keep the analysis session intact. Which mechanism?

A. --resume twice, each with a different follow-up prompt about one strategy. B. fork_session to create independent branches from the shared baseline. C. /compact with instructions focused on each strategy in turn. D. Two new sessions, each seeded with a copy of the analysis summary.

Q8. (Multi-Agent Research System) The coordinator always runs the full pipeline (web search, document analysis, synthesis, report generation) even for a query like "what year was the GDPR enacted?" Latency and cost are high for trivial queries. What should change?

A. Reduce each subagent's max_tokens so that trivial queries cost less to run. B. Have the coordinator assess query complexity and select which subagents to invoke. C. Add a caching layer in front of the web search subagent to avoid repeated searches. D. Merge web search and document analysis into one subagent to halve the pipeline.

Q9. (Code Generation with Claude Code) A task reads: "Add comprehensive tests to this legacy service." You do not know the module structure, the existing coverage, or the dependency graph. Which decomposition strategy fits?

A. A fixed prompt chain: generate unit tests, then integration tests, then end-to-end tests for the service. B. Dynamic decomposition: map the structure, rank high-impact areas, then adapt the plan as you go. C. Parallel subagents, one per directory, each writing tests independently for its own directory. D. A single prompt with the whole repository loaded into context so that nothing is missed or skipped.

Q10. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) A customer writes: "My order arrived damaged, I was double-charged, and I want to change my shipping address." Your agent addresses the damage and ignores the other two. Which design change follows the exam guide's recommended pattern?

A. Instruct the agent to ask the customer to submit one issue per message so each is handled alone. B. Split into items, investigate each in parallel with shared context, and synthesize one reply. C. Escalate any message that contains more than one issue to a human agent to handle. D. Process the issues strictly in the order stated, one per turn, finishing each before the next.

Q11. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) Select TWO. Your agent is escalating to human agents who cannot see the conversation transcript. Which two elements belong in the handoff?

A. The complete raw conversation transcript, verbatim. B. Root cause analysis. C. The agent's self-reported confidence score for the escalation decision. D. Customer ID, refund amount, and recommended action. E. A list of all tools the agent called, with timings.

Domain 2 — Tool Design & MCP Integration

Q12. (Multi-Agent Research System) Two tools, analyze_content ("Analyzes content") and analyze_document ("Analyzes documents"), are selected almost at random. What is the most effective first step?

A. Merge them into a single analyze tool that decides internally which backend to call. B. Rename them and rewrite the descriptions so each purpose is distinct, e.g. extract_web_results. C. Put a deterministic keyword-matching router in front of the model to pre-select the tool each turn. D. Set tool_choice: "any" so the model must commit to calling one of the two on every turn.

Q13. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) lookup_order times out against a flaky backend. Which error response best enables agent recovery?

A. A bare {"error": "Operation failed"} with no category, retry flag, or detail on what was attempted. B. isError: true, errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true, and what was attempted. C. Return an empty order list so the agent treats it as a successful query with no matches and carries on. D. Raise the exception to the top level and end the session so an operator can inspect the failing backend.

Q14. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) A customer requests a refund on an item outside the 30-day return window. The tool correctly refuses. What should it return?

A. errorCategory: "transient" with isRetryable: true, so the agent retries after a short backoff. B. errorCategory: "business", retriable: false, and a customer-friendly policy explanation. C. A generic failure message so the agent escalates the refund request to a human automatically. D. A successful empty result, because the call did not create any refund record.

Q15. (Multi-Agent Research System) Your synthesis agent has been given all 18 tools available in the system "so it never gets stuck." It now attempts web searches mid-synthesis and produces inconsistent reports. What is the best correction?

A. Add a system prompt line telling the synthesis agent not to run web searches, and keep the full 18-tool set. B. Scope it to its role's tools plus one narrow verify_fact tool, and route complex verification through the coordinator. C. Remove all tools from the synthesis agent so it can only write the final report from the findings it receives. D. Increase the synthesis agent's context window so it retains its instructions better across long inputs.

Q16. (Developer Productivity with Claude) Your team's custom MCP server exposes a search_internal_docs tool with the description "Searches docs." The agent keeps using Grep on the local repo instead. What fixes this?

A. Move the server from user scope to project scope in .mcp.json so the agent ranks it above built-in tools. B. Remove Grep from allowedTools so the agent has no other way of searching the documentation. C. Expand the tool's description to explain what it covers, what it returns, and when to prefer it over Grep. D. Set tool_choice: "any" to force the agent to call some tool on every turn.

Q17. (Developer Productivity with Claude) You need a shared GitHub MCP server available to the whole team, authenticated with a token that must not be committed. What do you do?

A. Add it to ~/.claude.json with the token inline and tell everyone to copy the file. B. Add it to .mcp.json with ${GITHUB_TOKEN} and commit that file. C. Add it to .mcp.json with the token inline and add .mcp.json to .gitignore. D. Write a custom MCP server that reads the token from a vault at runtime.

Q18. (Developer Productivity with Claude) You need to find every caller of calculatePremium() across a large TypeScript monorepo. Which tool?

A. Glob with **/*.ts B. Grep C. Read on each file, following imports D. Bash with find

Domain 3 — Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

Q19. (Code Generation with Claude Code) You documented your team's commit message conventions and Claude follows them perfectly for you. Two new hires report Claude ignores them entirely. Where are the conventions?

A. In .claude/rules/ without a paths: field. B. In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. C. In .claude/CLAUDE.md, but the new hires haven't run /memory. D. In a skill that requires manual invocation.

Q20. (Code Generation with Claude Code) Your repository has React components, API handlers, and database models, each with different conventions. Test files sit next to the code they test, scattered across every directory, and must all follow one shared testing convention. What is the most maintainable configuration?

A. A separate CLAUDE.md in each subdirectory, one per code type. B. All conventions in the root CLAUDE.md under a clear header per code type. C. .claude/rules/ files with paths: globs, including **/*.test.tsx. D. A skill per code type that holds that type's conventions.

Q21. (Code Generation with Claude Code) A /codebase-map skill produces 8,000 tokens of directory listings and dependency graphs every time it runs, crowding out the actual work. Which frontmatter option addresses this?

A. allowed-tools: Read, Grep B. argument-hint: [directory] C. context: fork D. model: haiku

Q22. (Code Generation with Claude Code) Which statement correctly distinguishes skills from CLAUDE.md?

A. Skills load at every session start; CLAUDE.md loads only when a task calls for it. B. Skills load on demand for task workflows; CLAUDE.md always loads universal standards. C. Skills can only be project-scoped; CLAUDE.md can be user- or project-scoped. D. Skills replace CLAUDE.md in projects that use them, making that file unnecessary there.

Q23. (Code Generation with Claude Code) You need to migrate the application from one HTTP client library to another. It touches roughly 45 files, and there are two viable migration strategies with different testing implications. What is the right approach?

A. Direct execution with one very detailed instruction listing every file and its change. B. Plan mode to design the approach, then direct execution to carry it out. C. Direct execution first, switching to plan mode only if something unexpected appears. D. Split the work into 45 single-file tasks, each run in direct execution.

Q24. (Claude Code for CI) Your pipeline runs claude "Review this PR" and the job times out with no output. What is the fix?

A. claude -p "Review this PR" B. export CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true C. claude --batch "Review this PR" D. claude "Review this PR" < /dev/null

Q25. (Claude Code for CI) You want Claude Code's review findings posted as inline PR comments by a downstream script. Which combination produces reliably parseable output?

A. --output-format json together with --json-schema B. A prompt instructing Claude to reply in JSON only C. --output-format text and a regex parser D. --json-schema alone, since it implies JSON output

Q26. (Claude Code for CI) Every time a developer pushes a new commit, the review bot re-posts the same twelve comments from the previous run. What change fixes this?

A. Run the review on the first push of each PR only, and skip every later commit. B. Feed in the prior findings and report only new or unaddressed issues. C. Deduplicate the comments in the posting script by hashing the text of each one. D. Limit the review scope to the files that were changed in the latest commit.

Q27. (Code Generation with Claude Code) You describe a data transformation in prose three times and get three different interpretations. What is the exam guide's recommended technique?

A. Move the description into CLAUDE.md so it is always loaded. B. Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples. C. Ask Claude to restate the requirement before implementing. D. Increase specificity by adding more prose constraints.

Domain 4 — Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

Q28. (Claude Code for CI) Your review bot flags too many false positives on the "misleading comment" category. Your current instruction is "check that comments are accurate." Which change most improves precision?

A. Append "be conservative and only report findings you are highly confident are real problems." B. Replace it with "flag comments only when the claimed behavior contradicts the actual code behavior." C. Require the model to output a confidence score with each finding and filter out anything below 0.8. D. Run the review three times and report only the issues that appear in all three runs.

Q29. (Claude Code for CI) Six months in, the "security" category is 92% precise and the "performance" category is 30% precise. Developers have started ignoring all bot comments. What is a legitimate immediate action?

A. Temporarily disable the performance category while you improve its prompt. B. Lower the overall reporting threshold so fewer findings show up across all categories. C. Switch to a larger model for the performance pass only. D. Post all findings but mark performance ones as "low confidence."

Q30. (Structured Data Extraction) Your extractor returns well-formed JSON that validates against the schema, but on 8% of invoices the line items do not sum to the stated total. What addresses this?

A. Enable strict mode on the tool schema so every field must match its declared type. B. Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and flag discrepancies in a validation step. C. Add additionalProperties: false to the schema so unexpected fields are rejected. D. Switch tool_choice from "auto" to "any" so the model must always call a tool.

Q31. (Structured Data Extraction) Roughly a fifth of your source contracts have no governing-law clause. The model invents a plausible jurisdiction for those. The governing_law field is currently required. What is the fix?

A. Add a few-shot example showing a contract with no governing law. B. Make governing_law optional/nullable so the model can return null. C. Add "do not guess" to the system prompt. D. Lower the temperature to 0.

Q32. (Structured Data Extraction) You receive three document types and cannot tell which type a document is until you read it. You have a distinct extraction tool per type and must never get conversational prose back. Which tool_choice?

A. "auto" B. "any" C. {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} D. "none" with a prefilled response

Q33. (Structured Data Extraction) Validation fails because total_paid is absent. Investigation shows the figure is in a payment remittance file that was never supplied to the model. What should the pipeline do?

A. Retry with the validation error appended to the prompt; the model will locate the figure. B. Retry up to five times with exponential backoff between attempts. C. Recognize that retry cannot recover absent data and route the document to human review. D. Make the field nullable and accept null as the correct extraction result.

Q34. (Structured Data Extraction) Select TWO. Which statements about the Message Batches API are accurate?

A. It offers 50% cost savings. B. It guarantees completion within one hour. C. It supports multi-turn tool calling within a single request. D. custom_id correlates requests with responses. E. It is appropriate for blocking pre-merge checks because it is usually fast.

Q35. (Structured Data Extraction) A batch of 100 documents completes with 7 failures, all because the documents exceeded context limits. What is the right recovery?

A. Resubmit the entire batch of 100 with a larger model that has more context. B. Identify the 7 by custom_id, chunk them, and resubmit only those. C. Process all 100 documents synchronously instead of through the batch. D. Reduce max_tokens and resubmit the whole batch to shorten each response.

Q36. (Claude Code for CI) Claude generates a module, then you ask it in the same session to review its own work. It finds nothing. What is the most effective architecture?

A. Enable extended thinking on the review request so the model reasons longer. B. Ask it to review the code three times in the same session and take the union of findings. C. Send the code to a second Claude instance that lacks the generator's reasoning. D. Add "be critical of your own work" to the review prompt in the same session.

Domain 5 — Context Management & Reliability

Q37. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) Forty turns into a billing dispute, the agent refers to "the disputed amount" and "the charge from last month" instead of $247.80 and 14 August. Summarization has been running throughout. What fixes it?

A. Truncate the history to the last ten turns and drop everything earlier, so recent detail stays sharp. B. Keep amounts, dates, order numbers and statuses in a case-facts block sent with every prompt. C. Instruct the summarizer to be more detailed and to keep more of each turn from every earlier turn. D. Move to a model with a larger context window so the full history fits without summarization.

Q38. (Customer Support Resolution Agent) Your agent responds to "I've had enough, put me through to a person" by first running lookup_order and offering a replacement. What is correct?

A. Escalate immediately, without first attempting investigation. B. Attempt one resolution; escalate if the customer repeats the request. C. Run sentiment analysis to confirm the frustration is genuine before escalating. D. Escalate only if the agent's confidence in resolving the case is below threshold.

Q39. (Multi-Agent Research System) A document analysis subagent times out after processing 3 of 5 papers. Which propagation approach best enables coordinator recovery?

A. Return structured error context: failure type, what was attempted, the 3 completed analyses, and alternatives. B. Retry internally with exponential backoff, then return a generic "document analysis unavailable" status once retries run out. C. Return the 3 completed analyses as a successful, complete result so the coordinator can proceed without delay. D. Propagate the timeout to a top-level handler that aborts the research run and reports the failure.

Q40. (Multi-Agent Research System) Two credible sources report the market size as $4.2B and $6.8B. Your synthesis agent silently picks $4.2B. What should it do instead, and what would have prevented the misreading in the first place?

A. Average the two figures into a single estimate; require confidence scores from each source. B. Pick the higher figure as a conservative upper bound in the report; require source URLs from subagents. C. Annotate both values with their sources and present the conflict; require publication or collection dates. D. Escalate to a human reviewer to pick one value; require the coordinator to deduplicate sources before synthesis.

Additional items — under-drilled task statements

Q41. (D4 · Claude Code for CI) Your review criteria are specific and well-defined, and precision is good on clear-cut cases. But on borderline code (a broad catch that is arguably intentional, a magic number that may be a domain constant) the bot's verdicts swing run to run. What most improves consistency?

A. Add "when uncertain, do not report the issue" to the criteria for borderline code. B. Add 2–4 few-shot examples of ambiguous cases that show the reasoning behind each verdict. C. Enumerate every borderline pattern in the codebase as an explicit exception list in the prompt. D. Increase the number of review passes and report only the findings that recur across them.

Q42. (D5 · Developer Productivity with Claude) Three hours into exploring a legacy payments service, the agent starts answering questions with "typically, services like this validate at the controller layer" instead of naming the PaymentValidator class it identified earlier. What is happening, and what fixes it?

A. The system prompt has been diluted over many turns; restate it every ten turns to refresh it. B. Context degradation; keep a scratchpad file of key findings and consult it for later questions. C. The model is hallucinating under uncertainty; lower the temperature to make answers more deterministic. D. Tool results were malformed along the way; add a PostToolUse normalization hook to clean them.

Q43. (D5 · Structured Data Extraction) Your extraction pipeline reports 97% overall accuracy and you want to cut human review. What must you verify first?

A. That the 3% of errors are evenly distributed across the human reviewers who handle them. B. That accuracy holds across document types and fields, since an aggregate can mask weak segments. C. That the model's self-reported confidence exceeds 0.9 on the 97% of correct extractions. D. That the validation set is at least 10,000 documents so the 97% figure is statistically stable.

Q44. (D5 · Structured Data Extraction) Having reduced review to low-confidence extractions only, how do you keep detecting new error patterns in the high-confidence bucket you no longer inspect?

A. Wait for downstream systems to report anomalies. B. Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions for ongoing error-rate measurement and novel pattern detection. C. Re-run every high-confidence extraction with a second model and compare. D. Raise the confidence threshold each quarter.

Q45. (D2 · Developer Productivity with Claude) Your internal MCP server fronts a documentation system with 4,000 pages across a deep hierarchy. Agents burn six or seven exploratory search_docs calls just working out what topics exist before asking a useful question. What is the appropriate MCP mechanism?

A. Increase the result count returned by search_docs so each call displays more of the hierarchy. B. Expose the documentation hierarchy as an MCP resource so agents see the catalog up front. C. Add a list_topics tool and instruct the agent to always call it before running any search. D. Cache search_docs results so repeated exploratory calls are cheaper and faster.

Additional items — full-length mock (Q46–Q60)

Q46. (D3 · Claude Code for CI) Select TWO. A nightly job runs claude -p to propose tests for the modules changed that day. The proposals keep repeating scenarios the suite already covers, pad the output with trivial getter tests, and ignore the team's shared fixtures. Which two changes address this?

A. Run the generation three times and keep only the tests that appear in every run. B. Pass the existing test files for the changed modules into the invocation's context so already-covered scenarios are not suggested again. C. Append "write high-quality, non-redundant tests" to the invoking prompt. D. Document the testing standards, what makes a test worth writing, and the available fixtures in CLAUDE.md so the CI-invoked session loads them. E. Pass the entire repository's source tree as context so the model sees every module.

Q47. (D3 · Claude Code for CI) A pipeline step runs claude -p "Implement the ticket" and, in the same job, resumes that session with "Now review the changes you just made and list any defects." The review step reports zero defects on 90% of runs, yet post-merge bugs keep appearing. Which redesign is most effective?

A. Keep the resumed session but turn on extended thinking for the review turn, so the model reasons longer about its own implementation before listing defects. B. Replace the review prompt with an adversarial persona ("You are a harsh reviewer; assume the code has bugs") that must list at least five findings, still in the resumed session. C. Run the review as a separate claude -p invocation that receives only the diff and the CLAUDE.md review criteria, without the implementing session's reasoning. D. Resume the same session and run the review turn three times with different phrasings, merging the findings so a defect missed once can be caught by another pass.

Q48. (D3 · Claude Code for CI) Select TWO. After each push, your review bot re-posts findings the developer already fixed or dismissed, and it also nitpicks formatting in generated protobuf files the team never reviews. Which two changes fix both complaints?

A. Supply the previous run's findings as context and instruct Claude to report only issues that are new or still unaddressed. B. Require a confidence score and drop any finding below 0.8. C. Restrict each re-run to the files touched by the latest commit only. D. Deduplicate in the posting script by hashing each comment's text. E. Record the review criteria in CLAUDE.md, including that generated files and formatting-only issues are out of scope.

Q49. (D1 · Customer Support Resolution Agent) Your system prompt says close_account must not run until verify_identity has succeeded and check_balance has confirmed nothing is owed. Measurement shows closures still run before both checks in about 3% of conversations. What is the most appropriate fix?

Restate the two-step rule in capitals at the start and end of the system prompt and add three few-shot examples showing the checks called in the correct order. C. Add a PostToolUse hook on close_account that flags closures lacking a prior identity or balance check in a nightly audit report for the compliance team. D. Switch to a larger model, which follows multi-step ordering instructions more reliably, and re-measure the skip rate on a sample of conversations.

Q50. (D1 · Customer Support Resolution Agent) Select TWO. lookup_order returns status as numeric codes (1, 2, 3) on one backend and as strings on another, with dates as Unix epochs or ISO 8601. Separately, finance requires that refunds above $500 never run without a human. Which two mechanisms give guaranteed behavior for these needs?

A. A system prompt table mapping every status code and date format, plus the $500 rule stated twice. B. A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that flags refunds above $500 for audit. C. A hook intercepting outgoing process_refund calls, blocking amounts above $500 and redirecting to escalate_to_human. D. A PostToolUse hook that converts numeric codes and epoch dates to one standard format before the model reads the results. E. Q51. (D1 · Code Generation with Claude Code) A file watcher deploys any change under db/migrations/ the moment it is written. Your CLAUDE.md says migrations must never be edited without human approval, yet about one session in thirty edits one anyway. Which approach guarantees the rule holds?

A. Repeat the rule in capitals at the top and bottom of CLAUDE.md and add a short example of a refused migration edit. B. Run sessions in plan mode so a human reviews the proposed plan, including any migration edits, before execution begins. C. Add a PostToolUse hook on Write and Edit that detects changes under db/migrations/ and reverts them, then notifies the on-call engineer. D.
