Q52. (D5 · Structured Data Extraction) Your extractor emits a self-reported confidence between 0 and 1 per field. You route anything below 0.9 to reviewers, but reviewers find that invoice_total is wrong in 1 of 12 documents the model rated 0.95, while vendor_name is rarely wrong even at 0.7. You must spend limited review capacity where errors actually occur. What is the best remedy?

A. Raise the single threshold to 0.97 for all fields so fewer uncertain extractions slip through. B. Measure actual accuracy per field on labeled validation data and set each review threshold from it. C. Ask the model to double-check each extraction and re-score it before routing to reviewers. D. Replace the extractor with a larger model, whose confidence scores are better calibrated.

Q53. (D5 · Structured Data Extraction) Select TWO. Overall accuracy is 97%, but your reviewers can only handle 15% of volume. A spot check shows handwritten scans are right only 71% of the time and make up 4% of traffic. Which two practices fit the plan to automate high-confidence extractions?

A. Route extractions with low field-level confidence, and those drawn from ambiguous or contradictory source documents, to human review first. B. Review a uniform random 15% of all documents and treat the overall error rate as the success metric. C. Review the longest documents first, since length correlates with error. D. Keep a stratified random sample of auto-approved extractions, stratified by document type and field, for continuing error-rate measurement. E. Automate everything above 0.9 confidence because the aggregate accuracy already exceeds 95%.

Q54. (D2 · Code Generation with Claude Code) You must change a 120-line configuration module in which the statement return DEFAULT_TIMEOUT; appears in six functions, and you want to alter only the one in loadRemoteConfig. Edit fails because the anchor text is not unique. What is the reliable approach?

A. Retry Edit with a shorter anchor so the match is more likely to succeed. B. Use Grep to find the line number and pass it to Edit instead of text. C. Read the whole file, make the change in context, and write it back with Write. D. Use Glob to locate the module file, then retry Edit with the same anchor text.

Q55. (D2 · Developer Productivity with Claude) Select TWO. You must find every place the pricing logic calculatePremium is used. pricing/index.ts re-exports it under the names calculatePremium, quotePremium, and premiumFor, and most callers import through that module. Which two steps trace usage reliably without reading the whole repository?

A. Grep for calculatePremium only, since renamed re-exports resolve to the same function. B. Read pricing/index.ts to identify every exported name for the function. C. Glob for **/*pricing* and read every matching file. D. Read every file under src/ first, then reason about which ones call it. E. Grep for each exported name separately across the codebase, then Read the callers to follow the flow.

Q56. (D5 · Multi-Agent Research System) A research subagent queries three sources (a patent database, a news archive and an academic index). Two return results; the academic index times out even after the subagent's retries. What should the subagent return to the coordinator?

A. The two sources' results plus structured error context for the third: failure type, query attempted, retries, coverage gap. B. Only the two successful sources' results, reported as overall success, since a failure note would add noise and the coordinator can ask again if it notices a gap. C. A generic "research failed" status for the whole task, discarding the two successful results so the coordinator never works from incomplete data. D. Nothing yet: keep retrying the academic index with growing backoff until it responds, then return all three sources' results together.

Q57. (D2 · Developer Productivity with Claude) Your documentation agent is given a generic fetch_url tool. Logs show it fetching arbitrary external pages and internal admin URLs when it only ever needs to load your knowledge-base documents. Which change fits scoped tool design?

A. Add a system prompt section listing hostnames it must never fetch, and tell it to refuse them. B. Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates the URL is a knowledge-base document. C. Remove fetch_url entirely and have the agent answer from existing knowledge, asking users to paste documents. D. Keep fetch_url and give the coordinator the same tool to audit the agent's fetches afterwards.

Q58. (D1 · Multi-Agent Research System) Select TWO. Your coordinator hands a synthesis subagent a prompt of the form "Step 1: read the notes. Step 2: list three themes. Step 3: write 400 words." Output is thin and loses attribution. Which two changes improve it?

A. Add a fourth step telling the subagent to search the web for additional detail on each theme, so thin sections are filled in with its own research. B. Give the subagent every tool in the system, including search and document analysis, so it can fill gaps itself instead of relying on the coordinator. C. Pass the complete findings from the search and document analysis agents in the prompt, in a structured format separating content from metadata (source URL, document name, page number). D. Replace the numbered steps with a longer, more detailed list of procedures covering each theme, a word budget per section and the exact citation format. E. State the research goal and quality criteria, such as coverage and well-supported claims, rather than prescribing steps, so the subagent can adapt.

Q59. (D4 · Structured Data Extraction) Contracts arrive continuously. Business requires extracted results within 28 hours of arrival. You use the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, and you submit on a fixed schedule. How often must you submit to guarantee the requirement?

A. Every 24 hours. B. Every 12 hours. C. Every 6 hours. D. Every 4 hours.

Q60. (D5 · Multi-Agent Research System) Your pipeline compresses each subagent's findings into a short summary before synthesis. The final report states figures confidently but cannot say which source each came from. Which change preserves provenance?

A. Have subagents emit structured claim-source mappings (URL, document, excerpt) that summarization and synthesis preserve and merge. B. Ask the summarizer to "cite sources where possible" in prose, and tell the synthesis agent to keep any citations it finds in the summaries it receives. C. Append an alphabetical bibliography of every source consulted to the end of the report, with a note that the figures come from these sources. D. Have the synthesis agent re-run searches for each figure to rediscover where it came from, and attach the URLs it finds to the final report.

Answers

Q1 — B. Loop control flow must be driven by stop_reason. The exam guide names "checking for assistant text content as a completion indicator" as an anti-pattern, because a tool_use response can and often does also contain text. A treats a structural bug as a prompting problem; C substitutes an arbitrary iteration count for a real signal; D still uses the wrong signal, just more carefully.

Q2 — C. Subagents operate with isolated context and do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history. The coordinator must include complete findings from prior agents directly in the synthesis prompt. B would work around the problem by making synthesis re-do the research, which over-provisions it and violates separation of concerns. D misunderstands the mechanism; there is no shared turn context.

Q3 — A. Parallel execution means emitting multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response. B invents a field. C is exactly the sequential pattern. D names a real Messages API parameter, but it governs parallel tool calls, not subagent orchestration, and it appears nowhere in the exam guide's API appendix.

Q4 — C. Deterministic compliance is required because the consequence is financial, and prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate. Tool-call interception blocks the action before it happens. A and B are both probabilistic. D uses the right mechanism too late: PostToolUse fires after execution, when the refund has already gone out.

Q5 — A. PostToolUse hooks intercepting tool results for transformation before the model processes them is the exam guide's named pattern for normalizing heterogeneous formats from different MCP tools. B is probabilistic and burns tokens on every turn. C may be impossible for third-party servers and is more work. D blocks useful tools rather than fixing their output.

Q6 — B. Resume when prior context is mostly valid, and inform the resumed session about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than full re-exploration. A wastes the benefit and risks stale reasoning. C solves a different problem (divergent branches). D overstates the case. The exam guide prefers a fresh session with a structured summary only when prior tool results are stale, and six changed files in a whole codebase do not necessarily make all of them stale.

Q7 — B. fork_session creates independent branches from a shared analysis baseline for exploring divergent approaches, which is the use case the exam guide states. A pollutes one session with two strategies. C compresses, it doesn't branch. D discards the detailed analysis you already paid for.

Q8 — B. The coordinator's role includes deciding which subagents to invoke based on query complexity, dynamically selecting rather than always routing through the full pipeline. A degrades quality without addressing the structure. C and D are narrower optimizations that leave the routing problem intact.

Q9 — B. Open-ended investigation calls for dynamic adaptive decomposition: map structure, identify high-impact areas, build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered. This is the exam guide's own worked example for "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase." A imposes a fixed chain on an unpredictable task. C guarantees duplication and no coherent prioritization. D invites attention dilution.

Q10 — B. Decompose multi-concern requests into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then synthesize a unified resolution. A and C push work back onto the customer or a human for a case the agent can handle. D is serial and slow, and risks the same drop-off.

Q11 — B and D. The exam guide specifies structured handoff summaries containing customer ID, root cause, refund amount, and recommended action, for human agents who lack transcript access. A is the raw dump the pattern exists to replace. C is an unreliable signal. E is operational telemetry that the human does not need in order to act.

Q12 — B. Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection; the exam guide's own repair for this exact pair is renaming and rewriting to eliminate functional overlap. A (consolidation) is a defensible architecture but more work than a first step. C over-engineers and bypasses the model's language understanding. D forces a tool call without improving which tool.

Q13 — B. Structured error metadata (category, retryable flag, human-readable description of what was attempted) is what lets the agent make an appropriate recovery decision. A is the named anti-pattern ("Operation failed"). C silently suppresses a failure as success. D terminates the workflow over a recoverable fault.

Q14 — B. Business errors are non-retryable and need a customer-friendly explanation so the agent can communicate rather than retry. A would cause pointless retries of a policy decision. C throws away the reason. D conflates a policy refusal with an empty result set.

Q15 — B. Too many tools degrades selection, and out-of-specialization tools get misused. The exam guide's pattern is scoped tool access plus a limited cross-role tool for a specific high-frequency need. A is probabilistic. C removes a real capability the agent needs 85% of the time. D misdiagnoses the cause.

Q16 — C. The named skill is enhancing MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs in detail, to prevent the agent from preferring built-in tools like Grep. A confuses scope with priority, since scope controls sharing, not selection. B cripples a useful tool. D forces a call without steering which.

Q17 — B. Project-scoped .mcp.json for shared team tooling, with environment variable expansion for credentials so nothing secret is committed. A is user scope and leaks the token. C loses the sharing that motivated the change. D reinvents what env var expansion already does.

Q18 — B. Grep searches file contents for patterns such as function names. Glob matches file paths, which finds the files but not the callers. C is the read-everything-upfront anti-pattern. D shells out where a dedicated tool exists.

Q19 — B. User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to that user and is not shared via version control. The exam guide names this exact diagnostic. A would still be committed and would still load (a rule without paths: just isn't conditionally scoped). C is contradicted by "ignores them entirely." D doesn't match "follows them perfectly for you" without manual invocation.

Q20 — C. .claude/rules/ with glob patterns applies conventions by file type regardless of directory location, which matters when test files are spread throughout. A is directory-bound and can't cover scattered tests. B relies on inference rather than explicit matching. D requires invocation and is not automatic.

Q21 — C. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing verbose skill output from polluting the main conversation. A restricts tools, not context. B prompts for arguments. D is not one of the frontmatter options the exam guide tests, and a cheaper model would still emit 8,000 tokens.

Q22 — B. Skills are on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows; CLAUDE.md is always-loaded universal standards. A inverts it. C is false, because personal skills go in ~/.claude/skills/. D is not a trade-off the exam guide draws.

Q23 — B. Plan mode is for large-scale changes with multiple valid approaches and architectural implications; combining plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation is a named skill. A assumes you already know the answer. C ignores that the complexity is stated in the requirements, not something that might emerge. D loses the cross-file coherence the migration needs.

Q24 — A. -p / --print is the documented non-interactive mode. CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch do not exist. Redirecting stdin is a Unix workaround that doesn't address the command syntax.

Q25 — A. --output-format json with --json-schema produces machine-parseable structured findings for automated posting as inline PR comments. B is unenforced. C is fragile. D drops half of the exam guide's pairing, and the guide only ever names the two flags together.

Q26 — B. Include prior review findings in context and instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. A abandons the feature. C hides the symptom and breaks when wording shifts slightly. D loses issues in unchanged files that interact with the change.

Q27 — B. Concrete input/output examples are the exam guide's remedy when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently, and it specifies 2–3 of them. A moves the ambiguous description somewhere else without making it any less ambiguous. C is the interview pattern, which is for finding considerations you have not thought of, not for pinning down a transformation you already know. D is more of what already failed.

Q28 — B. Explicit categorical criteria beat vague instructions. This is the exam guide's own before/after pair. A is named as a technique that fails to improve precision. C relies on poorly calibrated self-reported confidence. D suppresses real bugs that only some passes catch (the exam guide's reason for rejecting 2-of-3 consensus in sample question 12, the 14-file review).

Q29 — A. Temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while improving those prompts is a named skill. High false positives in one category undermine confidence in the accurate ones, so protecting trust is the priority. B degrades the good category too. C treats a criteria problem as a capability problem. D still spends the developer's attention.

Q30 — B. Schemas eliminate syntax errors but not semantic ones; the exam guide's named self-correction flow is extracting calculated_total alongside stated_total to flag discrepancies. A, C and D are all schema-level, and the JSON already validates.

Q31 — B. Designing fields as optional/nullable where source documents may not contain the information is the exam guide's stated way to prevent the model fabricating values to satisfy required fields. A helps at the margin but leaves the structural pressure in place. C is a prompt instruction against a schema-level incentive. D is not a lever the exam guide tests and wouldn't stop the fabrication.

Q32 — B. tool_choice: "any" guarantees the model calls a tool while letting it choose which. This is the exam guide's use for this case (multiple extraction schemas, unknown document type). A permits a text reply. C forces the wrong schema two thirds of the time. D disallows tools entirely.

Q33 — C. Retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source; the skill tested is identifying when retry will not help. A and B burn cost on an unrecoverable case. D would silently record a null for a value that exists, which is wrong and hides a real data-pipeline gap.

Q34 — A and D. 50% cost savings and custom_id correlation are both stated. B is wrong, since batches can take up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. C is wrong because batch does not support multi-turn tool calling within a request. E is the argument sample question 11 (batch vs a blocking pre-merge check) rejects.

Q35 — B. Handle batch failures by resubmitting only the failed documents, identified by custom_id, with appropriate modifications such as chunking oversized documents. A, C and D all reprocess 93 documents that already succeeded.

Q36 — C. A model retains its reasoning context from generation and is less likely to question its own decisions in the same session; independent review instances are more effective than self-review instructions or extended thinking. A is named as inferior. B is still self-review, three times. D is a self-review instruction.

Q37 — B. Extracting transactional facts into a persistent case-facts block included in each prompt, outside the summarized history, is the fix the exam guide gives for progressive summarization condensing numbers and dates. A discards exactly the early transactional detail the customer will hold you to, and the exam guide is explicit that complete conversation history matters for coherence. C asks the summarizer to keep the detail that summarizing exists to drop. D adds capacity when the problem is what gets kept.

Q38 — A. Honor explicit customer requests for a human immediately, without first attempting investigation. B is the correct behaviour for frustration without an explicit request, and this customer asked. C and D are the two named unreliable proxies.

Q39 — A. Structured error context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, potential alternatives) lets the coordinator decide whether to retry, substitute, or proceed with coverage annotations. B's generic status hides that context. C is silent suppression, the named anti-pattern. D terminates the whole workflow over one recoverable failure.

Q40 — C. Conflicting statistics from credible sources should be annotated with source attribution rather than arbitrarily resolved, and requiring publication or data-collection dates in structured outputs prevents temporal differences from being misread as contradictions. A fabricates a figure neither source reported. B is arbitrary selection with a rationalization. D escalates a case the system is designed to represent, and deduplication does nothing about sources that measured different things.

Q41 — B. Few-shot examples are the exam guide's named technique for demonstrating ambiguous-case handling, and it specifies 2–4 targeted examples that show the reasoning for why one action was chosen over a plausible alternative. A is a "be conservative"-class instruction, which the exam guide says fails to improve precision. C doesn't generalize to novel patterns, which is the benefit few-shot is credited with. D suppresses real intermittent findings.

Q42 — B. The exam guide describes context degradation in extended sessions as models "giving inconsistent answers and referencing typical patterns rather than specific classes discovered earlier", and the stem shows that symptom. The named remedy is scratchpad files persisting key findings across context boundaries. A, C and D all misdiagnose a context problem as a prompting, sampling, or data-format problem.

Q43 — B. Aggregate accuracy metrics can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields; the exam guide requires analyzing accuracy by document type and field before reducing human review. A misreads whose errors matter. C leans on uncalibrated confidence. D is volume without segmentation, which is exactly what hides the problem.

Q44 — B. Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is the named technique for ongoing error-rate measurement and novel pattern detection. A is reactive and slow. C costs as much as the review you just eliminated. D trades recall for a false sense of safety without ever looking at what's in the bucket.

Q45 — B. MCP resources expose content catalogs (the exam guide's examples are issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, and database schemas) specifically to reduce exploratory tool calls. Resources are for content catalogs and tools are for actions. A returns more noise per call. C adds a tool where a resource is the designed mechanism. D makes an unnecessary pattern cheaper rather than removing it.

Q46 — B and D. Providing existing test files in context stops the generator proposing scenarios the suite already covers, and documenting testing standards, valuable-test criteria and fixtures in CLAUDE.md is how CI-invoked Claude gets project context and avoids low-value output (3.6). A discards real but run-dependent tests and does not address redundancy against the suite. C is a vague quality instruction with no new information. E dilutes attention and still does not show what is already tested.

Q47 — C. The session that generated the code retains its reasoning and is less likely to question its own decisions (session context isolation), so an independent review instance, given only the diff and the documented criteria, is more effective (3.6, 4.6). A and B are self-review instructions in the same biased context, and the exam guide names independent instances as better than both. D repeats the same bias three times.

Q48 — A and E. Including prior findings and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues fixes the re-posting, and CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude review criteria, including what to skip (3.6). B depends on poorly calibrated self-reported confidence and would not remove already-reported findings. C misses issues in unchanged files that interact with the change. D hides the duplicates only while the wording stays identical and does nothing about generated-file nitpicks.

Q49 — A. Identity verification and a balance check before an irreversible account action need deterministic compliance, and prompt instructions have a measured non-zero failure rate; a programmatic prerequisite gate blocks close_account until both prerequisite calls have succeeded (1.4). B is still probabilistic. C is a PostToolUse audit that fires after the account has already been closed. D treats an enforcement problem as a capability problem.

Q50 — C and D. A hook intercepting outgoing process_refund calls blocks the over-threshold refund and redirects to human escalation, and a PostToolUse hook normalizes heterogeneous status codes and timestamps before the model processes them (1.5). A and E rely on probabilistic prompt compliance for both needs. B uses the right mechanism too late: it runs after the refund has executed.

Q51 — D. A guarantee needs a hook that intercepts the outgoing tool call and blocks the policy-violating action before it executes, then redirects to an alternative workflow, here human approval (1.5, 1.4). A is probabilistic. B shapes how work proceeds but does not deterministically block the write. C runs after the write, and the watcher has already deployed the file.

Q52 — B. Field-level confidence scores must be calibrated against labeled validation sets, and thresholds set from the measured accuracy per field, to route limited reviewer attention where errors occur (5.5). A applies one threshold to fields with very different error rates. C asks the same uncalibrated source to re-score itself. D assumes a bigger model's confidence is calibrated, which only a labeled set can show.

Q53 — A and D. Routing low-confidence and ambiguous or contradictory-source extractions to reviewers prioritizes scarce capacity, and stratified sampling by document type and field measures error rates in the auto-approved bucket and detects novel patterns (5.5). B samples uniformly, so the 4% handwritten segment is barely seen and the aggregate metric stays flattering. C uses an arbitrary proxy. E falls into the aggregate-accuracy trap, where 97% overall hid 71% on one segment.

Q54 — C. When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, Read the full file and Write it back with the change (2.5). A shorter anchor is more likely to match in several places. B is wrong because Edit matches on text, not line numbers. D finds a file path, which was never the problem. Read + Write is the exam guide's answer; current Claude Code would instead retry Edit with a longer unique anchor (or replace_all), which is not tested.

Q55 — B and E. Trace usage across wrapper modules by first identifying all exported names, then searching for each name across the codebase, reading callers to follow the flow (2.5). A misses callers that use the renamed exports. C is Glob, which matches file names rather than content. D is the read-everything-upfront anti-pattern; build understanding incrementally from Grep entry points.

Q56 — A. Subagents retry transient failures locally and propagate what they cannot resolve as structured error context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results), so the coordinator can retry, substitute or proceed with an explicit coverage annotation, and can tell a failed source from a valid empty one (5.3). B is silent suppression, the named anti-pattern, so the gap is invisible. C ends the whole task over one recoverable failure and discards good partial results (the other named anti-pattern). D never returns, so the coordinator is blocked on a source that has already failed after retries.

Q57 — B. Replace a generic tool with a constrained alternative, such as load_document validating document URLs, so the agent has only what its role needs (2.3). A is a probabilistic prompt guard. C removes a capability the agent needs. D spreads the over-broad tool to another agent.

Q58 — C and E. Subagents do not inherit context, so the coordinator must include complete prior findings in the prompt, in structured form that separates content from source metadata to preserve attribution, and should specify goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedure so subagents can adapt (1.3). A and B give the synthesis agent out-of-specialization tools and repeat the over-provisioning mistake. D adds more procedure, the opposite of the guidance.

Q59 — D. A document can wait one full submission interval before being batched and then take up to 24 hours, so interval + 24 must not exceed 28; the interval is at most 4 hours (4.5). A, B and C allow worst cases of 48, 36 and 30 hours.

Q60 — A. Attribution is lost when compression drops claim-source mappings; requiring structured mappings (URL, document name, excerpt) that downstream agents preserve and merge keeps provenance through summarization and synthesis (5.6). B is an unenforced prose request. C lists sources without tying any claim to one. D reconstructs provenance after the fact, expensively and unreliably.

Scoring yourself

Out of 60. Below 45, go back to the domain page for the section you missed most. Above 52, spend the remaining time on the domain pages' decision tables and "Things to remember" lists and the twelve official sample questions.

Resources — official prep, community material, and what to ignore

Checked 2026-10-21. Star counts are from the same date. Everything outside the exam guide is unofficial; the domain mappings below are interpretation.

Official (Anthropic)

Resource Notes
Exam guide PDF, v1.0 The authority for what is tested. Linked from the certification page. No newer version exists. Re-check before booking.
Certification FAQ Live logistics (fee, retakes, cancellation). Outranks the PDF where they differ.
Practice exam None. The old one was retired in the move to Pearson. The only official sample items are the 12 in the exam guide.

Community articles and practice-test vendors

  • Experience write-ups (themes only, unofficial): re-cinq.com/blog/claude-certified-architect-foundations-exam; itone.substack.com/p/lessons-from-the-anthropic-architect; levelup.gitconnected.com (2026-06-24); medium.com/@johnelanji (2026-05-20).
  • Udemy practice tests: few reviews, unverified accuracy.
  • Third-party banks contain wrong answers. Claude-generated drills run easier than the real exam.

How to use these

  • Read the exam guide first.
  • Do this guide's 60 practice questions.
  • Add one external bank for volume: utkarsh1agarwal.
  • Use the aderegil labs to close the API/SDK hands-on gap.
  • Check any external "fact" against the exam guide and the out-of-scope list before adopting it.
